In such cases, it should be continuously connected to the internet which needs ‘Any PLACE Connection,’ ‘Any TIME Connection,’ and ‘Any THING Connection.’ With the technological advancements, various devices and board are attaining communication capabilities which can help in implementing an IoT environment at a very low cost.

Figure 2.2 Definition of internet of things

2.1.1 IoT – architecture

The structure of an IoT solution is described in its architecture. It includes various aspects including physical, the THINGS and virtual, the communication protocols. The IoT architecture is shown in Figure 2.3. As shown in the figure, the IoT architecture contains three different aspects which are connected to each-other by Internet. The THINGS comprise of the physical components which include the sensors, actuators, and various IoT devices. The sensors and actuators are connected to the IoT devices which help gather the data. The IoT devices are smart devices which can process the data that is collected from the sensors. Various sensors and actuators are connected using wired or wireless connectivity. Different levels of abstractions of an IoT model are shown in Figure 2.4.

Figure 2.3 Architecture of internet of things

Figure 2.4 Architecture levels of internet of things

There are various devices that communicate with the cloud and other IoT devices in different ways as shown in Figure 2.5. Some of the sensors and devices communicate directly to the cloud and transmit the data. Such devices will have high performance and can also do some of the data processing before uploading the data to the cloud. There are gateway devices which act as an intermediary devices between them and the sensors. These play a major role in data acquisition. After preprocessing the data, it is then sent to the cloud. Various cloud applications are available which can provide an interface for the end-user of the data to interact with it. Using the application programming interface (API), the client will have much exploratory choices and process the data further if needed.

Figure 2.5 Various aspects of internet of things

IoT, fog computing, and edge computing are three different concepts that provide the functions to control and transfer the data to the cloud storage as presented in Figure 2.6. The cloud computing is extended to the edge; thereby, giving it the secure control and management of software, domain specific hardware, and standard compute. While edge computing is the management and control of the standalone device either individually or by software in the fog domain.

Figure 2.6 Fog computing versus edge computing versus cloud computing

2.1.2 IoT – driving technology

In an IoT environment, every THING will have a unique IP address as discussed above. Every sensors would not have the capability of communication. In such cases, the sensors combined with a device that has the capability of communication will become the THING that is necessary in an IoT environment. There are various aspects to IoT. It has spread its wings to various domains like smart city, smart healthcare, smart transportation, smart home, and so on. As shown in Figure 2.7, various sensors are connected to different single computer boards or microcontrollers which have the capability of having a unique IP address and transmit the data over internet to form a THING. In the figure, the sensor is connected to a smart watch which will collect the data from the sensor and transmit the same to the cloud or other devices.

Figure 2.7 Driving technologies of internet of things

Various sensors and devices are the driving technologies for IoT. There are various sensors and devices for IoT, and those are called as smart devices. One of the main concerns of these devices is security (Sivaraman et al., 2018). Research is being conducted for a very long time in this aspect of IoT driving technology, various IoT smart devices, and their security (Almajali et al., 2018; Sivaraman et al., 2018; Surendran et al., 2018; Valea et al., 2018). Another aspect of driving technologies in an IoT architecture is the communications. Figure 2.8 shows various communication technologies that are used in the IoT environment (RS Components, 2015). Most of the components are using low-power Bluetooth and WiFi components in the single-board computers and boards for communication, but other communication protocols are also used in IoT. Low-power Bluetooth is not suitable for data transfer of large files, but can be used for smaller data packets. Zigbee is another protocol that is widely popular in the industrial scenario. It offers a low-power operation, robust security, and scalability. For home environments, Z-wave is employed. 6LowPAN is an Internet Protocol-based communication technology, unlike Bluetooth, operates over the network defining the encapsulation and header compression. WiFi and cellular are the options that are explored where ever they can be employed. Unlike other protocols, NFC does not have a wide range and also not capable of sending high chunks of data (RS Components, 2015). Long-range wide area network (LoRaWAN) is getting popular due to its low-energy consumption and long range.

Figure 2.8 Communications of internet of things

2.1.3 IoT – applications

INTERNET and THINGS are the two main aspects of IoT architectures. Based on them, two different architectures can be proposed. When the Internet is given the main focus and network aspects are given a priority in the IoT architecture, it is called as an internet-centric architecture (Gubbi et al., 2013). With the cloud at the center of the whole architecture, the full potential can be brought out. With the introduction of cloud, the entire system becomes highly scalable and also makes it simple and flexible to divide the costs associated. When the smart devices or ‘THINGS’ are the main focus of the architecture, it is called as an object-centric architecture (Lopez et al., 2012). Internet of everything (IoE) as depicted in Figure 2.9 will advance IoT to even more broader scope with human and process integrations.

Figure 2.9 Internet of everything

The smart devices or THINGS have been around for a very long time (Carter et al., 2008; Lee and Ke, 2018; Luo et al., 2009; Obuchi et al., 2018). With RFID becoming the leading technology, many smart devices are taking advantage. Developments in technology and high-performance devices have been a great advantage in developing IoT applications (Mohanty, 2017; Mohanty et al., 2016). Many areas use the concept of IoT to perform actions with more accuracy and acquire more data that was not at all possible before. Figure 2.10 shows different applications of IoT. Smart healthcare is a growing area which takes advantage of smart devices to develop medical devices for improving the quality of life, diagnosing, and providing treatment to various diseases and health conditions (Catarinucci et al., 2015; He et al., 2018; Sundaravadivel et al., 2016). There are various components of a smart city, which includes infrastructure, buildings, energy, transportation, technology, education, governance, and citizens (Mohanty et al., 2016). Economy, governance, society, and environment are different themes of a smart city. Each of the components and themes uses the concept of IoT in a very efficient way to improve the quality of living in a smart city. In a smart home environment, controlling various devices securely can be achieved through IoT (Al-Kuwari et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2017; Son et al., 2016). IoT can also be implemented for various military applications where LoRaWAN, as presented in the previous section, can be used (Jalaian et al., 2018). IoT in military applications is also sometimes referred as Internet of Battlefield Things or Internet of Battle Things (Bolisetti et al., 2017; Farooq and Zhu, 2018; Kott et al., 2016).

Figure 2.10 Applications of IoT

2.1.4 IoT – challenges

Technological advancements have made developing IoT applications and devices much simpler, but there are a lot of challenges to overcome in this area. Connectivity is a major issue in this regard. IoT devices or Things needs to have a unique IP address of their own which means they should be connected to internet or cloud storage. But, a high-range wireless communication requires more energy consumption and low-power communication protocols will have a transmission rate or range as a trade-off (RS Components, 2015). Sensors have improved since the beginning of IoT, but a need for better sensing devices has not yet been developed. Moreover, accuracy of the sensors has to be improved in various ways as well. Figure 2.11 shows various challenges that are present in an IoT environment (Mohanty, 2017). Various IoT architectures are proposed based on different aspects and focus of IoT (Gubbi et al., 2013). Selecting an architecture based on the environmental conditions and devices being used in the environment is an uphill task and a challenge. There are various dependencies in the IoT architectures.

Figure 2.11 Challenges in designing IoT

When various devices are connected to each other through a network, they are vulnerable to various threats. Security issues are a great challenge and addressing them should be considered as a primary priority. Various solutions are available for IoT security but with the implementation of better security solutions, power consumption is going to increase for the entire module (Yanambaka et al., 2017). Collecting the data and sending it to the cloud is part of the challenge for which the later part is going to be process the data that is being collected. First, the data is sent to the cloud where it can be processed, employing high-speed servers, and storing huge amounts of data will increase the cost of design and overall IoT design. Processing the data needs high-performance computing, wherein some cases, the data should be processed in real-time that will increase the operational and overall cost of the design.

2.2 Security, privacy, IPR in IoT, and consumer electronic systems – a big picture

Security has been one of the major issues that has been around for a very long time, and it is still the main focus of the research. New devices are developed every day with the advancements in technology, and better solutions are resulted in various domains as discussed in Section 2.1. Even with the introduction of many security primitives, attackers are finding ways to hack and perform successful attacks on various secured devices. This has been a major issue since many times. Cryptography has been the solution where the main text message intended for the end-user is encrypted with a key and the end user will decrypt the text with the same key or a different private key. This has been the in practice for a very long time (Yanambaka et al., 2017). The first lock and key found was 4,000-year-old, and again now in this digital era; here, the locks and keys are also digital, however the underlying concept remains the same. It may be noted that security, privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights (IPR) are not necessarily the same (Bhargava et al., 2018; Mohanty, 2017, 2018) as depicted in Figure 2.12. Data security is typically referred to as the confidentiality, availability, and integrity of data. System security often deals with trustful, safe, normal operations of a system (e.g., smart car), etc. Data privacy is defined as the appropriate use of data as agreed for different purposes. System privacy can be making location and functions of unknown system, e.g., location of a smart car should be unknown to adversaries. Confidentiality is assured only if the information is not made available or disclosed to unauthorized individuals, entities, or processes. IPR or ownership rights deals with the preservation of ownership of the owner of a particular hardware or media which is analogous to the copyright or authorship of a book that of a publisher or author.

Figure 2.12 Security versus privacy

2.2.1 IoT security – attacks and countermeasures

The debate of security and privacy has been going on for a very long time (Notario, 2016). The definitions of privacy and security are still in debate, and the most center-point is the confidentiality part. Both security and privacy are important parts of any system. In the case of an IoT environment, these are paramount as the devices in IoT are continuously connected to a network and online. This leaves much room for the attacker to attack the system in various ways. There has been a lot of research going on in this area (Asplund and Nadjm-Tehrani, 2016; Schinianakis, 2017; Schneier, 2017; Sivaraman et al., 2018; Unwala et al., 2018). There are various security attacks that are happening around the world. Number of cybercrime attempts have increased, and so have been the security solutions to fight against them (Andrews, 2017; Heartfield et al., 2016; Kundu et al., 2018; Mazurczyk et al., 2016).

Figure 2.13 shows different types of attacks that are possible on an IoT environment (Nawir et al., 2016). There are many threats where unauthorized and unrecognized malicious devices can enter the network and tamper the system both externally and internally. So, therefore, identifying the users that are in the IoT environment is an important prerequisite. Research is being conducted extensively in detecting and preventing the IoT botnets (Moon et al., 2015; Prokofiev et al., 2018). The device should be tamper resistant. There are various types of attacks like side channel attacks and memory exploitations that can be successfully executed by tampering with the device itself (Li et al., 2011; Sengupta and Kundu, 2017). Hence naturally, the IoT device should be tamper proof, so that the attacker cannot perform such attacks. Software that is used in the IoT devices should be extensively scrutinized before executed on the device. This can lead to unauthorized usage of the device, data loss, or device failure. The network and the device security are of highest important. But increasing the security of the device may also increase the power consumption of the overall module. This should be avoided as the IoT devices are usually battery operated and cannot be used with a continuous power source. This makes it difficult for the development of security primitives for IoT devices. Low-power hardware security modules are being developed for these devices (Yanambaka et al., 2017) so that the attacks are mitigated. Communication and device network authentication should also be given highest priority such that unauthorized devices cannot be in the network and the communication channel is not compromised (Yanambaka et al., 2016a). Identity management is also a key factor in this scenario. The identity of the device should be secured such that cloning attacks are prevented.

Figure 2.13 Taxonomy of security attacks in IoT

Hardware trojans are another issue that should be dealt within the IoT environment. Figure 2.14 shows various types of hardware trojans that are currently active, the location where they will be introduced, and the phase where there is a chance of insertion (Mohanty, 2015). A hardware trojan is an unwanted and malicious design that is introduced into the main design in different phases of manufacturing by the attacker to render the entire module useless or steal the data from the module. A hardware trojan can be introduced in processor, memory, I/O devices, power supply, and clock grid. Each of these components is the important modules of the device, which play a vital role in the overall functioning of the device. Introduction of a malicious design can prove fatal to the efficient working of device. There are two different types of trojans, one which is always on when the device itself is on and the other where it can be triggered with an event or with a signal. There are many ways in which the hardware trojans can be detected and avoided (Dupuis et al., 2018; He et al., 2017; Sengupta, 2016, 2017; Shen et al., 2018; Xue and Ren, 2018). There are many phases where the hardware trojans can be inserted as shown in Figure 2.14. Changing functionality, downgrade performance, leak information, and denial of service are some of the effects of hardware trojans. These can prove fatal for many cases where the device cannot function at the full potential in times of need.

Figure 2.14 Hardware trojans

2.2.2 Trustworthy consumer electronic systems

Besides high- and low-power consumption, any consumer electronic system should also have the properties of trustworthiness and security. Figure 2.15 shows different aspects of security, privacy, and protection (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Mohanty, 2015). There are different layers in the system, application, operating system (OS), firmware, digital signal processor (DSP), embedded processor, memory, and radio frequency (RF) components. At each of the stages, there are different kinds of attacks that can be successfully performed on the system. Application and OS attacks are possible on the OSs and its applications. Between the OS and applications or firmware and OS, there is a network which connects them to perform operations. This network can be attacked with different kinds of attacks: application attacks and network attacks. Some of them were discussed in the previous sections. Firmware is an integral part of the system. This acts as a bridge to the board or system to talk to other components or peripherals and describes its functionality. There are different kinds of firmware attacks possible on the devices.

Figure 2.15 A selected attacks on a typical CE system – security, privacy, IPR

Different hardware components of the device such as DSP, embedded processor, memory, and RF components, can become targets to various attacks as shown in Figure 2.15. IP attacks, side channel attacks, physical attacks, and memory attacks are some of them that are performed at the hardware level. After the output is produced, the data in the output can be subject to many copyright attacks. The RF components can also be subject to various network threats which will be discussed in the proceeding sections.

A selective attributes of CE system to be trustworthy (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Mohanty, 2015):

  1. The integrity of the data that is being processed by the system should be maintained.

  2. The device will be prone to side channel and power analysis attacks once it is deployed in the field. So the data that is being processed should be secured and concealed during processing.

  3. The functionality of the device should be restricted to the intended functionality. Additional operations should not be performed by the device.

  4. The device should be reliable at all times and especially at times of critical operation.

  5. The transparency of the device must be restricted to the owner and no one else.

  6. Trusted vendors should be approached for different parts while manufacturing the device to avoid introduction of unwanted trojans.

  7. Trusted fabrication facilities should be approached.

2.2.3 Hardware-assisted security and protection

With the increased security threats, software-based security alone is not going to fight against them. Hardware-assisted security plays a crucial role in mitigating the threats caused by the attackers. There are two different kinds of attacks that can be performed on the system: software-based attacks and hardware-based attacks (Chang et al., 2017; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017). The software attacks are performed usually from the communication channel. As IoT is connected through a network, this can easily be under threat by the attacker. These attacks are typically originated remotely and the device is affected. As the attacker need not be present at the device to perform them, they can be performed regularly and remotely. Denial of service attack, routing attacks, malicious injection, spoofing, snooping, and brute force are some of the software-based attacks.

Hardware-based attacks are typically on the device itself and most of them has to be performed at the location of the device. Some kinds of hardware attacks can also be performed remotely. In an IoT environment, the devices are deployed in areas where human interaction is very minimal and so it is highly prone to the attacks. Side channel attacks, backdoors, eavesdropping, inducing faults, and hardware trojans are some of the hardware attacks.

For the two kinds of attacks, software and hardware, the solutions available are also two different types: software solutions and hardware solutions (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017). The software-based security solutions are easy to use, update, and also upgrade. This gives the flexibility to increase the robustness offered. As the software-based applications are dependent on the OS, they are widely supported and can be designed for cross-platform applications. The recurring operational costs are high in case of software securities. They can be used for general purpose processor but one of the main drawbacks is it will not be able to save the system against reverse engineering and other hardware attacks. In case of a hardware-security solutions, they are very fast when compared with software solutions, consumes less power, high flexibility in optimization, and low cost when an field programmable gate array or application-specific integrated circuit is used. They cannot be used to stop the software reverse engineering and are highly prone to side channel attacks.

Figure 2.16 shows the security-aware design trade-offs and describes different aspects of the design. An example of hardware-assisted security is shown in Figure 2.17. Major concerns when designing a system is low-power consumption and high performance, reliability, low cost of manufacturing and easy integration. In the design of a secure camera system, the watermarking chip is the main focus as most of the security is offered by it. The trade-offs that are present are power consumption, performance, chip area, integration into the system, and the memory. Integration of more memory into the system will increase the battery life, chip area, and design cost of the camera. Increased security will also increase the battery consumption and the other parameters as shown in Figure 2.16. Thus, a design should be designed keeping all the parameters in view and trade-offs for security, and include additional hardware components, that will perform voltage and frequency scaling like technology for security, energy, and performance optimization (Figure 2.17; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017).

Figure 2.16 CE system security – aware design tradeoffs

Figure 2.17 CE system design and operation tradeoffs: camera system example

2.2.4 Different aspects of security and privacy

Security and privacy are two different aspects and are always up for a never-ending debate. The debate regarding them is going on for a very long time, and might not end anytime soon. The definitions and differences between them have not yet reached a conclusion. Different aspects of security are shown in Figure 2.18 (Mohanty, 2017, 2018). The data that are stored in the memory should be secure and confidential. It should not fall into the wrong hands and attacker should not be able to retrieve the data stored in the memory. The data that is stored should also be authentic, i.e., no unauthorized person should have tampered with the data and changed it. The integrity of the data should also be intact. The data should always be available. The storage should not be affected by the attacker and the storage must not wipe-off any of the data. Non-repudiation is another issue where the owner of the data cannot deny it. Access to the personnel should also be controlled and only authorized people should be able to access the data.

Figure 2.18 Different aspects of security

Different aspects of privacy are shown in Figure 2.19 (Mohanty, 2017, 2018). Privacy of anyone should not be compromised with the data that is being collected and stored. In case of a smart healthcare device, the patient’s data will be collected over a period of time and sent to the doctors. The only people that should have access to the data are the patient and doctor. The cloud storage server where the data is stored should not be accessed by the attacker, and the privacy of the patient must not be compromised. In such case, the data should not reveal or lead to the patient and not be traceable. The data that is stolen from the storage should not lead to any additional details or data. The data can also be encrypted or scrambled so that the patient information or any other data cannot be retrieved from any patterns and data. Anonymity of the patient and doctor should always be maintained at the storage node.

Figure 2.19 Different aspects of privacy

2.2.5 Different aspects of intellectual property (IP), ownership right, or copyright protection

Ownership, IPR, and copyright protection are the main issues that are present in many different areas. Not only media but electronics are also highly susceptible to the counterfeiting (Mohanty, 2015, 2018; Mohanty et al., 2017; Sengupta and Roy, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2018). This has been around for a very long time. Copyrights management has been around and various laws are established such that the ownership of the entity remains intact. But attackers are finding different ways to counterfeit devices and media and sell the items on their own ownership. Figure 2.20 shows the concept of IPR, ownership and copyright protection. Consumers and researchers are having the trouble in maintaining the rights. There are cases where the user is not aware of the copyright laws and is not using the entity for their own commercial purpose. But in most of the cases of copyright infringement, the attacker takes advantage of the laws that vary from region to region and claim ownership of the device or media. Identical designs are used for the electronic components, which makes the consumer to wonder whether the hardware is legitimate or not. These are also an issue of the media where a photograph is debated for ownership by the owner and the attacker (Mohanty, 2015). Watermarking the images is a way to protect the media but this is also susceptible to many attacks where the attacker can remove the watermark and claim the ownership of the media.

Figure 2.20 Intellectual property (IP), ownership right, or copyright – media versus IP hardware cores

2.3 Memory security

Memory is the integral part of every system. Different types of memory, primary, and secondary memories are available and are present in almost every IoT device. Non-volatile, static random access memory (SRAM), etc., are employed to improve the performance and increase the storage capabilities of the IoT devices where they will have the capabilities to store the data collected and send to the cloud at a later time. There is no IoT device without memory. But different types of memories are subject to different types of attacks. It is a highly vulnerable part of an IoT device. This section describes various kinds of attacks and solutions that are available in the market.

2.3.1 Memory security attacks

Various attacks are possible on the memory modules of the embedded systems. Figure 2.21 shows various attacks that are possible on the memory of an embedded system (Nimgaonkar et al., 2013). The attacks can be broadly classified as passive and active attacks. The passive attacks may include snooping and cold boot attacks. Snooping attacks happens when an adversary is able to read and interpret confidential information in memory. The cold boot attacks, which is also a type of side channel attack, a hacker who has physical access to a computer retrieves encryption keys from a running OS after using a cold reboot to restart the computer. The attack relies on the data remanence property of random access memory (cache, SRAM, or dynamic random access memory (DRAM)) to retrieve memory contents that remain readable in seconds to minutes after the power supply has been removed. This happens as the memory chips used in the computers retain their contents for seconds to minutes after power is lost even if these are volatile, leaving the contents available for malicious or forensic acquisition. Active attacks include spoofing, splicing, replay, and denial of service. In the active attacks, an adversary is able to change the contents of memory so it would not perform the intended functions. In spoofing attack, an adversary exchanges a block of memory with an arbitrary fake block. The block of memory at one location is replaced with another block from a different location in splicing attack. In replay attacks, an adversary stores the value of a block of memory at a given address at one time, and writes that value at exactly the same address at a different time. Replay attack is the hardest attack as it is difficult to trace and protect. The denial of service attack memory refers to a scenario, when a malicious process takes most of the memory bandwidth, leaving other processes without the required resources and thus effectively slowing them down.

Figure 2.21 Attacks on the memory of an IoT device

2.3.2 Memory security solutions

The nonvolatile memory (a.k.a., hard-drive or solid state drive) is protected by different hardware and software methods which rely primarily on encryption as depicted in Figure 2.22. In this kind of solutions, an encryption hardware is integrated in the storage which then allows access through a password or personal identification number (PIN). Similarity, an encryption software can run in the system that uses the storage drives for data security purposes. The software then allows access to the data through password or PIN.

Figure 2.22 Nonvolatile solutions for attacks on the memory of an IoT device

There are various solutions available to sense an attack and defend against it. In a typical embedded system, there are various sensors that are deployed around the entirety of the system. These different sensors are used to detect various parameters of the system. When the system is being attacked by the attacker, there will be changes in various parameters of the system like current fluctuations, increased power consumption, and thermal variations. These parameters can be constantly monitored with the help of sensors and detect any abnormal variations in them. The memory integrity verifications are performed only when these values sensed by the sensors are abnormal. In a traditional embedded system, the integrity verification is performed for all the blocks of memory which will increase the power consumption of the entire module for the preservation of data integrity in the memory.

The definition of any memory integrity verification approach can be structured as follows. Initially, the memory ‘M’ is communicated by a processor. There are two attributes to the memory ‘M,’ the contents of memory ‘V,’ and addressed ‘A.’ M[R,A] denotes that the memory at the address A is read and it will return the data that is associated at A. M[W,A,V] denotes that the value V is written into the address A. To return the value V, the write of value V should be immediately followed by address A. The writes and reads of the memory have a notion of time. In order to associate the same into the reads and writes, it should be addressed as: M[W,A,V,T] and M[R,A,T]. The association between the values that is present in the memory locations and the addresses of the locations is called as splicing attack. Let us consider an example, address A should return the value VA and A′ should return the value , when the memory is subjected to a successful splicing attack, the A will return the value . When the value that is stored in the memory location associated with an address A is changed to a random value , this is called spoofing attack. When the association between the value and the time is disoriented, it is called as replay attack. For example, let us consider VA as the value at the address location A at a time TA and the value of the same location at the time TB as and TA < TB. When a successful replay attack is performed on the memory, at a time T > TB, the value that will be returned is VA.

Implementing various sensors in a trusted environment boundary of the embedded system for monitoring various parameters of the processor have been around for a long time (McGowen et al., 2006; Oh et al., 2010). Research has been conducted to use the variations in power consumption and current fluctuations to monitor the attacks that are being performed on the devices. Figure 2.23 shows the implementation of such a system that can perform the memory integrity verification when the sensors detect an abnormal values of the parameters (Nimgaonkar et al., 2013).

Figure 2.23 On chip memory solutions for attacks on the memory of an IoT device

As shown in Figure 2.22, various sensors that are present in the hardware is represented as sensor module (SM). The memory bus is constantly monitored by the sensors present in the SM for the fluctuations. The memory integrity verification mechanism is present in the special cache, the ‘hash cache.’ The hash addresses are present in the hash cache. Hash of the memory block is written to the off-chip memory. The hash and the hash addresses are used to verify the integrity of memory. The processor in the embedded system is a trusted chip. So, the cache and the SM are present in the processor boundary. An encryption/decryption block is present in the architecture.

The read and write operations performed on the memory are described in Figure 2.22. When data are being written to the memory, the hash address and the hash are computed by the processor and are stored in the hash cache. After storing them, the memory block is encrypted and stored. During the read operation, the memory block which is read is decrypted. During this decryption operation, the SM continuously monitors the memory bus for any abnormalities. If the voltage fluctuations in the memory bus cross a previously set threshold value, the system is considered to be under attack and in this scenario, the hash address is computed again. It is verified with the previously stored hash addresses in the cache. If there is a hit, the hash of the data itself is checked and verified using the hash stored. In case if these two did not match, the system is under attack and the data get corrupt. All the operations that are being performed by the processor are aborted. Once the voltage fluctuations in the memory bus are reduced below a threshold value, the processes stop and the threat is considered to be stopped or mitigated.

2.4 Radio-frequency identification (RFID) security

Radio-frequency identification (RFID) is an old technology and has been used in various applications. It can be said to be a starting for IoT in some ways. Tracking, security, and locating are some of the applications of RFID. In IoT, RFID is implemented in many ways. Even though the range of RFID is very less, it can be used for various purposes in IoT environments. But like every communication protocol, RFID is also vulnerable to many attacks and threats. This section discusses various security vulnerabilities and threats of RFID and solutions to some of them.

2.4.1 RFID security attacks

There are different security threats for RFID (Jayakrishnan et al., 2018; Li et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2014). Figure 2.24 shows various attacks on RFID (Mohanty, 2015). The attacks are categorized into three types: physical threats, channel threats, and system threats.

Figure 2.24 Attacks on the RFID modules of an IoT device

Physical threats are the security threats that are performed on the physical RFID device, transmitter, or receiver (Li et al., 2012). Due to the low cost of the devices, the RFID tags are not tamper resistant and can be easily exploited. There is a great chance of reverse engineering the RFID tags and clone them. This allows the attacker to get the data that is stored in the tag. Every RFID tag will have a unique identification number and copying the label is not a difficult task with the device itself in hands of the attacker. The RFID tags can be easily disrupted with the electromagnetic waves which can disable them temporarily making them vulnerable. To disrupt the RFID tag, the electromagnetic radiation should be of the same frequency as that of the RFID system.

There are two components in an RFID system: the tag and the reader. The channel to communicate between them can be taken as an advantage and the vulnerabilities are exploited by the attacker. These are called as channel threats. Eavesdropping is a vulnerability of the RFID tag as the communication between the RFID tag and the reader is wireless. The information retrieved by eavesdropping can be used for different attacks like counterfeiting, copying the tag, track, etc. The transmitting power of the reader is high when compared with the RFID tag. so reading from the tag is going to be easier comparatively. To avoid the data being stolen, the data transmitted should be encrypted between the reader and the tag.

One other major vulnerability of the RFID tag is the replay attack. First, the data is collected by performing an eavesdropping attack on the RFID channel. This collected data is again replayed to the reader which is illegal and a false deception is achieved. The attacker can deceive the reader by impersonating the original tag and gain access. One time password, stamp program, and so on, are some of the solutions for these types of attacks. Man in the middle attacks, popularly known as relay attack is another security vulnerability of RFID, where the attacker can intercept the data between the reader and the tag but the attacker is far from the devices themselves. By using the devices, the data intercepted can be forwarded to another device and used for various reasons. This is called relay attack.

2.4.2 RFID security solutions

It is said that any system is as secure as its weakest element. So to secure the entire system and increase the robustness, its weakest elements should also be made secure. The two different communication channels of RFID are front-end and back-end, respectively (Vattem and Anjali, 2017). Readers collect the data from the RFID tags. This is the front-end part of the communication. Once the data is collected from the tags; the data is transmitted to the servers to process it. This is called as the back-end of the system. The back-end communication is already made secure by using secure shell and secure socket layer. This is already standardized and secure. But the front-end is prone to many issues as discussed above. This can be considered the weakest part of the RFID systems.

There are many security solutions available for RFID systems (Jayakrishnan et al., 2018; Sun and Zhong, 2012). Figure 2.25 shows various solutions for the RFID attacks that can be implemented to prevent the attacker to succeed in taking advantage of the vulnerabilities. Killing the RFID tags when a security threat is detected can be one of the ways of saving the security measures that can be implemented easily. The communication between the reader and the RFID tag can be temporarily stopped and necessary measures can be applied before continuing the communication again. The RFID tags themselves that does not contain any power source and hence the reader should be very near to the tag which needs the attacker to be near to the devices. Faraday cages can be implemented as a security measure. Faraday cages for security has been around for a very long time (Ahmadi et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2001). Figure 2.26 shows the structure and working of a Faraday cage. When it is implemented, the electromagnetic waves cannot pass through it as it is canceled out by the electric field generated around the Faraday cage. Cryptographic primitives like encrypting the communication between the tag and the reader can be implemented which can render the data collected by the attacker unless without the proper decryption. Blocker tags that block-out the unauthorized reader requests can be placed in proximity and can protect the authentic tags from being vulnerable.

Figure 2.25 Solutions for attacks on the RFID modules of an IoT device

Figure 2.26 Solutions for attacks on the RFID Modules of an IoT device using Faraday cage and blocker tags

There are also other solutions for security of RFID (Halevi et al., 2013). In some cases of applications, access to the system can be blocked to certain conditions. In a scenario of a patient with an implantable medical device, access can be granted to the reader when the patient is lying down or in a specific predetermined posture which can prevent the attacker from gathering data or tampering with the system in other conditions (Halevi et al., 2013). In the case of a keyless entry car, this context can be taken as an advantage (Yang et al., 2012). There are various steps for the driver before starting the car engine, for example, opening the door of the car, sitting in the driver’s seat, etc. In this scenario, the posture of driver sitting in the driver’s seat can be considered for starting the car’s engine. Obviously, this can prevent any unauthorized usage of the vehicle by the attacker. This scenario can also be implemented for starting the car from a distance or home of the user (Yang et al., 2012). The human actions and interaction with the world is an involuntary action which need not require the user to perform any additional actions for the purposes of security.

2.5 Near-field communications (NFC) security

Near-field communication, often also referred as NFC, is a short-range communication system. NFC is a contactless technology that allows data communication between the devices without internet connection. Features like Android Beam can be used in the NFC which allows for the users to transmit the data between devices. There are various applications of NFC which are shown in Figure 2.27 (Harbison, 2016). The foundation for developing NFC is RFID technology. There are some drawbacks to the NFC technology which include smaller range and low data rates.

Figure 2.27 Various applications of NFC modules in IoT

There has been a lot of research conducted in the area of NFC. There are various attacks that can be performed on NFC modules even though they are considered difficult to perform, NFC relay attack being one of them. Figure 2.28 shows various attacks that are performed on an NFC module. A trojan relay can be installed on a mobile device equipped with NFC and can initiate payments using the properties in the device of the victim (Harbison, 2016). This issue was addressed immediately but recent studies show that NFC can be used to steal the currency from various physical credit cards in the pockets of the victims. A point of sale (POS) machine which has the capability to accept payments through NFC and a mobile phone having NFC built into it are the only things needed to execute this attack (Harbison, 2016). This is possible with the NFC relay attacks which will forward the wireless communication over a large distance in contrary to the small distance of the NFC which are discussed further in the section.

Figure 2.28 Attacks on the NFC modules of an IoT device

2.5.1 NFC security attacks

Figure 2.29 shows the relay attack on the NFC module. As explained above, the attacks allow the data to be transmitted over a large distance. There are various parts of the attack, viz., honest prover, honest verifier, dishonest prover, and dishonest verifier. The cards of the victim and the point-of-sale terminal of the attacker are the honest prover and verifier in the scenario. The dishonest prover and verifiers are the NFC capable mobile phones of the victim and the attacker.

Figure 2.29 Relay attacks on the NFC modules of an IoT device

ISO/IEC14443 protocol of the NFC is taken as an advantage by the attacker in the relay attack. First, the attacker will forward the reader’s request to the victim and the answer from the victim is sent back to the reader in real-time. In the attack scenario, the attacker should be near the victim’s card and relay data over another communication channel which is sent to the second NFC reader. This secondary NFC reader has to be in the original readers’ proximity. For example, in case of cashless payment, an attacker could have an accomplice covertly holding one of the relay devices in range of somebody else’s payment card (i.e., by holding it near their wallet). Once this is done, the attacker could then use their relay device to purchase an item against the victim’s card. The disadvantage to this type of attack is the time taken to transmit the data. Due to the increased distance that the data has to travel, the time taken to transmit the data will also be increased.

In case of data-modification attack, the data that is being exchanged by the two parties is captured by the attacker and modified. The device used by the attacker will inhibit the data that is exchanged through the NFC channel for a brief amount of time. Another way of interfering with the data exchange over the NFC channel is to use an RFID jammer. The data modification can be easily detected by monitoring the strength of the signal that is being transmitted.

Figure 2.30 shows the eavesdropping attack of the NFC applications. In this case, an antenna is used to monitor the traffic between two parties by the attacker. The small distance between the two devices does not reduce the possibility of this attack. In some cases of attacks, the data that is being exchanged will be corrupted rendering it as useless. Using a secure channel for transmission, the data integrity can increase.

Figure 2.30 Eavesdropping attacks on the NFC modules of an IoT device

In a spoofing attack, the attacker pretends to be a different entity and taps the device against the tag. This can be made possible if the tag is compromised allowing it to run the malicious code. Even though the distance between the sender and receiver is very small, in some cases, man in the middle attacks is also possible in NFC. The attacker can use the antennas to intercept the information and manipulate it before sending it to the original receiver.

2.5.2 NFC security solutions

Figure 2.31(a) shows the architecture of Swing-Pay, a digital card module which uses biometric authentication combined with NFC for peer-to-peer payments (Ghosh et al., 2017). Various components of the Swing-Pay system are shown in the figure. For prototyping, Arduino Due board was used for the modules (Ghosh et al., 2017). The prototype of Swing-Pay was presented using the off-the-shelf components (Ghosh et al., 2017).

Figure 2.31 Various aspects of internet of things

In the design, E-Ink display was used for reducing the power consumption by the modules. The displays are bistable, and the power is consumed only when a change of state is required. A global system for mobile communication (GSM) modem, Adafruit Fona was implemented in the design for communications with a small size and a wide variety of capabilities. For interaction, a capacitive touch sensor was implemented in the design. A battery, lithium ion battery, was used as a power source.

In the framework of Swing-Pay, the fingerprint of the payee is activated initially. The card will be activated once the fingerprint is authenticated. Once payer selects pay-money, the payee will select the receive money in the respective module. The payee is authenticated using the fingerprint sensor and tap his card with the payer’s card. Upon successful authentication, the Payee’s ID will be transferred using NFC P2P mode to the payer module. If the authentication fails, the transaction will be blocked. Upon successful authentication, a message is sent through GSM module. In this prototype, the Android application was used and data is put in a Web Service using HTTP.

Once the data is received by the cloud server, it proceeds with the transaction. The details of bank for both payer and the payee are stored in the cloud server. Details are sent to the respective bank servers using the API. The payer’s bank will transfer the money to the payee account.

A Crypta tag architecture is shown in Figure 2.32 (Plos et al., 2013). One of the main components of the tag is analog front-end. This is connected to the antenna and is responsible for various tasks, extracting power supply, modulation, and demodulation of data and providing stable reset and clock signals. The digital part is attached to the analog front-end. The received demodulated data is processed in the digital part of the tag. The requested operations are performed on the data received and the responses are prepared. The digital part of the tag consists of an 8-bit Microcontroller, crypto unit (CU), framing logic (FL), and a memory unit. Internal memory stores the microcontroller program and AMBA bus is used for the communication between the FL and memory unit. Various cryptographic operations are performed on the data by the CU. An interface to the microcontroller is provided by FL and also handles some of the commands that are at lower levels.

Figure 2.32 Crypta tag

2.6 Smart transportation security

This section discusses the security threats and solutions for smart transportation. The category of vehicles that are discussed here, include smart cars and UAV. Research is being conducted where smart vehicles are being designed to reduce human interaction in driving the vehicle on road or in the air. This means the system will be doing all the driving and the dependence on circuitry increases exponentially. They are also connected to the internet for constant updates and also communicate with the servers. This makes them vulnerable to many kinds of attacks (Storm, 2015; Wu and Horng, 2017; Xiao et al., 2009). If the smart car or a UAV are attacked and taken control by the attacker, the results can be catastrophic.

2.6.1 Smart car security

There are various attacks that can be performed on a smart car or an autonomous car (Petit and Shladover, 2015). Figure 2.33 shows a typical autonomous car system (Storm, 2015). Various parts of an autonomous car include global positioning system (GPS), LiDAR, on-board unit, Emaps, radar, camera, wheel encoder, etc. LiDAR is a ranging system which uses laser. It shoots laser pings which when echoed back, gives the readings from reflection of the objects that are present around the vehicle. Radars and camera are also used to detect the obstacles in the surroundings while the vehicle is in motion. Now-a-days, smart vehicles have around 100 electronic control units (ECUs) and 10 million lines of code. When such a massive system is in place there are various chances of security breaches possible. The software updates are usually Over-The-Air updates, which also means the communications of the car has to be protected. Advanced threats should also be mitigated and each module that is present in the vehicle should be secured and protected such that the attacker does not gain access to them.

Figure 2.33 Various aspects of an autonomous car

2.6.1.1 Smart car security attacks

There are various threats when it comes to the smart transportation (Petit and Shladover, 2015). Figure 2.34 shows some of the attacks that a smart car is vulnerable to. GPS spoofing and jamming are considered to be high threats in a smart transportation environment. Cost of the simple jamming equipment is very less, but highly effective (Petit and Shladover, 2015). Costlier jammers do not only jam the signal but also give fake coordinates which can increase the risk. This is called GPS spoofing where false locations are given to the car. The antitheft system of a car can be easily blocked by using a GPS jammer combined with a GSM jammer. Detecting this kind of threat is highly difficult due to the environmental constraints (Petit and Shladover, 2015). Using the GPS modules, the attacker will also be able to track the location of the vehicle affecting the privacy and security of the smart vehicle. Tracking a vehicle is also possible by merely eavesdropping the communications and enabling the remote identification and tracking (Figure 2.35).

Figure 2.34 Security attacks on autonomous car

Figure 2.35 Privacy issue in an autonomous car

Cameras are used in the smart car to constantly monitor the environment and perform the necessary operations. It is responsible for many processes like detecting pedestrians, nearby cars, and so on. A camera lens is highly susceptible to many issues. Like any camera, the lens can be distorted using a high-intensity light which may render it useless. There are various off-the-shelf components available, infrared light sources that are able to incapacitate the camera. This may lead to under performance of the vehicle or even cause an accident due to the malfunctioning of car. There are solutions available for this issue.

When an autonomous vehicle is designed, specific decision chains are also required to be incorporated. Figure 2.36 shows the design chain of a smart car. When a human is driving the vehicle, the decisions can be made by the human, but when an autonomous vehicle is driven by the actuators and they are controlled by algorithms. This decision chain involves different sensors, perception, planning, and actuation. The sensors will collect the data from the surroundings and store it or send it for processing. Once the data is processed, the algorithms are used for planning the next operation that should be performed by the vehicle. Depending on the decision made, the appropriate actuators will be activated to perform the action.

Figure 2.36 Smart car decision chain

Figure 2.37 shows the data-exchange process between different autonomous vehicles and the areas that can be attacked by the attacker (Petit et al., 2014). The sensors will collect the data about the surroundings and the data is processed at the ECU in the vehicle. Data at rest is the data that is stored when the vehicle is not in motion or stopped. This data is then sent to the other vehicles and the server through the communication module. When this data is sent to another vehicle, same process repeats and data is stored as encrypted data. Each of the different layers are subject to different attacks by the attacker.

Figure 2.37 Data exchange between smart vehicles

2.6.1.2 Smart car security solutions

Smart transportation is a fast-growing area with many researchers working on it. Secure components development is also one of the main focus of this area (Kong et al., 2016; Pacheco et al., 2016; Petit et al., 2014; Satam et al., 2017). Security of an autonomous vehicle cannot be compromised, or else, public can get into danger. There are many solutions available for most of the attacks performed on the smart vehicles. The cameras can be incapacitated using high-intensity IR emitters. This can be blocked by implementing the filters before the camera which can block the IR light. Securing the communication between the vehicles and to the server can help in fighting against the eavesdropping attacks. This can be achieved by implementing the hardware-assisted security which can increase the encryption strength (Yanambaka et al., 2016a, 2016b, 2017).

There are also various frameworks that are available to develop more secure services for the smart autonomous vehicles (Ferreira et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2014; Soliman et al., 2013). There are four different layers when designing a smart car framework (Satam et al., 2017). They are the application, services, communications, and devices layers. At each of these layer, attacks can be performed. But with the abstraction of the layers, the security can be increased and entire system can be made more robust to the attacks. The sensors and other physical devices are responsible for collecting the data that is required to control the vehicle. The next layer is responsible for the communications to the other vehicles and the servers for updates. Various communications can be used like WiFi, Bluetooth, etc., as discussed in the previous sections. The services layer is responsible for performing all the middleware operations and functions that are used in smart car between the communications and applications layer. The top layer is the applications layer which has different applications that the user will need.

Various encryption modules are available for the smart vehicles as shown in Figure 2.38 and 2.39 (Freescale, 2013). A cryptographic services engine is shown in Figure 2.38, which implements the encryption of the flash modules and prevents the access to other blocks or attackers. A secure communication can be made possible between the components using the ECU and master ECU. A random number is generated and is sent to the central ECU immediately when the car is turned on. Then, the sensor will collect the data and send to the sensor ECU which are encrypted by the CSE module with the random number generated. The central ECU then receives the message that is secured by the CSE. Then, the central ECU will decrypt the message using the CSE that is present in central ECU and receives the message.

Figure 2.38 Block diagram of cryptographic services engine

Figure 2.39 Secure communication

2.6.2 UAV or drone security

There are many different types of UAV and drones. Drones and UAVs are used in various applications of day-to-day life from military grade to home grade (UAV, https://www.theuav.com/). These applications are designed to reduce human interaction in dangerous situations such as hostile areas and also to increase efficiency in day-to-day applications. But the drones and UAVs are susceptible to many different attacks like other smart vehicles as discussed in the previous sections. This section describes different security threats for Drones and UAVs and security measures that can protect against them.

2.6.2.1 UAV security attacks

The illustration of an UAV with selected components and attached is presented in Figure 2.40. There are various parts of an UAV that are connected to the network or a satellite that can be used to breach the security and take control of the UAV. Communications protocol connects to the satellite to receive and send data to the base station, GPS module communicates with the GPS satellites. The different logic components that are necessary for computations are shown in Figure 2.40. The control systems and security modules are shown in Figure 2.40.

Figure 2.40 UAV security – a big picture

Many of these components are vulnerable to various attacks originated from a computer. So the attacks can be originated from a remote source and the attacker need not be near to the devices while attacking. Different actions can be performed by the attacker like:

  • Change the control rates by performing a distributed DoS (DDoS) attack.

  • The data that is being collected from the sensors can be modified which can make the flight dangerous.

  • The data from the drone can be analyzed for any design flaws that can be taken advantage of in a later attack.

The attacks that can be performed on a UAV can be broadly classified into two categories: integrity attacks and denial of service attacks (Sedjelmaci et al., 2017). The integrity attacks compromise the functionality of the vehicle by changing and sending a false information. Figure 2.41 shows different types of attacks on a UAV. GPS spoofing is a common attack that can be performed on the UAVs receiver which can send the vehicle false coordinates which can make the flight difficult. By performing this attack, the UAV can be led to believe it is in a different location than the original location. Such attacks are performed and vehicles were compromised because of this attack (Shepard et al., 2012). But to perform the attack the spoof signal should be aligned precisely with the original signal and increase the strength of the spoofing signal gradually to control the target. After gaining control, the counterfeit signal can be moved away from the original signal which controls the drone (Nighswander et al., 2012; Shepard and Humphreys, 2011). Detecting this attack by the drone is highly difficult as the drone’s navigation system will not raise any alarm when this attack is being performed.

Figure 2.41 Security attacks on a UAV

UAVs can also be attacked by similar UAVs which can lead to the authentic vehicle transmitting falsified data to the receiver. A counterfeit UAV can be used to communicate with an authentic vehicle and send false data. The authentic vehicle then communicates the falsified data to the base station which can be catastrophic in some conditions. This is called the injection attack. The position of the UAV and other collision avoidance systems are handled by the ADS-B controller which is present on the UAV (Sedjelmaci et al., 2016). These can be taken advantage by the attacker to perform an ADS-B attack that will send false position data to the system. This is called spoofing attack.

Another common attack that can be performed on the UAV is the denial of service attacks. This can be performed by sending huge packets of data which will disrupt the communications of the UAV rendering it useless. Jamming, gray hole, and black hole attacks are some of the DoS attacks. Jamming will jam the communications to the base station which can make it loose control and block any new commands. A gray hole and black hole attacks will initialize a node which can lure the UAV into sending the data and forward the data to the server, but then drop all the data or steal it when received at the node.

Security of a UAV can be increased but with the increase of security there can be many issues as shown in Figure 2.42. With added security modules, the weight of the entire UAV increases. When it comes to the aerial vehicles, weight plays a major role in the flight to destination. With an added weight, the aerodynamics are changed. With more components added to the system, more battery consumption is a major issue. With the more battery added, again it loops back to the aerodynamics.

Figure 2.42 Effects of increased security

2.6.2.2 UAV security solutions

Intrusion detection system is a way of stopping the attackers from getting into the system’s network (Sedjelmaci et al., 2017). In the delay tolerance network, the communications are sparse and hence to deploy a distributed intrusion detection system is a better approach. When a distributed intrusion detection systems (IDS) is employed, different nodes will be able to fire the IDS and then monitor various behaviors of the incoming data. Each of the UAV will be able to monitor the neighbors and secure the entire network. When a malicious UAV is detected in the network, it then sends the data regarding the UAV and the malicious UAV loses the ability to be in the network. Hence, the entire network can be secured easily. Different rules are written for detecting the GPS spoofing and jamming (Hartmann and Steup, 2013; Kim et al., 2012). There are different characteristics of a spoofing attack: it generates a signal with a high strength and signal strength intensity (SSI) is very high from that of a satellite. The attacker will also send multiple signals from the same directions and from the same antenna. All of those signals will have the same signal. So while detecting such attackers, the UAV detection agent first selects all those signals and their signal strength, SSI, are determined and calculated. Then, the mean and variance of the signals are calculated and if they lie within the range of ±3σ, they are correct, and if not they are not correct and are from an attacker.

2.7 Smart healthcare security

IoT, the interconnection of various sensors that collect data, transmit it to the cloud, and store or process the data, is becoming an integral part of various industries including the healthcare. The idea of smart healthcare using the internet of medical things (IoMT) or internet of health things (IoHT) is presented in Figure 2.43. It is estimated that there are more connected devices on this planet than there are people (Li et al., 2011) and the number is keep on increasing day-by-day. Among all the data that is being collected by the sensors, health data is one of the most sensitive information. The health conditions of the patients should be kept under high security making sure the data does not leak. If medical records of patient are leaked, it can lead to major problems like social exclusion, insurance, adverse employment, and so on.

Figure 2.43 Internet of medical things (IoMT) or internet of health things (IoHT)

Previous sections discussed various security flaws that can be exploited and data stolen. This infers no system is 100% secure. An IoT network means network of connected devices and sensors. If one device is attacked and breached, the entire network will be in jeopardy. When it comes to a healthcare device, this can lead to catastrophic results where the patient’s life may fall into danger. Many healthcare devices will monitor a certain parameter of the patient and deliver the drug at a preprogrammed dosage. If such devices are attacked, the configuration can be changed leading to health deterioration. Hence, the health information of the patient should be confidential.

Thoughts around health information privacy and security automatically turn to the Health Information Privacy and Security Act (HIPAA), together with the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act amendments. Administered by the Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights (OCR), the HIPAA Rules regulate privacy, security, individual rights, and breach notification for some (but not all) health information. Moreover, they require certain (but not all) persons who process that health information to put physical, administrative, and technical safeguards in place to protect it in all forms, and to institute a security management process (including risk analysis and risk management) to protect it in electronic form.

2.7.1 Smart healthcare security attacks

There are many different risks when it comes to a smart healthcare system (Alamri, 2018; Chaudhary et al., 2018; Ghoneim et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018). Figure 2.44 shows different kinds of attacks that can be performed on a smart healthcare system. Data eavesdropping is the process where the attacker will listen to the communications between the medical device and the receiver and steal the data from the communication. This can be avoided using a secure communication. Data privacy, data confidentiality, and location privacy are major issues in healthcare. There is a lot of data that is collected in the case of a medical device (Sundaravadivel et al., 2016). All this data needs to be securely transmitted to the doctor. The data should not fall into the hands of an attacker. It should be confidential and privacy should be given a highest priority. Every device will be given a unique identification which is also subject to counterfeiting attacks and spoofing attacks that were discussed in the case of RFID tags. RFID tags may also be used in the medical healthcare devices which are subject to different attacks that can lead to identity threats. Access and control of the device can be taken by the attacker which will be discussed further in the section.

Figure 2.44 Attacks on smart healthcare systems

Figure 2.45 shows the design of an insulin delivery system that is used by various diabetes patients to monitor and control the insulin levels in the body (Li et al., 2011). There are various components in the system, a glucose monitor, which can monitor the levels of glucose in the blood and a pump which is used to pump glucose into the blood when necessary and a remote control. The glucose monitor will have glucose sensors, which senses the levels of glucose in blood and transmit the data to the insulin pump and to the computer when necessary. The pump will autonomously administer the insulin in prescribed doses by the doctor and is programmed. There are two different ways of administration, bolus dose, which administers quickly when the glucose levels rise quickly and basal dose which administers the dose slowly during night and between meals. These are preprogrammed into the pump and are administered accordingly. There are different ways of programming the device, buttons on pump, through a computer with a wireless connection, remote control, and wireless connection to a blood glucose monitor. Figure 2.46 shows two different kinds of attacks that are possible on the insulin pump which can affect the health of the patient. Passive attack is where the remote control is taken into control and send signal to the insulin pump (Li et al., 2011). A universal radio peripheral is used in this scenario where the remote sends a malicious signal to the pump which can change the program of system and administer an unprescribed dosage of insulin. Active attack is where the same radio peripheral is used to send the signal directly to the pump and change the program of the system. Both these attacks are dangerously harmful to the patient.

Figure 2.45 Insulin delivery system

Figure 2.46 Passive and active attacks on smart healthcare

2.7.2 Smart healthcare security solutions

There are many solutions available for the security threats of smart healthcare. As the smart healthcare itself is a growing field, many researchers are aiming toward securing the system (Ghoneim et al., 2018; He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2011; Rauf et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018). Many hardware-assisted security solutions are discussed in different sections above which can be deployed in case of smart healthcare devices as most of the components in this case are discussed previously. Data eavesdropping, privacy, security, and location privacy can be handled by employing more secure measures to encrypt the communication. But added security modules can increase the power consumption and require more battery which is a major issue in the smart device especially healthcare (Sundaravadivel et al., 2016; Yanambaka et al., 2015, 2016a, 2017). So, low-power modules should be used for this purpose.

Figure 2.47 shows the ways of securing the insulin administering system (Li et al., 2011). Using a different pin at a timely manner will help securing the system without adding more to the security modules already present in the system (Alrabady and Mahmud, 2005). The remote and the insulin pump shares a communication channel which can be encrypted for a better security measure. There is a sequence counter in the remote and a key is used to encrypt the number generated by the counter. When a data is sent to the pump, the counter increased by 1 and the insulin pump will have the same key to decrypt the number shared with the pump. There may be some dropped signals between the remote and the pump which can have some difference in the numbers but if that difference is large it can be assumed the system is under attack. By employing a rolling code technique, the attacker will not be able to retrieve the pin to launch any attack. But the encryption and decryption algorithms should be more sophisticated to avoid the attacker reading the pins.

Figure 2.47 Encryption and decryption modules in an insulin delivery system

2.8 Firmware

Technology scaling has allowed us to design smaller and more powerful application devices that has network capabilities (Mohanty, 2015; Yanambaka et al., 2015). These devices have allowed us to develop huge number of applications that has become an integral part of our lives. When a network capability to the device was added, this entity has given access to a whole new level of attackers. The attacker can now access the devices remotely and attack them. All the embedded systems are equipped with firmware nowadays. Firmware is the software that is embedded in the hardware and acts as a middleware between the hardware and the outer world applications or an OS, if necessary. This firmware will not be updated as often as the other applications. When updating the firmware, there can be many attacks possible which will be discussed in this section.

2.8.1 Firmware attacks

There are a growing number of attacks being performed on the firmware of the devices. The network capabilities of the devices have allowed them to be attacked from a remote location. When the firmware has been attacked, the entire hardware can be compromised. The hardware can be taken into control, or tampered with, data loss, and so on are some of the results of a successful attack. There is also a chance that the attacker can take control of the embedded system to create and send spam messages to many other devices or emails across the network (Kaspersky, 2014). Denial of service attacks are one of the most common ones that are happening (Shila et al., 2016). A ThingBot can also be used to create a DDoS attack that can incapacitate a server (Kaspersky, 2014). It is a fact that the majority of these attacks are possible, because the firmware and firmware updates are insecure, low security in Internet web interfaces, insecure web applications, and so on (OWASP, 2018). There are many research facilities that are developed for the security flaws in the firmware and their updates (Choi et al., 2016; Dacus and Yannakogeorgos, 2016; Danese et al., 2017; Guin et al., 2017).

The firmware attacks are broadly classified into two different types of attacks: static and dynamic (Figure 2.48). The static attacks are the kind where the firmware that is present in the memory of the embedded system is attacked during the update process or when it is being patched. This can be avoided by implementing a trusted environment when updating and patching the software (Greene, 2016). But using them will fail when a dynamic attack is launched on the firmware of the system.

Figure 2.48 Firmware and attacks

In a dynamic attack, the attacker will divert the flow of control from the firmware to the code that he has injected and will execute it. There are two different types of dynamic attacks on the firmware of a system: code reuse and code injection. In case of a code injection attack, as the name suggests, the attacker will inject his own code into the memory of the system and will change the flow of control to execute the malicious code. Data execution prevention, Stack Canaries are some of the ways to protect the hardware against such attacks. In code reuse attacks, the attacker will try to execute the already existing code on the memory by changing the flow of control. This can compromise the functionality of the entire system. Various code snippets or gadgets can be combined and a new arbitrary logic can be developed (Shila et al., 2016). This allows the attacker to avoid injecting any new code into the system.

2.8.2 Firmware solutions

There are many defenses that are being developed for firmware security as stated above (Choi et al., 2016; Dacus and Yannakogeorgos, 2016; Danese et al., 2017; Guin et al., 2017). Commonly used security solution is the Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) which will randomize the address lotions of data and code segments. This will render the attacker impossible to create some of the attacks that have been discussed. Figure 2.49 shows the implementation of programming protocol of flash memory. In the process, an open channel is used between the microcontroller and the programmer (Soja, 2014). An RSA encryption scheme is used in this scenario for security. For the software image that is to be loaded onto the microcontroller, a hash is generated using SHA-256 algorithm. The hash is generated in a secure offline environment. A signature is added to the hash value which is used to identify the owner of the software. The signed hash value and the software image are transferred to the destination.

Figure 2.49 Firmware security solutions

The destination then uses the public key and verifies if the code sent to it is authentic or is tampered with. The hash value must match with the hash generated by the embedded module. If they are not matching, then the software would have been tampered, and thus, cannot be used in the system. This method does not use any power intensive mechanisms to encrypt and decrypt the entire software which uses more power and performance from the embedded system. The initially generated hash of the software image is generated in a secure offline environment which can prove very limited chances of attacks from a remote location. Access to the original software is restricted before generating the hash. All systems can be provided with a public key which can be used to authenticate the software and RSA key. This also does not demand much processing power from the embedded system.

2.9 Blockchain technology

Transactions have been around for a very long time. Especially, financial transactions and banks have been around making it easier to transfer funds between accounts. With the advent of internet, online transactions have increased lately. Huge number of financial transactions is happening in the internet for online shopping, transfer funds between accounts and overseas. An intermediary or bank is given the responsibility of transferring the funds securely from the sender to the receiver. These are accurate, responsible, legitimate, and secure. But there are questions rising lately:

  • What happens when the trusted party goes rogue?

  • When an attacker steals all the data, and who is held responsible?

  • There is a delay between sender to intermediary and to the receiver.

  • Can the intermediary be trusted for authenticity?

As an answer to all these questions, the blockchain technology was introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto with Bitcoin (Barber et al., 2012; Bitcoin, 2008). It uses an open ledger or shared distributed ledger that contains the records of every transaction that occurred. There is no presence of intermediary in this scenario. This section discusses the Blockchain, its applications, and issues in implementations of blockchain.

2.9.1 Blockchain – overview

Blockchain is the concept of shared ledger where all the participants or users will have a copy of the ledger which contains all the transactions that occurred till date. There is no trusted intermediary in this case which eliminates all the questions that raised. A public key infrastructure is implemented in the case of Bitcoin which is used for the authentication of the users and control the access. Every owner will sign and authenticate the transaction with his private key. A ‘block’ contains multiple transactions that happened along with its hash and is time stamped. For a transaction to be approved, majority of the users or nodes has to agree to the consensus. Miners are responsible to calculate the hash value of the block according to the consensus algorithm. The hash computed will be less than a threshold that was previously agreed to avoid any issues among the users. The value is set such that the miners will be able to calculate it in a less period of time, in this case, 10 min (Li et al., 2017). Figure 2.50 shows the process of blockchain. A selected characteristic of the blockchain technology is shown in Figure 2.51.

Figure 2.50 Blockchain operation and data flow

Figure 2.51 Blockchain characteristics

2.9.2 Blockchain – application
