There are various applications to the blockchain. Mainly, the security it offers makes it suitable to be implemented in different domains. Figure 2.52 shows different applications of blockchain. It can be implemented in asset management where the security in managing and transferring the assets among different business networks is a priority. A software image or a physical entity like a computer or laptop can be an asset. It can be implemented from serialization until the step being deployed on the floor and it mainly focuses on the following issues: receiving and validating the assets, manufacturing serialization of assets, asset capitalization, installation of asset, and warranty activation.

Figure 2.52 Blockchain applications

Financial transactions can be a huge hassle when it comes to real estate. There are many entities from government databases, brokers, title companies, and so on. Blockchain will eliminate most of these entities, where every person and property can be digitally addressed and it may contain anything from financial, occupancy, legal, building performance, and physical attributes. Blockchain is mainly useful in financial transactions where the transfers of funds can be performed without the help of an intermediary. The blockchain implementation in financial transactions is not only cheap but also extremely fast. In case of a bank transaction, it takes 2–3 days where in the case of blockchain, it takes only about 5 min to complete a transaction.

Blockchain can also be used to improve the efficiency of IoT. There is a huge amount of data that is being collected in case of an IoT device. This data can be stored securely and trusted that no alterations are made to it. Blockchain-assisted weddings can also be made easy where searching for a bride and groom online then meeting them and made arrangements for wedding (Ngo, 2014). Healthcare is another domain where blockchain can be proven to be very useful. Patient’s data should be stored securely and without compromise. This technology allows for such storage and also makes sure the data is protected from alterations.

2.9.3 Blockchain as a security framework

The consensus is a distributed and decentralized network where the user is the only entity that can determine the future updates of the state can occur. Figure 2.53 shows the process of adding a new value to the already existing chain and Figure 2.54 shows the consensus algorithm. In the blockchain, practical byzantine fault tolerance algorithm (PBFT) is responsible for establishing the consensus among different users or nodes. Each of the user will maintain a state which when receive a new message, is fed with the message data that is necessary for computing the value and reach a decision. Once a decision is reached, it is broadcasted to the network and when majority of the decisions match it leads to the next consensus. A consortium for businesses, blockchain technology is used and PBFT as its base is being developed by Hyperledger Project (https://www.hyperledger.org/).

Figure 2.53 Blockchain process of adding a new value

Figure 2.54 Blockchain consensus algorithm

Proof-of-work was initially the decentralized consensus protocol that was proposed by the developer of blockchain, Satoshi, for the consistency and security of Bitcoin. As the transactions of the bitcoin blockchain, they require a consensus for the validation of blocks. There are different nodes in the network and several of them compete with each other to calculate the value of the newly added block. Once a node calculates the value of hash, it waits for the other nodes to complete and verify the values together. Then, the generated hash is added to the blockchain. If an appropriate solution is found by multiple nodes, then there may be multiple blocks generated in the network which can cause a temporary branch. In such scenarios, all of them are acceptable and nodes closer to the miners accept the solution they receive and forward the same to other peers. At any time, the longest chain is accepted by the users in the network. Proof of stake has been developed to avoid the issues of high-power consumption by Proof Of Work in bitcoin. Etherium uses the Proof of Stake as the consensus. In case of a POS, the cryptocurrency is bought and then used in the network which reduces the high-power consumption in calculating the hash.

2.9.4 Blockchain – issues

As discussed in this section, there are various advantages to blockchain technology. But there are also some disadvantages when comes to this and the main being scalability. There is also need of the entire blockchain, i.e., the entire list of all the transactions that happened till date for the consensus and validation. This requires huge amounts of storage capacity. Restriction of block size can decrease the entire problem of scalability. But this also decreases the speed of transactions and increases the fees of transaction. But with a high block size, the entire transaction can take very long to execute. Bitcoin-NG was proposed which has a reduced block size and increased security. This can be achieved by dividing the block into two different parts.

When a Fork is created in the blockchain, a long time should be waited to confirm which chain is the longest and correct branch by all the nodes. This can cause much higher delay to the entire transaction. There is also a 50% attack problem in the blockchain where 50% of the nodes can fake the block and also reverse the transactions. In this case, the power of computation holds all the power so legitimate users might face a problem. Power consumption of bitcoin miners is very high. To mine a bitcoin needs very high amount of computational power which can also increase the power consumption drastically. This can lead to the problem where investment can be higher than the return.

2.10 Conclusions

This chapter discussed different security flaws of the IoT devices and modules. Appropriate solutions were also presented for the security issues for each of the module. Still there are many security issues that need addressing. There can also be some zero-day vulnerabilities which are still yet to be found. The attackers who find the security flaws can take the advantage of them and need not share the flaw with the world. There may be many security flaws and vulnerabilities that are present but not known to the security community which are not addressed in the solutions. There is a vast scope of future research in this domain where security can be increased, and robust design is implemented in an IoT environment.

Chapter 3
Trojan security aware DSP IP core and integrated circuits

This chapter discusses different security approaches to designing digital signal processing (DSP) cores that have detection capability against functional-type hardware Trojans in a global supply chain. In the current design and fabrication supply chain, design houses, circuits and system core vendors, and manufacturing houses are globally scattered. It is quite possible that Trojans can be inserted in this design and manufacturing supply chain by anyone involved at any phase. Such Trojans can give backdoors to hackers and affect the operation of the system that uses the infected hardware. In a worst case, in critical applications, such as aircrafts and medical devices, functioning can be completely stopped, causing catastrophic consequences. The chapter is organized as follows: Section 3.2 discusses different features and threat models of hardware Trojans; Section 3.3 explains how a Trojan could be inserted in a 3PIP core and why it is difficult to detect; Section 3.4 discusses different hardware Trojan security approaches that are available in the literature with emphasis on DSP cores; Section 3.5 presents definition, goal, and design evaluation models for Trojan security aware DSP IP cores; Section 3.6 discusses the design process of Trojan secured DSP IP cores; Section 3.7 presents analysis and comparison of different Trojan security approaches for DSP IP cores; the chapter concludes with Section 3.8.

3.1 Introduction

The use of heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) architecture in modern consumer electronics (CE) devices such as smartphones, gaming consoles, tablets, and digital cameras has become a common practice in the semiconductor industry. The in-house SoC designer or the system integrator mostly imports intellectual property (IP) cores from third-party IP vendors to minimize design time and to meet strict product delivery deadlines. These third-party IP (3PIP) cores can be DSPs/media processors, such as JPEG image compression-decompression (CODEC), finite impulse response (FIR) filters, infinite impulse response (IIR) filters, fast Fourier transformation (FFT) algorithms, Haar wavelet transformation (HWT) algorithms, and discrete cosine transformation (DCT) algorithms, or they can be micro IP cores/blocks, such as adders, multipliers, and comparators. However, these 3PIP cores have severe trust issues, because an untrustworthy IP vendor may insert malicious logic elements known as “hardware Trojans” into their IP cores to introduce malfunctioning/failure of the SoCs (Tehranipoor and Koushanfar, 2010; Liu et al., 2014; Sengupta, 2016, 2017; Chakraborty et al., 2009; Sengupta and Kundu, 2017) (a thematic representation of the aforesaid statement during an SoC life cycle is shown in Figure 3.1). Moreover, a Trojan-infected IP core may leak confidential information by creating a backdoor in the design or may degrade the performance of the processor (Bhunia et al., 2013). The typical trusted and untrusted phases in the life cycle of a SoC design are shown in Figure 3.2.

Figure 3.1 Design flow of a SoC

Figure 3.2 Life cycle of a SoC for a CE product and its possible vulnerabilities (Chakraborty et al., 2009)

Detection of a hardware Trojan is not always easy or straightforward, because an intelligent adversary always inserts malicious logic that will be activated under sporadic conditions (Wolff et al., 2008) and/or exhibit its effect for a small duration to evade detection. Additionally, thorough analysis, test, and verification of a complete SoC is complex and time-consuming. The Trojan activation condition is termed the trigger condition and, once triggered, the effect of the Trojan is termed the payload (Narasimhan et al., 2010). Logic testing (Banga and Hsiao, 2009) and side-channel analysis (Narasimhan et al., 2010; Koushanfar and Mirhoseini, 2011) are two commonly used techniques to detect hardware Trojans (Narasimhan et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014). In the first approach, functional or structural testing is performed (Chakraborty et al., 2009a; Wolff et al., 2008; Banga and Hsiao, 2009) to generate rare conditions, so that the effect of hardware Trojan logic gets reflected in the output. This type of detection approach is effective for ultra-small Trojans (Narasimhan et al., 2010). In the second approach, detection of hardware Trojans is performed by measuring physical “side-channel” parameters such as delay (Jin and Makris, 2008; Rai and Lach, 2009) or power signature (Agrawal et al., 2007; Banga and Hsiao, 2008; Rad et al., 2010). In this type of approach, detection of a hardware Trojan is possible without activating the Trojan logic and monitoring its effect on the output.

There are multiple classes of hardware Trojans which we discuss in Section 3.2.1; however, we mostly focus on how to provide security (detection) against a particular type of Trojan that changes the functionality or output of a DSP-based IP core. More specifically, we discuss the design process of a low-cost hardware Trojan secured datapath design for a DSP core through the dual modular redundant (DMR) schedule and vendor allocation processes (Rajendran et al., 2013; Sengupta et al., 2017b). To obtain a low-cost Trojan secured design, a particle swarm optimization (PSO)-based design space exploration (DSE) (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011, 2013) is performed for the DSP cores.

3.2 Types of hardware Trojans

This section discusses the different types of hardware Trojans, the advantages of handling this type of Trojan security for DSP cores at higher abstraction level, and details of the threat model of hardware Trojans.

3.2.1 Trojan features

We discuss here the major classification of Trojan-based hardware threats (shown in Figure 3.3) (Chakraborty et al., 2009; Sinanoglu et al., 2013; Sengupta, 2017). Digital hardware Trojans are classified into two types: trigger-based and payload-based. As mentioned earlier, triggering of a Trojan indicates activating it, which can be performed either through a combinational or a sequential mechanism. Similarly, the payload of a Trojan that indicates the effect of Trojan logic can change the functionality, degrade the performance, or leak secret information without changing the functionality.

Figure 3.3 Broad classification of digital hardware threats

Combinational-triggering-based hardware Trojan: This type of Trojan gets triggered under a very rare condition or event. Until that condition arises, the circuit works correctly. For example, as shown in Figure 3.4, the original output (Q) will be same as the Trojan-infected output (Q*) for all input combinations of A and B except A = B = 0. In this particular case, the inserted Trojan logic triggers and the incorrect output in Q* will be generated as payload. Therefore, in this circuit, A = B = 0 is the triggering condition.

Figure 3.4 Combinational-triggering-based hardware Trojan under a rare event (Chakraborty et al., 2009)

Sequential-triggering-based hardware Trojan: This type of Trojan gets triggered at a particular count of the counter. Once triggered, the circuit produces an incorrect output (Chakraborty et al., 2009). For example, as shown in Figure 3.5, there are p counters and all the counters execute synchronously using a clock signal. Once the counter reaches 2p−1 count, the Trojan logic gets triggered and the incorrect output in Q* will be generated as payload instead of Q. As this type of Trojan gets triggered in a certain time period, it is also known as a “time-bomb hardware Trojan.”

Figure 3.5 Synchronous counter sequential-triggered hardware Trojan

Functionality changeable payload-based hardware Trojan: This type of Trojan affects the payload of a circuit by causing output malfunction. For example, as shown in Figure 3.6, the BCD adder has two primary inputs, A and B, each of 4-bit size (A3−A0 and B3−B0), one enable signal En of one bit and one primary output O of 4-bit size (O3−O0). The BCD adder will work correctly when the En signal is set to 1, but when the En signal is set to 0 to disable the component/module, the Trojan gets triggered and starts introducing malfunctioning. The system integrator would keep the component enabled (En = 1) during the testing phase, because he/she may assume that the En signal is for enabling and disabling the component (Sengupta, 2017); however, it is a covert triggering signal for the Trojan. Therefore, the rare condition test could evade and pass the functional simulation and test (explained later in greater detail).

Figure 3.6 Trojan-infected BCD adder resulting in functionality change

Performance degradable payload-based hardware Trojan: This type of Trojan affects the payload of a circuit by degrading its performance. In other words, this type of hardware Trojan may increase execution delay or power consumption of a circuit without altering the correctness of the output. Therefore, this type of Trojan may go unnoticed during the functional verification phase. For example, as shown in Figure 3.7, for input values A = 1 and B = 0 or 1, the Trojan logic will not get triggered; therefore, there is no degradation of performance in terms of propagation delay of the 1-bit adder while calculating the sum (S). However, for input values A = 0 and B = 0 or 1, the Trojan logic gets triggered, therefore the propagation delay to calculate S will increase, thus degrading the performance of the circuit. However, in both the cases, the correct output will be generated, therefore, identification of this type of Trojan through functional/simulation verification could be evaded. This type of Trojan may result in an occasional timing violation of the circuit (Sengupta, 2017).

Figure 3.7 Hardware Trojan resulting in performance degradation

Leaking confidential information and launching denial of service (DoS) payload-based hardware Trojan: This type of Trojan, which leaks confidential information, is designed in such a way, that it can bypass the encryption process applied on the confidential information. The Trojan could be a big threat for sensitive information. For example, as shown in Figure 3.8, once the Trojan is triggered, the plaintext may skip the encryption process, thus disclosing confidential information (Sinanoglu et al., 2013).

Figure 3.8 Hardware Trojan resulting in leakage of confidential information (Sinanoglu et al., 2013)

The Trojan which launches DoS is designed in such a way that it forces the circuit to provide no output. For example, as shown in Figure 3.9, when the enable signal (En) is set to 0, it will trigger the Trojan. The effect of the payload is that data are not allowed to pass through the muxes, as for both the muxes, the second input is left uninitialized. Therefore, no output will be generated for the BCD adder.

Figure 3.9 Trojan-infected BCD adder resulting in no output or denial of service (DoS). (The BCD adder available to a designer as a black box is shown on the right)

3.2.2 Benefit of Trojan security at higher abstraction level

As mentioned earlier, most of the CE devices integrate IP cores from the DSP and multimedia domain in their SoC design process, such as JPEG CODEC (Sengupta et al., 2018b), FIR, IIR, FFT, DCT, and HWT (Sengupta et al., 2018a).These IP cores contain complex algorithms that are very challenging and time-consuming to design if the design process starts from the register transfer level or lower abstraction layer. Additionally, multiple design architectures (hardware variances) are possible for implementing these IP cores. Selecting arbitrary hardware design architecture may result in large overheads in terms of design implementation cost (area, delay, power etc.). A high-level synthesis (HLS) process integrated with a DSE engine is capable of exploring and designing a low-cost (in terms of power, performance, energy, and area) hardware architecture for DSP/multimedia IP cores within an acceptable runtime. Thus for designing of hardware for complex algorithms, within design constraints, while concurrently satisfying time-to-market pressure, HLS is the key.

While designing a DSP IP core, multiple 3PIP cores are usually available in the module library of an HLS tool. As these IP cores are imported from 3PIP vendors, which are untrustworthy, there is high possibility of their containing hardware Trojan (Rajendran et al., 2013). In a typical case, the vendor of the HLS tool imports IP cores/blocks available in its library from 3PIP vendors. Again, as mentioned earlier, these IP cores may also contain hardware Trojan. As designing a DSP IP core is vulnerable to such Trojan, handling hardware Trojan for DSP cores is necessary (Rajendran et al., 2013; Sengupta et al., 2017b, 2017c). In Section 3.4, we discuss different Trojan secured DSP IP core design processes that are available in the literature.

3.2.3 Threat model

There are different variations of hardware Trojan as discussed in Section 3.2.1. However, in the context of DSP, since hardware Trojan threats affecting the output functionality is a well-studied topic, in this chapter we lay emphasis only on those type of Trojans which change the computational (functional) output of an IP core circuit. As mentioned earlier, this type of Trojan can be available in the library of an HLS tool inside an IP block/module. Insertion of Trojan logic into the IP block/module is possible in two ways: (i) through an adversary within the HLS design house team; or (ii) when the design team of the HLS tool vendor imports the IP block/module from a 3PIP vendor. As this type of Trojan is triggered under very rare conditions, its detection is not always possible (i.e., the chances of evasion are high). The literature has studied the Trojan threat model on DSP cores that consider 3PIP vendors as untrustworthy. Thus the in-house design integrator team and foundry are considered trustworthy and the 3PIP vendor is considered an untrustworthy entity in the SoC design cycle.

3.3 Hardware Trojan in a 3PIP module

This section describes examples of Trojan-infected 3PIP cores which change the functionality of a circuit and gives reasons why such Trojans could evade detection during regular validation. As already mentioned, in this chapter, we discuss only that type of Trojan which alters the functionality of an IP core but does not leak any secret information. Literature so far has studied the effect of these Trojans on DSP IP cores (Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2015).

3.3.1 Example of a hardware Trojan

As discussed earlier, owing to several reasons, the HLS framework has become integral in efficient DSP IP core design processes. There are multiple successful academic and commercial HLS tools available for designing DSP IP cores. Generally, these HLS frameworks shave some pre-defined modules or blocks available in their library. These pre-defined modules or blocks are also known as micro IPs. While designing a complete DSP IP core, the DSP IP designer directly uses these micro IPs to increase reusability and reduce design effort. If HLS tool vendor imports these micro IPs from another vendor who is non-trustworthy, then in such a scenario, these IP cores could be vulnerable to hardware Trojan. Thus there is no guaranteeing that a 3PIP core in an HLS library will be 100% Trojan-free.

Let us assume there is a BCD adder IP available in the module library of an HLS framework as a black box. It contains three inputs and one output: (i) the enable signal (En) which switches on/off the execution of the adder, (ii) the first primary input A of bit width 4 (A3A2A1 A0), (iii) the second primary input B of bit width 4 (B3B2B1 B0), and (d) one output O of bit width 4 (O3O2O1 O0). In a general scenario, during functional/simulation verification and test, the En signal is set (En = 1) to start the execution of the BCD adder IP. Once the verification process is completed, the En signal is reset (En = 0) to stop the execution of the BCD adder IP. Now, let us consider a BCD adder that is designed as shown in Figure 3.10. In this case, the BCD adder IP would behave correctly during its verification process as the design verifier will set the En signal “ON” during functional simulation. He/she may falsely believe that the En signal truly starts and stops the execution of the IP. However, an adversary could design an IP in such a way that the Trojan will be triggered when the En signal is reset. Therefore, whenever the system designer/integrator resets the En signal, it may maliciously generate the wrong output thereby impacting the output of the DSP IP core design. Moreover, other than the aforementioned case, triggering of the Trojan can also be achieved through the finite state machine (FSM) counter, external antenna, and so on. Moreover, there is no golden IP (i.e., with a guarantee that it is100% Trojan-free) available in the open market; thus detecting this type of Trojan is difficult during lower abstraction level. There are several other reasons as well, which are discussed in the following.

Figure 3.10 Trojan logic inserted by an adversary in a BCD Adder IP (inputs A and B). Note: When Enable (En) = 0 (rare event), the Trojan blocks get activated and produce incorrect computational output

3.3.2 Trojan detectability in a 3PIP module at RTL/lower levels

Detection of hardware Trojan logic which corrupts the functional output of a 3PIP module is difficult during RTL validation or lower design abstraction level verification/tests for the following reasons:

  1. A Trojan logic-infected 3PIP produces functionally correct output in normal condition, that is, until the Trojan logic is triggered.

  2. The Trojan logic is triggered under very rare and specific time/condition (discussed earlier), therefore identifying such a condition or event is difficult during functional verification (Tehranipoor and Koushanfar, 2010).

  3. During functional verification, in most cases, only the functionality of the entire SoC is verified; each and every IP/module used (imported) in the system (after system integration) is not checked.

  4. Normally, the Trojan logic is set in an IP in such a way that it remains dormant during functional verification and triggered when the complete SoC is deployed in a real-time situation.

  5. As there is no trustworthy golden IP (i.e., guarantee of a 100% Trojan-free IP) model available, the evasion of detection of hardware Trojan in a 3PIP during HLS design for DSP core is possible.

  6. Physical inspection and reverse engineering, a very costly and complex procedure, does not guarantee the detection of such Trojans.

  7. The testing process to detect manufacturing faults (i.e., bridging faults, delay faults, stuck-at faults, etc.) also does not guarantee the detection of such Trojans.

  8. Due to evolution in technology, the physical feature size of a 3PIP decreases. The analysis of parametric signals to detect such Trojans is not considered very effective (Tehranipoor and Koushanfar, 2010).

3.4 Selected Trojan security approaches

In this section, we discuss Trojan security approaches for DSP IP cores and few selected Trojan security approaches for other hardware types such as combinational/sequential circuits. We first view multiple Trojan detection approaches for DSP cores and next, we discuss selected Trojan detection approaches for combinational/sequential circuits.

3.4.1 Trojan security approaches for DSP cores

The Trojan detection approaches for DSP cores discussed in the following is based on the threat model where hardware the Trojan is capable of producing functional (computational) changes in the DSP core output. In other words, the Trojan payload considered for these approaches is one that causes functional (computational) changes in the DSP core output.

3.4.1.1 Trojan security approach—Rajendran et al. (2013) and Liu et al. (2014)

Rajendran et al. (2013) and Liu et al. (2014) have devised duplication-based concurrent error detection (CED) techniques to achieve a Trojan secured design through HLS. The hardware Trojan that is available in a 3PIP core and affects its output or denies service is handled in this approach. In the duplication-based CED technique, replication of the same design is performed and both the designs are fed with the same set of inputs. The incorrect/dissimilar outputs due to activation of Trojan logic can be identified by comparing their outputs. However, generally an untrusted third party vendor makes a single Trojan infected IP core design and then exports multiple copies of it to the system integrator/SoC designer. Therefore, normal replication of the design cannot detect the Trojan (as both the designs will produce the same malicious outputs). In Rajendran et al. (2013), the source of the 3PIP core is diversified in such a way so that the same operation of both the design uses 3PIP cores coming from different sources. This process not only detects the malicious output of a 3PIP core caused by a hardware Trojan but also can prevent the activation of the Trojan by preventing collusion. Two types of collusion are prevented in this approach, that is, parent-child collusion and parent-parent collusion. The binding rules to prevent collusion are as follows:

  • A parent operation and its child operations in a design must be bound to the 3PIPs of different 3PIP vendors.

  • At least one of the parent operations of a child operation in a design must be bound to a 3PIP from a different 3PIP vendor.

The generic overview of this approach is shown in Figure 3.11. Although this approach is capable of achieving Trojan detection and collusion prevention, it may incur some design overheads as no low-cost design architecture is explored during the scheduling phase of HLS. Moreover, distinctness during 3PIP vendor allocation can be achieved in multiple ways which have a direct impact on the overall design cost. In this approach, no optimal vendor allocation is explored to minimize the overall design security cost. Further, this approach does not handle loop-based control data flow graph digital signal processing (CDFG DSP) applications.

Figure 3.11 Top-level diagram of the Trojan security approach of Rajendran et al. (2013)

3.4.1.2 Trojan security approach—Sengupta et al. (2017a)

Sengupta et al. (2017a) devised a hardware Trojan security aware approach that is capable of detecting the Trojan for DSP cores. It accepts a non-loop-based DSP application in the form of a data flow graph (DFG), user constraints, bacterial foraging optimization algorithm (BFOA) control parameters (such as step size, # of chemotactic steps, # of elimination-dispersal steps, # of replication steps, terminating criteria, and population size), and a module library. It then obtains a low-cost Trojan secured design based on the input DSP core (fed as DFG).

To obtain low-cost Trojan secured DSP IP core, a design solution consisting of hardware architecture configuration and vendor allocation mode is explored iteratively through BFOA. This approach explores an optimal vendor allocation procedure using variable Mv in bacterial encoding. More explicitly, in this process, each bacterium is encoded with the number of resources of a particular resource type and the vendor allocation mode. The encoding of each bacterium can be represented as B = (Rn, Mv), where Rn indicates the hardware configuration and Mv indicates the vendor allocation mode. Here, the vendor allocation mode includes two variances (Mv = 0 or 1). Before discussing the vendor allocation process, let us assume the scheduled design includes DMR logic consisting of the original unit (indicated as UOG) and the duplicate unit (indicated as UDP).

The rules for vendor allocation mode at Mv = 0 are as follows:

  • In each control step for a particular unit (either UOG or UDP), alternate vendor allocation would be performed for similar types of operations. For example, if in control step 1, three addition operations (opn.1, opn.2 and opn.3) are available, then opn.1 and opn.3 would be allocated to hardware of same vendor and opn.2 would be allocated to hardware of another vendor.

  • In the other unit, orthogonal vendor allocation is performed to maintain distinctness. In others words, the same operation of both the units must be allocated to different vendors. For example, if in UOG, opn.1 and opn.3 are allocated to hardware of vendor type 1 (V1) and opn.2 is allocated to hardware of vendor type 2 (V2), then in UDP, opn.1 and opn.3 must be allocated to hardware of V2 and opn.2 must be allocated to hardware of V1.

The rules for vendor allocation mode at Mv = 1 are as follows:

  • All operations of a particular unit (either UOG or UDP) must be allocated to hardware of the same vendor. For example, all operations of UOG must be allocated to hardware of V1.

  • Similar operation of both the units must be allocated to distinct vendors. For example, if all operations of UOG are allocated to hardware of V1 then all operations of UDP must be allocated to hardware of V2 and vice versa.

The generic overview of this approach is shown in Figure 3.12. Although this approach is capable of handling hardware Trojan during HLS for non-loop based DSP applications, it does not provide any process to handle loop-based CDFG DSP cores.

Figure 3.12 Top-level diagram of Trojan security approach of Sengupta et al. (2017a)

3.4.1.3 Trojan security approach—Sengupta et al. (2017b)

Sengupta et al. (2017b) overcome the aforementioned shortcoming in their devised hardware Trojan security aware approach. This approach is capable of accepting single loop-based DSP applications in the form of a CDFG, user constraints, maximum loop iteration count (I), PSO control parameters (such as inertia weight, cognitive factor, and social factor), and module library. It finally produces a low-cost Trojan security aware DSP RTL design as output.

This approach obtains a low-cost design solution through a PSO-based DSE process within the user-specified design constraints (the details of the PSO-DSE approach is available in Section 3.6.3.1). The design solution in each iteration of the PSO-DSE contains not only hardware configuration and vendor allocation mode but also loop-unrolling factor, which is a crucial design parameter for loop-based CDFG. Moreover, in this approach, instead of searching among all the possible values of the unrolling factor, a list of selected unrolling factors is obtained through a pre-processing algorithm as shown in Figure 3.13(a). The input to the pre-processing algorithm is the maximum loop iteration count and the output is the screened list of unrolling factors. The algorithm works as follows: the unrolling factors with the higher number of sequential execution and ones which increase code complexity without significantly improving the performance are not included in the screened list. This is because increase in sequential execution results in delay overhead, while increase in code complexity results in higher area/power. Further, large unrolling factors are not always monotonically increasing functions of performance. For example, the output of the pre-processing algorithm of an FIR filter is shown in Table 3.1. The C-code and CDFG of the FIR filter are described in Section 3.6.1.3 (Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2015).

Figure 3.13(a) Pre-processing algorithm for screening unrolling factors

Table 3.1 Preprocessing of unrolling factors for FIR filter

In this approach, distinctness during vendor allocation is achieved in two ways which are similar to that of Sengupta et al. (2017a). The encoding of each particle can be represented as P = (Rn, Mv, U), where U indicates the unrolling factor value; Rn and Mv have already been defined. The generic overview of this approach is shown in Figure 3.13(b). Although this approach is capable of handling hardware Trojan for single-loop CDFG-DSP cores, there are multiple nested loop-based CDFG applications available in DSP domain, which cannot be handled through this approach. Moreover, the authors here have presented only two-vendor allocation rules/modes for obtaining reduced design cost of Trojan secured architecture.

Figure 3.13(b) Top-level diagram of Trojan security approach of Sengupta et al. (2017b)

3.4.1.4 Trojan security approach—Sengupta et al. (2017c)

Sengupta et al. (2017c) overcome the aforementioned shortcoming in their devised hardware Trojan security aware approach. This approach is capable of accepting nested-loop DSP applications in the form of a CDFG, user constraints, maximum loop iteration count for all nested loops (I1, I2, … In), PSO control parameters (such as inertia weight, cognitive factor, and social factor), and module library, finally producing a low-cost Trojan secured DSP RTL design as output.

As this approach handles nested loop-based applications, screening of unrolling factors for all the loops is performed to discard the unfit unrolling factors of each respective loop. The input to the pre-processing algorithm is the maximum loop iteration count of each loop and the output is the screened list of unrolling factors for that respective loop. Compared to Sengupta et al. (2017b), in this approach, the screening algorithm needs to be executed multiple times corresponding to multiple loops. Thus the implementation complexity of this approach is higher than that in Sengupta et al. (2017b). Further, in this approach, similar to that of Sengupta et al. (2017b), a low-cost design solution is obtained through a PSO-based DSE process within the user-specified design constraints. However, the encoding of each particle in this approach is significantly different from that of Sengupta et al. (2017b) and can be represented as P = (Rn, Mv, UF1, UF2, …UFn), where UF1 indicates the unrolling factor value for the outermost nested loop and UFn indicates the unrolling factor value for innermost nested loop. Moreover to achieve distinctness, this approach uses four vendor allocation modes to obtain low-cost Trojan secured design architecture for DSP cores. Here, the four different vendor allocation modes are Mv = 00, 01, 10, and 11, where Mv = 00 and 01 are the same as Mv = 0 and 1, respectively (discussed earlier). The remaining of the vendor allocation modes are defined in the following.

The rules for vendor allocation mode at Mv = 10 are as follows:

  • In a particular unit (either UOG or UDP) all critical path operations must be allocated to the hardware of one vendor and all non-critical path operations must be allocated to the hardware of another vendor. For example, if all critical path operations of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 then all non-critical path operations of UOG must be allocated to the hardware of V2.

  • Similar operation of both the units must be allocated to distinctive vendors. For example, if all critical path operations of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 then all critical path operations of UDP must be allocated to the hardware of V2 and vice versa.

The rules for vendor allocation technique at Mv = 11 are as follows:

  • In a particular unit (either UOG or UDP) alternate vendor allocation is performed for the operations belonging to subsequent unrolled nested-loop iterations. For example, if all the operations of the first unrolled loop of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 then the operations of the second unrolled loop of UOG must be allocated to the hardware of V2, following which the operations of the third unrolled loop of UOG must be allocated to hardware of V1, and so on.

  • Similar operation of both the units must be allocated to distinctive vendors. For example, if all the operations of the first unrolled loop of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 then all the operations of first unrolled loop of UDP must be allocated to the hardware of V2 and vice versa.

The generic overview of this approach is shown in Figure 3.14. However, unlike Cui et al. (2014), this approach does not perform Trojan recovery during run-time. Nevertheless, Trojan correction through CED can be performed using TMR logic.

Figure 3.14 Top-level diagram of the Trojan security approach of Sengupta et al. (2017c)

3.4.2 Trojan security approach for combinational/sequential circuits

Code-coverage analysis is one of the promising Trojan-detection approaches that are available in the literature. Hu (1997) has identified the list of suspicious signals from the RTL design. In this process, if a signal remains stable (does not change its state) during coverage analysis, it is identified as a suspicious signal. The reason for selecting these types of signal as suspicious is that a Trojan usually does not change its states until triggered. Thereafter, uncovered parts of the design are activated by adding test vectors. However, this approach suffers from huge verification time.

Equivalence analysis on only suspicious signals (instead of all the available signals of a design) can detect Trojan logic in an efficient way (Bushnell and Agrawal, 2013). However, this approach also incurs some runtime overhead. Additionally, all suspicious signals may not always be a Trojan logic. Moreover, the number of suspicious signals will increase with the complexity of the inserted Trojan. Thus, achieving 100% code-coverage for all IP cores through this approach is difficult. Salmani et al. (2009) devised a Trojan-detection mechanism by inserting dummy flip-flops to increase the Trojan activity. Dummy flip-flops are inserted in such a way that they increase the transition probability of nets. Finally, they are capable of increasing Trojan activity while reducing Trojan activation time. Multiple Trojan secured methodologies for C-series benchmarks at lower design abstraction are also available in the literature (Agrawal et al., 2007; Narasimhan et al., 2010; Jin and Makris, 2008; Wang et al., 2008). The Trojan detection process by Agrawal et al. (2007) is performed on the basis of comparison of characteristics of the manufactured chip, such as path delay and power consumption with the expected value. In detecting Trojans, Narasimhan et al. (2010) rely on the fact that the hardware Trojan inserted into a design will change the design parameters of the circuit. This approach is capable of detecting Trojans in the presence of large process variation-induced noise. Wang et al. (2008) devised a multiple-supply transient-current integration approach to detect hardware Trojan. This approach is capable of isolating the Trojan through a localized current analysis approach. However, process variations for detection and isolation of very small size Trojan circuits (less than few gates) can be negative.

3.5 Trojan security aware DSP IP core

In this section, we discuss the definition of “Trojan security aware DSP IP core design,” objectives that must be satisfied while designing it, the design problem to achieve a low-cost Trojan secured DSP IP core, and the fitness models required to evaluate different design solutions (Sengupta et al., 2017b; Rajendran et al., 2013).

3.5.1 Definition

We discuss here one of the established methodologies to handle hardware Trojan (which corrupts the functional output of a DSP IP core) by generating a Trojan secured scheduling design. A Trojan secured schedule can be obtained in three consecutive steps: firstly, performing duplication of all the operations of the original CDFG to generate a duplicate CDFG, collectively known as a dual modular redundant (DMR) system; secondly, performing scheduling of operations of the DMR system based on the resource configuration (DSE-generated) to obtain the scheduled DMR; finally, achieving distinctness during hardware allocation of operations of the DMR schedule such that similar operations of the original CDFG and duplicate CDFG must have hardware of distinct vendors. Therefore, to achieve distinctness during hardware allocation, IP cores must be imported from a minimum of two distinct third-party vendors. As both the third-party vendors are not trustworthy, it may be possible that both the 3PIP cores are Trojan infected. However, having *exactly* the same Trojan payload in both the 3PIP cores is nearly impossible as both third-party vendors are mutually exclusive (unknown) to each other. Therefore, Trojan detection can be achieved by performing an equivalence check of the output of both the original CDFG and duplicate CDFG during the runtime. In other words, hardware Trojan detection can be achieved by assigning different sets of 3PIP vendors for similar operations in DMR design during the hardware-allocation step of HLS.

Trojan detection achieved through DMR for loop-based CDFG introduces duplication of all the operations, adding steering logic and internal buffering that results in incurring design overhead. Additionally, loop-based CDFGs can be implemented for different unrolling factor (UF) values, where different UF value have a different impact on the design latency, which may also incur design overhead (if not selected intelligently). Moreover, distinctness during vendor allocation can be achieved in several ways. However, each distinct vendor-allocation procedure may result in different area and execution delay of the Trojan secured design. The reason is that the same hardware imported from two different vendors may have different area and latency. Considering all these factors, to optimize the design overhead as well as to design a low-cost Trojan secured DSP IP core, an optimal design solution comprising of resource configuration, unrolling factor, and vendor allocation mode needs to be explored.

3.5.2 Goal

The goals of Trojan security aware design are as follows:

  1. Generate a low-cost Trojan secured DMR schedule to detect hardware Trojan for DSP IP core.

  2. The Trojan secured design should satisfy the user-specified design constraints (such as area, delay, and power).

  3. For single- and nested-loop-based applications, an optimal unrolling factor should be additionally explored to optimize the Trojan secured DSP core design.

  4. Perform distinct vendor allocation of the original and the duplicate unit of the DMR schedule.

  5. Explore an optimal distinct vendor-allocation process out of several available possibilities.

  6. Provide low-cost Trojan security aware solution.

  7. Minimize the design overhead of Trojan secured DSP IP core.

3.5.3 Formulation

To generate a low-cost, Trojan secured DMR schedule for a DSP application (given in the form of a C-code or CDFG) within the user-specified constraints, which accepts module library and PSO control parameters as inputs, the formulation is as follows:

where ATDMR and TEDMR indicate the total area and total execution delay of the DMR design respectively; Acons and Tcons indicate user-specified area and execution-delay constraints respectively.

On the basis of the DSP application type, the design solution Xi can be represented in different ways, such as the following:

where N(RD) indicates the number of resources of resource type RD, U indicates the unrolling factor of single-loop-based CDFG, Un indicates the unrolling factor of nth loop of n-times nested-loop-based CDFG and Mv indicates the vendor-allocation mode. The loop unrolling factor of both single and nested loops directly impacts the delay in a design, therefore the optimal design solution (Xi) depends on the unrolling factor. Mv is essential to provide distinctness in vendor allocation while designing the Trojan-secured DMR schedule. As the Trojan-secured DMR schedule designed using different vendor-allocation modes can have different design costs, an optimal design solution (Xi) also depends on Mv. There is a detailed discussion on different modes of vendor allocation in Section 3.6.3.2.

3.5.4 Models

On the basis of the hardware resource configuration, loop unrolling factor and vendor allocation mode, the total area and execution delay of a Trojan secured design is calculated. Thereafter, the implementation cost of the design is evaluated using the calculated area and delay of the design. (Note: area and delay have been considered as orthogonal design parameters for evaluating the design cost). In this section, we discuss the evaluation models of total design area, latency and design cost.

3.5.4.1 Design area evaluation model

Total design area consumed by a Trojan secured DSP IP core can be expressed by the following model (Sengupta et al., 2017c):

where indicates the area of resource type Ri corresponding to vendor type vj, indicates the number of instances of resource type Ri corresponding to vendor type vj used in the design. It is assumed there are 3PIP cores of n distinct vendors that are available in the module library, however 3PIP cores from a minimum of two different vendors are required to achieve distinctness. Here resource type Ri consists of functional resources (such as adder and multiplier), internal storage elements (latch, register), interconnecting units (multiplexer and de-multiplexer), and comparators (for error detection). Sengupta et al. (2017c) assessed the total design area with respect to a 90-nm CMOS-based technology node.

The solution design cost of a Trojan secured DSP IP core is estimated using the following function (Sengupta et al., 2017b):

The remaining variables are defined in Section 3.6.3. As the objective of a Trojan-secured design is to satisfy the user-provided design constraints as well as minimizing the design cost, a higher negative value of Cf(Xi) indicates a better design solution.

3.6 Design process of Trojan secured DSP IP core

In this section, we discuss the complete end-to-end design process of a Trojan secured DSP IP core. Each DSP IP core executes an algorithm or mathematical function during processing. These DSP IP cores could be realized as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) or SoC, which accepts appropriate inputs and, after executing the algorithm/function, produces the corresponding output (s). In the following, we discuss how to derive or generate a CDFG of a DSP IP core from its mathematical function. Next, we explain how to generate a DMR of a CDFG and finally we explain the process of generating a Trojan secured DSP IP core from the DMR CDFG through an illustrative example.

3.6.1 Deriving the CDFG of a DSP core

In this section, we discuss how to obtain the DFG/CDFG of some well-known transformation techniques used in DSP from the corresponding mathematical expressions (transfer functions) through examples. We demonstrate the process through three popular DSP core applications: the 8-point forward DCT function, the 8-point Decimation in Time (DIT) Discrete Fourier Transformation (DFT), and the FIR filter.

3.6.2 Generating the DMR of the CDFG

For designing a Trojan secured DSP IP core, we already discussed how to obtain the CDFG of a DSP core from its mathematical equation/transfer function or C-code. The next step is to construct the DMR of the application. In order to obtain the DMR CDFG, complete duplication of all the unrolled operations is performed. The unrolling factor is obtained from the candidate design solution Xi (explained earlier in Section 3.5.3). For example, the DMR of the FIR filter for unrolling factor 2 is shown in Figure 3.24, where UOG indicates operations of original unit and UDP indicates operations of the duplicate unit.

Figure 3.24 DMR CDFG of the FIR benchmark for unrolling factor 2

3.6.3 Trojan secured scheduling of DMR CDFG

After obtaining the DMR CDFG, the next step is to schedule all the operations of the original and duplication units simultaneously on the basis of the resource configuration. The resource configuration is obtained from the candidate design solution Xi. Once the scheduling of the DMR is performed, the next step is to allocate 3PIP cores imported from different vendors. In this context, four distinct vendor allocation rules, devised in Sengupta et al. (2017c) are used (discussed earlier in Section 3.4.1.2). As the same functional resources (3PIP cores) imported from different vendor have different area, delay and power, each vendor allocation mode has an impact on the final Trojan secured design. Hence, to obtain a low-cost Trojan secured DSP core, optimal hardware resource configuration, unrolling factor(s), and vendor allocation mode must be explored. In Sengupta et al. (2017c), this is obtained through a PSO-DSE approach (explained in the next paragraph).

Particle initialization

To explore a low-cost Trojan secured design for a loop-based DSP core (CDFG), each particle of the PSO process is encoded through hardware resource configuration, unrolling factor(s), and vendor allocation mode. Particle movement

The fitness of each particle is calculated using (3.5).The particle position which has the highest fitness (lower cost value indicates higher fitness) among its positions so far is known as local best particle. Further, among all the local best particles the particle having highest fitness is known as global best particle. On the basis of the local and global best, the velocity of each particle is calculated. Each dimension (d) of a particle velocity (Vdi) is updated using the following expression:

where V+di and Vdi are new and current velocity of the ith particle in the dth, dimension respectively; Rdi is the resource value of the ith particle in the dth dimension; Rdlbi is the local best position of the ith particle in the dth dimension; and Rdgb is the global best of the dth dimension; ω is the inertia weight, b1 and b2 are social and cognitive factors; r1 and r2 are random numbers between 0 and 1. On the basis of the updated velocity of a particle calculated in Eqn. 3.16, the updated particle position is calculated. The updated particle position can be determined as follows:

where R+di is the updated resource value of ith particle in dth dimension.

Velocity clamping

To control unwanted exploration drift of a particle, velocity clamping is required. Velocity clamping is required when the new velocity (V+di) of a particle crosses its maximum (+Vmaxdi) and minimum (−Vmaxdi) limits. Velocity clamping can be performed as follows:

In the above expression,

Terminating criteria

PSO searches for a low-cost hardware architecture design solution for DSP cores iteratively. In each iteration, it explores an equal or better solution in terms of design cost. However, this iterative searching process terminates on the basis of the following two conditions: (i) the number of iteration exceeds the maximum count (Imax); (ii) the global best remains unchanged for the maximum consecutive iteration count (δ). In Sengupta et al. (2017b), the used value of Imax and δ during the experimental setup is 100 and 10, respectively.

3.6.3.2 Vendor allocation procedure

As mentioned earlier, scheduling and hardware allocation are performed for the DMR CDFG on the basis of resource configuration and vendor allocation mode. For example for the DMR of the FIR filter, the hardware resources required to schedule are the adder, multiplier and comparator (shown in Figure 3.24) . Now to implement distinctness during hardware allocation, the same 3PIP cores (adders, multipliers and comparators) are imported from two different vendors. Let us assume the two different vendors are V1 and V2; the multiplier and adder imported from V1 have area = 2468 au and 2034 au, latency = 10,000 ns and 265 ns, respectively; while the multiplier and adder imported from V2 have area = 2464 au and 2032 au, latency = 11,000 ns and 270 ns, respectively (Note: the values are used based on 90 nm technology scale; assuming 1 au = 1 transistor; ns = nanosecond).

Now consider the Trojan secured DMR CDFG of the FIR that is designed on the basis of the candidate solution Xi = 2(+), 2(*), 1(<), U = 2, Mv = 00 (illustrated in Figure 3.25(a)). This indicates that the DMR CDFG of the FIR filter is unrolled two times, scheduled based on two adders, two multipliers, and one comparator, and vendor hardware allocation is performed using mode ‘00’. The corresponding execution delay and area of the design is: TEDMR = 45,080 ns and ATDMR = 13,064 au. As shown in Figure 3.25(a), based on the vendor allocation rule in mode 00 (all modes are explained in Section 3.4.1.2), operations of UOG are allocated to the vendor in an alternative way in a control step (CS). For example, opn.1 and opn.3 of UOG are allocated alternatively to hardware of V1 and V2 in control step 1. Further, opn.1′ and opn.3′ of UDP are allocated to hardware of V2 and V1, respectively.

Figure 3.25(a) Scheduling and binding of the FIR for Xi = 2(+), 2(*), 2(<), U = 2, I = 4 based on vendor allocation mode Mv = 00; TEDMR = 45,080 ns and ATDMR = 13,064 au

If the same DMR CDFG of the FIR filter is designed based on the candidate solution Xi = 2(+), 2(*), 1(<), U = 2, Mv = 01 (illustrated in Figure 3.25(b)), the corresponding execution delay and area of the design are TEDMR = 43,080 ns and ATDMR = 17,996 au. As shown in Figure 3.25(b), based on the vendor allocation rule in mode 01, all operations of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 and all operations of UDP are allocated to the hardware of V2.

If the same DMR CDFG of the FIR filter is designed based on candidate solution Xi = 2(+), 2(*), 1(<), U = 2, Mv = 10 (illustrated in Figure 3.25(c)), the corresponding execution delay and area of the design is: TEDMR = ’45,080 ns and ATDMR = ’13,064 au. As shown in Figure 3.25(c) based on vendor allocation rule in mode 10, all the critical path operations, that is, opn.1, opn.2, and opn.4 of UOG (marked in a dotted circle) are allocated to the hardware of V1 and all non-critical path operations, that is, opn.3, opn.5, and opn.6 of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V2. The hardware of the distinct vendor is allocated in UDP.

If the same DMR CDFG of the FIR filter is designed based on candidate solution Xi = 2(+), 2(*), 1(<), U = 2, Mv = 11 (illustrated in Figure 3.25(d)), the corresponding execution delay and area of the design are TEDMR = 45,070 ns and ATDMR = 15,096 au. As shown in Figure 3.25(d) based on vendor allocation rule in mode 11, alternate vendor allocation is performed to the operations belonging to subsequent unrolled loop iterations, for example all operations of the first unrolled loop, that is, opn.1, opn.2, opn.5, and opn.6 of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V1 and all operations of the second unrolled loop, that is, opn.3, and opn.4 of UOG are allocated to the hardware of V2. 3.7 Analysis of case studies/test cases

In this section, we analyze and compare four different Trojan security approaches for DSP cores that are available in the literature in terms of their security and design cost. This section is divided into four sub-sections: (i) DSP core applications and system setup, (ii) security analysis of Sengupta et al. (2017b), (iii) design cost analysis of Sengupta et al. (2017a), Rajendran et al. (2013) and Sengupta et al. (2017c) (iv) comparative study among them.

3.7.1 DSP applications and system setup for the case studies

Results of approaches HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013), LC-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017a), TL-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017b) and NL-TS (Sengupta et al., 2017c) reported in the literature were based on the implementation carried out in Java 8 and executed on Windows platform with Intel Core i53210M CPU, 4GB DDR3 primary memory, and processor frequency of 3.20 GHz. The design parameters were evaluated with respect to 90 nm CMOS-based technology node. The design cost of Trojan secured DSP core is calculated based on (3.5) where w1 and w2= 0.5. The design area is calculated based on (3.1), design latency for single-loop CDFG is calculated based on Eqn. 3.3 and nested-loop CDFG and non-loop CDFG is calculated based on Eqn. 3.4. During the PSO-DSE approach, each design solution is run 15 times to obtain low-cost design solution. Further, the optimal PSO control parameters are set as follows: ω = linearly decreasing between 0.9 and 0.1; b1 and b2 =2; r1 and r2 = 1; terminating criterion Imax = 100 and δ = 10 (Sengupta et al., 2017b). (Note: all the variables are defined in Section 3.6.3).

3.7.2 Security analysis

Authors on TL-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017b) presented security analysis to show the robustness of their approach. The number of vulnerabilities detected by this approach is proportional to its robustness. In the design flow of an SoC, each 3PIP core used is considered as potentially untrustworthy. The number of 3PIP cores used in a design is directly proportional to the number of operations in the DMR design. In Sengupta et al. (2017b) such vulnerable 3PIP cores are detected using their devised concept. Figure 3.26 shows the numbers of vulnerable 3PIP cores that are detected through this approach for different non-loop CDFG, single-loop CDFG, and nested-loop CDFG benchmarks. As it can be observed from Figure 3.26, the maximum numbers of vulnerable 3PIP cores are detected for the DHMC nested-loop CDFG.

Figure 3.26 Total number of vulnerable 3PIPs detected through TL-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017b)

3.7.3 Design cost analysis

3.7.3.1 Non-loop CDFG DSP core

The design cost of a non-loop Trojan secured DSP core for the LC-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017a) and HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013) approaches is reported in Table 3.2. In HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013), no low-cost design solution is achieved while designing the Trojan secured DSP core. Moreover, no optimal vendor allocation is performed during this approach. On the other hand, in LC-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017a), a low-cost design solution is explored through a BFOA-based DSE approach. Moreover, out of the two devised vendor allocation modes (Mv = 0 or 1), the optimal vendor allocation mode is also explored. For this reason, Sengupta et al. (2017a) achieve lower design cost than Rajendran et al. (2013). The design cost of less than zero indicates it satisfies the user-provided design parameter constraints such as area, delay, and power.

Table 3.2 Design cost analysis of LC-HLS (Sengupta et al., 2017a) and HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013) for non-loop CDFG

3.7.3.2 Single- and nested-loop CDFG DSP cores

The design cost of single- and nested-loop Trojan secured DSP cores for NL-TS (Sengupta et al., 2017c) and HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013) approaches is reported in Table 3.3, where FIR, FFT, and differential equation applications are single-loop CDFGs and auto-correlation filter and DHMC applications are nested-loop CDFGs. As is evident from the table, because of lack of optimization framework, the design cost for Trojan secured DSP core of HLS-ST approach is higher than that of Sengupta et al. (2017c). In the NL-TS approach, low-cost design solution, the optimal loop unrolling factor, and optimal vendor allocation mode (out of the four devised security rules) are explored through PSO-DSE. Owing to the PSO-driven multi-dimensional optimization framework, NL-TS (Sengupta et al., 2017c) achieves lower design cost than HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013). In Table 3.3, UF1 indicates the optimal unrolling factor for the outermost loop and UF2 indicates the optimal unrolling factor for the innermost loop for auto-correlation filter and DHMC applications, while U indicates the explored optimal loop unrolling factor for FIR, FFT, and differential equation applications.

Table 3.3 Design cost analysis of NL-TS (Sengupta et al., 2017c) and HLS-ST (Rajendran et al., 2013) for loop-based DSP cores (CDFGs)

3.7.4 Comparative perspectives

We now highlight some state-of-the-art approaches by providing a comparative perspective on them. To present a comparative perspective, design latency parameter has been used by the authors. The comparative analysis between LC-HLS and HLS-ST is presented for non-loop DSP cores (DFGs) and highlighted in Figure 3.27. It was observed that for almost all the reported DSP/multimedia applications, LC-HLS achieves lesser design latency than HLS-ST does, owing to optimal hardware configuration and vendor allocation mode. The comparative perspective between LC-HLS and HLS-ST in terms of design latency for single- and nested-loop DSP cores (CDFGs) is also highlighted in Figure 3.28. It was observed by authors that, for all the reported benchmarks, the NL-TS approach achieves lesser design latency than HLS-ST does, except for the auto-correlation filter and DHMC applications. The underlying reason was found out to be that for both the benchmarks, the hardware resource configuration used in HLS-ST is higher than that in NL-TS. However, this results in higher design area of HLS-ST than that of NL-TS. Thus overall, the final design cost of both these benchmarks is better in NL-TS than in HLS-ST as reported in Table 3.3.

Figure 3.27 Comparison between HLS-ST and LC-HLS in terms of design latency

Figure 3.28 Comparison between HLS-ST and NL-TS in terms of design latency

3.8 Conclusion

This chapter presents multiple Trojan security approaches, with emphasis on DSP IP cores. The mechanism mostly used to design a Trojan secured DSP IP core is the CED- or DMR-based approach. Authors have mentioned different types of vendor allocation techniques to achieve that. Rajendran et al. (2013) devised collusion prevention in addition to CED, while Sengupta et al. (2017a) devised a BFOA-driven low-cost Trojan secured design for non-loop DSP cores. Further, Sengupta et al. (2017c) devised a Trojan secured design for nested-loop DSP cores and multiple vendor allocation rules to obtain a PSO-driven low-cost DSP IP core. Finally, it can be observed that both Sengupta et al. (2017a) and Sengupta et al. (2017c) obtained better design solution in terms of design cost.

Chapter 4
IP core and integrated circuit protection using robust watermarking

This chapter discusses robust watermarking approaches for the ownership protection of hardware cores [a.k.a. intellectual property (IP) cores]. Watermarking ensures some additional attributes inserted in the hardware core such a way that it can be used to verify ownership of the hardware core when required. Robust watermarking approaches have been discussed as these are resilient to various attacks that happen in global supply chain for various reasons. The remaining chapter is structured as follows: Section 4.2 provides an overview on selected hardware/IP core watermarking approaches; Section 4.3 discusses design process of watermarked IP core; Section 4.4 analyses the hardware watermarking approaches on case studies/test cases; and finally, Section 4.5 draws the conclusion.

4.1 Introduction

A watermark is a secret mark implanted into an entity such as official documents, currency notes, postal stamps, audio/video files, etc., to protect ownership right of an owner. Usually, a watermark embedded into an entity is expected to preserve its quality and functionality. However, for the domains in which watermarking is applied such as audio/video, documents, etc., slight degradation of the quality is usually noticed. Given the advantages of a watermark, it may be considered an extremely useful tool for protecting hardware [e.g., digital signal processor (DSP) core] ownership as well. However, the prime difference from watermarking in other domains is zero tolerance toward modification of quality/functionality of the hardware design. This makes hardware watermarking challenging but extremely useful for protecting legal rights of an IP vendor/owner. It is widely acknowledged that complex consumer electronics (CE) system design relies heavily on DSP IP cores realized as system-on-chip (SoC). Thus, hardware watermarking plays an integral role in IP core protection of CE devices (Mohanty et al., 2017; Voyatzis and Pitas, 1999; Cox et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2013; Sengupta, 2017; Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011; Sengupta et al., 2013).

In the modern era of CE, use of DSP IP cores in global supply chains become an inexorable part of complex SoC design process. IP cores not only speedup the design productivity massively but also decreases the design period immensely. Importing these IP cores from third-party IP vendors by the system integrator or SoC designer has become a common industry practice. Previously, IP vendors have mainly focused on IP performance and IP functionality but have neglected IP security. As evidence it can be observed that in a typical IP design flow, measurement of performance and functionality is only included in the IP specification. However, prevailing usage of IP cores in SoC design process increases the rivalry between multiple IP core vendors, which invites security threats like IP core forgery, dishonest claim of ownership, etc., which can be tackled by hardware watermarking. Thus, the threat model can be defined as:

Threat model: The targeted threat models for watermark-based IP core protection mechanism are: (i) false claim of ownership, (ii) ownership conflict, and (iii) IP piracy/forgery in IP cores.

The designing process of an IP core involves many man-hours of research, investment, and substantiation; therefore, this effort must be protected. As IP core can be copied easily, IP piracy and ownership abuse is a rising security concern now. Hence, protecting the ownership of an original IP owner is very crucial. For example, after importing an IP core from a third-party IP vendor, a SoC integrator may claim himself as the original owner of the IP or may reuse the IP core without acknowledging the original IP owner. Thus, nullifying false claim of ownership or detecting the illegal misuse of an IP core is essential and complex for an original IP owner. One popular way to safeguard an IP core against aforementioned potential threats is embedding vendor signature in the IP core during its design process in the vendor house itself (Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2008; Koushanfar et al., 2005; Sengupta, 2016; Guajardo et al., 2008; Sengupta et al., 2017; Sengupta and Roy, 2017).

4.2 Selected watermarking approaches

This section discusses few selected watermarking mechanisms for IP core protection. Ziener and Teich (2008) devised an IP core watermarking methodology for field programmable gate array (FPGA) architecture. The IP owner signature as a watermark is embedded in the netlist and the bit-stream file of the IP core. The watermarking algorithm embeds the signature into the functional part of the IP core in such a way that it becomes challenging to remove the watermark without destroying the IP core. The signature is identified from the power supply pins of the watermarked FPGA. More specifically, the authors have devised a signature detection algorithm that decodes the watermark through voltage trace with high reliability. Additionally, two robustness enhancement algorithms are also devised so that the signature can be decoded correctly in the presence of significant noise. The overview of Ziener and Teich (2008) approach is shown in Figure 4.1. Two in-synthesis IP core watermarking methodology: a low-cost watermark and a costless watermark are possible (Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012). The vendor signature in the form of a watermark is embedded based on the ‘temporally free’ IP output slot. In low-cost watermarking approach, the watermark is characterized by a set of arbitrarily selected internal computation values of the IP which get transferred through a ‘temporally free’ output slot. In costless watermarking approach, the watermark uses dynamic transient outputs unit to drive selected data to the output ports when the slots are temporarily free which can be achieved by modifying the IP control. As high level synthesis (HLS) tools design a control unit using a finite state machine, therefore, the costless watermarking approach only influences the finite state machine of an IP core. The desired mathematic relations used to generate watermarked IP core can be validated using equality-checking tests of the ‘temporally free’ IP output slots. A watermark can be represented as (Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012):

where Mi(n) indicates ith sub-mark or mathematical function and Ci indicates the clock cycle number during which the sub-mark is sent to a ‘temporally free’ IP output port. Different DSP applications are used as the benchmark to embed this watermarking approach and the result is compared with the approach (Koushanfar et al., 2005) in terms of area and timing overhead. The overview of Le Gal and Bossuet (2012) approach is shown in Figure 4.2.

Figure 4.1 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Ziener and Teich (2008)

Figure 4.2 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Le Gal and Bossuet (2012)

Koushanfar et al. (2005) devised a dynamic watermarking process to shield a DSP IP core (Coussy et al., 2009). A set of design and timing constraints in the form of vendor watermark is embedded in the IP core. In this approach, a vendor’s signature is transformed into its equivalent binary form where each digit (0 or 1) indicates a watermarking constraint. More specifically, these watermarking constraints are embedded in register allocation and binding phase. This is achieved by adding additional edges in the equivalent colored interval graph (CIG) of the IP design. In a CIG, each node indicates a storage variable. The lifetime of a storage variable lies between the time it is created (value written into it) and the last use (value read from it). An edge between two nodes indicates there is an overlap in lifetime between those storage variables. The color of the node indicates the allocated register of that corresponding storage variable. Therefore, two storage variables whose lifetimes overlap cannot be stored in the same register. In other words, two nodes having a common edge between them cannot have same node color. Thus, adding additional edges in the CIG as watermarking constraints will force to execute two storage variables in two different registers. The overview of Koushanfar et al. (2005) approach is shown in Figure 4.3.

Figure 4.3 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Koushanfar et al. (2005)

Unlike dual variable (0 and 1) signature encoding rule in Koushanfar et al. (2005), Sengupta and Bhadauria (2016) devised a single phase multi-variable (combination of four) watermarking methodology to protect a reusable IP core. Each variable which carries a unique encoding rule (unknown to an attacker) adds an additional edge between two node pair in the CIG. Thus, Sengupta et al. (2016) embed a more robust and tamper-proof watermark compared with Koushanfar et al. (2005). Due to insertion of watermarking constraints in both Sengupta et al. (2016) and Koushanfar et al. (2005) area overhead may occur. Therefore, to minimize the design cost, a low-cost design solution is explored through particle swarm optimization in Sengupta et al. (2016). The embedded signature can be detected by inspecting the datapath hardware description language (HDL) file of the watermarked IP. As the encoding rules are hidden to an attacker, it is almost impossible to identify the watermarking constraints from its datapath. The overview of Sengupta et al. (2016) approach is shown in Figure 4.4.

Figure 4.4 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Sengupta et al. (2016)

Sengupta et al. (2018) devised a triple-phase watermarking process to secure a DSP IP core (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011). In this approach, vendor signature consists of 7-variables. The IP owner signature as watermarking constraints is embedded in three dissimilar (but interconnected) phases of HLS, i.e., scheduling phase, hardware allocation phase, and register allocation phase. Due to insertion of watermarking constraints in three different phases, vendor signature is distributed throughout the IP core design. Thus, complete removal or malicious alteration of the watermark is extremely difficult. Besides, embedding 7-variable encoding makes this approach tremendously strong. Additionally, the watermark in scheduling phase is independent of the watermark in hardware allocation and register allocation phase. Similarly, the watermark in register allocation phase is independent of both scheduling and hardware allocation phase watermarks. Due to these benefits, the triple-phase watermarking approach is tremendously robust as well as tamper resistant. The embedded signature can be detected by inspecting the datapath and controller HDL file of the watermarked IP. As the watermarking constraints are well dispersed in the IP design and the encoding rules are hidden to an attacker, it is extremely difficult to identify the watermarking constraints from its datapath and controller by an adversary. The overview of Sengupta et al. (2018) approach is shown in Figure 4.5.

Figure 4.5 Top level diagram of watermarking process of Sengupta et al. (2018)

4.3 Design process of watermarked IP core/hardware

As mentioned earlier, IP/hardware watermarking is a process of embedding owner’s signature covertly in the design of an IP/hardware to proof his/her ownership in case of any conflict (Sengupta et al., 2017). In this section, we discuss problem formulation and design process of two (i.e., single-phase and triple-phase) IP core watermarking processes in detail. Both the approaches are demonstrated through a motivational example.

4.3.1 Problem formulation

Inputs: (i) DSP application, (ii) resource configuration, (iii) module library, and (iv) vendor signature.

Output: Watermarked IP core design.

Sengupta et al. (2016, 2018) accepted DSP application in the form of data flow graph (DFG), module library in the form of NanGate 15-nm technology (NanGate Open Cell Library, 2018) or 90-nm library/other library, and user-specified resource configuration (R). Here, R is represented as: N(X1), N(X2), …, N(XD), and N(XD) indicating the number of resources of type XD. Sengupta et al. (2016) proposed a vendor signature that contains four encoding variables used for generating watermarking constraints. These watermarking constraints are embedded in a single HLS phase of a DSP IP core design process. On the other hand, Sengupta et al. (2018) proposed a vendor signature that contains seven encoding variables. These watermarking constraints are embedded in three different HLS design phases of a DSP IP core design process. Figure 4.6 depicts the inputs and output of an IP core watermarking process.

Figure 4.6 Inputs and output for watermarked IP core

Target platform: The targeted platform for Sengupta et al. (2016, 2018) watermarking approach is any modern computer-aided design (CAD) tool. Both watermarking approaches generate the final watermarked DSP IP core design in HDL; therefore, any HDL-based CAD tool used for generating IP core can easily adopt these watermarking algorithms.

4.3.2 Design process of single-phase watermarked IP core/hardware

In this section, we describe the design of a watermarked DSP IP core/hardware (especially for DSP/multimedia applications).
