4.3.2.2 Watermarking process for DSP IP core

As an example, we have used single-phase watermarking approach presented in Sengupta et al. (2016) to demonstrate the design process. Watermark in DSP IP core can be embedded as additional design constraints in one of the HLS design phases. Sengupta et al. (2016) embed watermarking constraints in the register allocation phase of HLS. To embed additional constraints, a register allocation table is generated using the aid of CIG. In CIG, the nodes indicates the storage variables of the scheduled design, the edges indicates existence of overlapping of lifetime between two storage variables, and the color of the node indicates allocated register of that corresponding node. Therefore, if there is an edge between two storage variables (nodes) then the same register cannot be assigned between them. In other words, if there is an edge between two nodes, then the color of them must be different.

In Sengupta et al. (2016) and Koushanfar et al. (2005), watermarking constraints are added as supplementary edges between the nodes of a CIG. The color of the nodes are adjusted after embedding additional edges and the register allocation table of an IP core is generated from the final modified CIG. More specifically, inserting each edge as watermarking constraints, force two storage variables of a CIG to execute through distinct registers. Thus, embedding additional edges in a CIG affect the allocation of the register of a design. However, these additional edges should be derived from a vendor’s hidden signature. This mandates designer to design a strong signature encoding process. Sengupta et al. (2016) devised a multi-variable signature encoding scheme to embeds a robust watermark. Compared with the authors in Koushanfar et al. (2005), who have used two variables signature encoding scheme, a more robust and stronger signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta et al. (2016). The signature encoding scheme of Sengupta et al. (2016) is discussed in the rest of this section.

4.3.2.3 Signature encoding scheme

A four variables signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta et al. (2016) where each variable indicates an encoded watermarking constraint. More specifically, each decoded signature digit inserts an additional edge between two nodes of a CIG as a watermarking constraint. An IP core owner can select his desired signature using any random combination of four variables, i.e., ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’. The encoded rule of each variable is as follows:

  • ‘i’ = Add an additional edge between (prime, prime) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘I’ = Add an additional edge between (even, even) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘T’ = Add an additional edge between (odd, even) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘!’ = Add an additional edge between (0, any integer) node pair of CIG.

In Sengupta et al. (2016), as IP sellers signature is embedded based on multi-variable signature encoding scheme and distributed throughout the DSP design, it is harder for an adversary to detect and remove the complete watermark. Thus, provides significant robustness and stronger encoding.

4.3.2.4 Watermark embedding process for DSP IP core

In the previous sub-section, we have discussed the signature encoding rule using four variables. Here, we discuss how to embed an IP seller’s signature into an original (non-watermarked) IP design. As mentioned earlier, all the aforesaid encoding variables embed watermarking constraints in the register allocation phase of HLS; the phases of HLS appearing before register allocation phase, is described as the pre-processing steps of watermark. Therefore, watermark embedding process is divided into two parts, viz., pre-processing steps and watermark embedding steps. Detailed steps of the complete watermarking process (Sengupta et al., 2016) are as follows:

  • A. Pre-processing steps

    1. Accept an original/non-watermarked DSP application in the form of CDFG with resource configuration as input.

    2. Schedule the CDFG of DSP application based on the resource configuration (constraint).

    3. Assign storage variable for each operation of the scheduled CDFG.

    4. Construct the CIG to identify the minimal registers essential for register allocation.

    5. Generate the register allocation table from the constructed CIG.

    6. Sort storage variables in ascending order according to their number.

    7. Accept an n-digit vendor’s signature as a combination of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ variables.

  • B. Watermark embedding steps

    1. Extract the decoded meaning of each signature digit based on encoded rule of each variable.

    2. Construct a list of additional edge from the decoded value of vendor’s signature by traversing the sorted nodes.

    3. Insert those additional edges in the CIG (constructed in pre-processing step 4) one by one as watermarking constraints and adjust the CIG if required.

    4. After embedding all the additional edges in the CIG, modify the register allocation table (constructed in pre-processing step 5) based on the updated CIG.

After following the above steps, IP owner’s watermark gets embedded into the DSP IP core. The watermarking constraints are embedded into the register allocation phase of HLS. Each constraint forces two storage variables to be executed through a distinctive register. Thus, manipulates the register sharing which creates an impact on the final datapath of the IP core and its corresponding gate-level structure (netlist). Therefore, embedding this watermark retains the correctness and functionality of a DSP IP core.

4.3.2.5 Didactic example of single-phase watermarking process

In this sub-section, we demonstrate end-to-end single-phase watermark embedding process through a representative example. The CDFG of FIR-2 filter adopted from DSP Benchmark Suite (2018) shown in Figure 4.12.

Figure 4.11 is taken as input (according to step A.1). The accepted CDFG is then scheduled based on two adders and two multipliers (according to step A.2). Storage variables (V0–V30) are assigned to each operation of the scheduled DFG (according to step A.3). A CIG is constructed (according to step A.4) with 31 nodes, i.e., V0–V30 and eight registers, i.e., register purple (Reg_P), register dark_blue (Reg_DB), register light_blue (Reg_LB), register green (Reg_G), register yellow (Reg_Y), register red (Reg_R), register orange (Reg_O), and register black (Reg_B). The corresponding CIG is shown in Figure 4.12. The scheduled CDFG after performing storage variable assignment and register allocation is shown in Figure 4.13. The number of control steps (cs) required to schedule the FIR-2 CDFG is 9. The register allocation table corresponding to the constructed CIG (shown in Figure 4.12) is reported in Table 4.1 (according to step A.5). All the storage variables (V0–V30) are sorted in ascending order according to variable number and a list is generated (according to step A.6). As an example, a 14-digits vendor signature: ‘i I I T I TT I IT ! TTT’ is selected which is a combination of four aforementioned signature variables (according to step A.7). All the pre-processing steps to embed single-phase watermark is performed now. The next step is to decode the 14-digits signature, based on aforementioned encoding rules (according to step B.1). The vendor’s signatures and its corresponding decoded meaning are shown in Table 4.2. According to the decoded signature shown in Table 4.2, the list of additional edges are between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), (V2 and V8), (V1 and V4), (V1 and V6), (V2 and V10), (V2 and V12), (V1 and V8), (V0 and V1), (V1 and V10), (V1 and V12), and (V1 and V14) (according to step B.2). Although according to the vendor’s signature, there are 14 additional edges to be added in the CIG, however, by default eight edges (i.e., edge between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), (V2 and V8), (V1 and V4), (V1 and V6), and (V0 and V1)) are already present in the graph. Hence, the constraints for these eight constraints are satisfied by default. Therefore, the objective is to satisfy the other six remaining constraints (i.e., edge between nodes (V2 and V10), (V2 and V12), (V1 and V8), (V1 and V10), (V1 and V12), and (V1 and V14)) in the IP core design. It can be observed that edge between node (V2 and V12) forces storage variable V2 and V12 to be executed through distinct register, therefore node color of V2 and V12 must be different which is green (G) now (see Figure 4.12). Hence to accommodate this constraint, the allocated register for storage variable V2 (Reg_G) needs to swap with other storage variable of same control step. Scanning the storage variables from left to right, we can observe that swapping V2 with V0 is violating a constraint (due to edge between nodes V2 and V8), similarly, swapping V2 with V1 is violating a constraint (due to edge between nodes V1 and V12). However, swapping V2 with V3 does not violate any constraints; therefore, storage variable V2 is allocated to Reg_LB and storage variable V3 is allocated to Reg_G. Similarly, edge between nodes V1 and V14 forces storage variable V1 and V14 to be executed through distinct register which need swapping. Swapping V14 with V15 does not violate any constraints, therefore storage variable V14 is allocated to Reg_G (previously allocated to Reg_DB) and storage variable V15 is allocated to Reg_DB (previously allocated to Reg_G). (Note: If no storage other variable is found to swap with the conflicting storage variable, a new register should be added in the CIG and assigned to that conflicting storage variable.) After embedding all these additional edges in the CIG, the final modified graph (according to step B.3) is shown in Figure 4.14. The register allocation table corresponding to the modified CIG (shown in Figure 4.14) is reported in Table 4.3 (according to step B.3). The scheduled CDFG after modifying storage variable assignment and register allocation is shown in Figure 4.15. The corresponding multiplexing schemes of ‘Reg_G’, ‘Reg_DB’, and ‘Reg_LB’ before and after embedding watermark are shown in Tables 4.4(a), 4.4(b) and 4.4(c), respectively. The multiplexers and demultiplexers of ‘Reg_G’, ‘Reg_DB’, and ‘Reg_LB’ before embedding watermark are shown in Figures 4.16(a), 4.17(a), and 4.18(a), respectively. The corresponding multiplexer and demultiplexer of ‘Reg_G’, ‘Reg_DB’, and ‘Reg_LB’ after embedding watermark are shown in Figures 4.16(b), 4.17(b), and 4.18(b), respectively. The change in datapath after embedding watermark is marked as dotted lines to the mux inputs. For example, due to the swapping of storage variable V2 and V3 (due to the insertion of edge between nodes V1 and V12), input IN3 of Reg_G moved Reg_LB, similarly input IN4 of Reg_LB moved to Reg_G. The reflection of this alteration is also visible in the gate structure of the design. The partial gate structure of Mux of Reg_G before embedding watermark is shown in Figures 4.19(a) and (c). The corresponding gate structure of the same part of Mux of Reg_G after embedding watermark is shown in Figures 4.19(b) and (d).

4.3.3 Design process of triple-phase watermarked IP core/hardware

In this section, we describe the design process of another watermarked DSP IP core/hardware. We describe a more robust triple-phase watermarking approach presented in Sengupta et al. (2018) to design a DSP IP core. This approach does not protect non-HDL IP cores such as standard/pre-defined blocks or symbols that are present in the in-built library of a logic CAD tool. The triple-phase watermarking methodology protects the ownership of an IP core (especially for DSP/multimedia applications). In the process of embedding triple-phase watermark, it is presumed that same type of micro-IPs are available from at least two different third-party vendors to design a macro-IP core (which is a common practice in the industry).

Unlike single-phase watermarking approach (Sengupta et al., 2016), triple-phase watermarking approach (Sengupta et al., 2018) for DSP core embeds watermarking constraints in multiple phases of HLS. More specifically, triple-phase watermarking approach embeds watermarking constraints in the scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation phase of HLS. In addition to implanting watermarking constraints in three different phases of HLS, the signature encoding scheme consists of seven different variables, where each variable carries a unique encoding rule. Thus, triple-phase watermarking approach enhances the robustness and minimizes the chance of malicious alteration or removal of the signature. Furthermore, for an adversary, it is also difficult to recognize the synthesis phase and in what way watermark constraints are implanted in the design.

In Sengupta et al. (2018), watermarking constraints are embedded during scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation phases by modifying three information: (a) ‘Non-critical operations (μm > 0)’ timing table (μm = the mobility of an operation), (b) ‘Functional unit allocation’ table, and (c) ‘Register allocation’ table (adopted from Sengupta et al., 2016). As mentioned earlier, this watermarking approach has seven different variables, viz. ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’. Variable ‘γ’ modifies the timing table of ‘non-critical operations (μm > 0)’ thus embedding watermarking constraints during scheduling (first phase). Variables ‘α’ and ‘β’ modifies the ‘functional unit allocation’ table thus embedding watermarking constraints during hardware allocation (second phase). Finally, variables ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, ‘!’ modify the ‘register allocation’ table thus embedding watermarking constraints during register allocation (third phase). The signature encoding process of each variable is described below (Sengupta et al., 2018).

4.3.3.1 Signature encoding scheme

A seven variables signature encoding scheme is devised in Sengupta et al. (2018) where each variable embeds decoded watermarking constraint in any of the three phases (scheduling, hardware allocation, and register allocation) of synthesis process. More specifically, each decoded signature digit inserts a watermarking constraint by modifying any of the aforementioned tables. An IP owner can select his desired signature using any random combination of these seven variables, i.e., ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’. The encoded rule of each variable is as follows:

  • ‘γ’ = Move/shift a non-critical path’s operation with the highest mobility into immediate next control step (cs).

  • ‘α’ = In odd control steps only: Even operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 2 (U2) and odd operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 1 (U1).

  • ‘β’ = In even control steps only: Even operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 1 (U1) and odd operation must be allocated to the hardware of vendor type 2 (U2).

  • ‘i’ = Add an additional edge between (prime, prime) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘I’ = Add an additional edge between (even, even) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘T’ = Add an additional edge between (odd, even) node pair of CIG.

  • ‘!’ = Add an additional edge between (0, any integer) node pair of CIG.

In Sengupta et al. (2018), 3rd phase watermarking variables, i.e., ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’ are independent of both 1st phase watermarking variable, i.e., ‘γ’ and 2nd phase watermarking variables, i.e., ‘α’ and ‘β’. Similarly, watermarking variable of 1st phase is independent of both watermarking variables of 2nd and 3rd phase. These advantages make the triple-phase watermarking approach exceptionally robust and tamper tolerant for an adversary. However, watermarking variable of 2nd phase is dependent on watermarking variables of 1st phase. Therefore, watermarking constraints of 2nd phase may be affected due to alteration of 1st phase watermark which is a limitation of this approach. Nevertheless, as mentioned earlier, it is tremendously tough for an adversary to detect in which step of synthesis, the 1st phase watermark is implanted, and how. Moreover, if 1st phase watermark is tampered somehow by an attacker, then still 3rd phase watermarking constraints (which is independent of 1st- and 2nd-phase watermark) are capable of resolving the ownership conflict and identifying the real IP core owner. Thus, triple-phase watermark provides a strong tamper tolerant watermarked IP core design.

4.3.3.2 Watermark embedding process

In the previous sub-section, we have discussed encoding rule of seven variables of the triple-phase watermark. In this sub-section, we will discuss about how to embed a triple-phase watermark in a non-watermarked IP design. The triple-phase watermark embedding process is divided into four parts, i.e., pre-processing steps, 1st phase watermark embedding steps, 2nd phase watermark embedding steps, and 3rd phase watermark embedding steps. Detailed steps of this watermarking process are as follows (Sengupta et al., 2018):

  • A. Pre-processing steps

    1. Accept a non-watermarked DSP application as CDFG and schedule it based on user resource configuration.

    2. Perform functional unit allocation and register allocation.

    3. Construct the timing table for ‘non-critical operations (μm > 0),’ ‘functional unit allocation’ table, and ‘register allocation’ table from the non-watermarked IP core design.

    4. Sort the operations control stepwise based on their number in increasing order.

    5. Accept an n-digit vendor’s signature as a combination of ‘α’, ‘β’, ‘γ’, ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’ variables.

  • B. 1st phase watermark embedding steps

    1. For each occurrence of ‘γ’, shift an operation of the non-critical path into its very next control step while checking from control step 1 onward (without re-occurrence), if both of the following conditions satisfied:

      •  (i) Respective operation does not have any child operation in very next control step.

      • (ii) Shifting does not violate the hardware resource constraints.
        (Note: In case more than one operation is eligible to be shifted in the next control step, the operation with the highest mobility will be given the priority).

    2. Adjust the timing table of ‘non-critical operations (μm > 0)’ after embedding all ‘γ’ variables.

  • C. 2nd phase watermark embedding steps

    1. Accept the 1st phase watermark embedded scheduled design as input to embed 2nd phase watermark.

    2. For each occurrence of ‘α’ and/or ‘β’ variable in the vendor’s signature, re-allocation of functional unit needs to be performed according to the encoding rule of ‘α’ and ‘β’.

    3. Modify the ‘functional unit allocation’ table after embedding all ‘α’ and ‘β’ variables.

  • D. 3rd phase watermark embedding steps

    1. Accept the dual phase (1st and 2nd phase) watermark embedded design as input to embed 3rd phase watermark.

    2. Rest of the steps is similar to single-phase watermark embedding steps B.1–B.4 (refer Section 4.3.B).

4.3.3.3 Signature detection process

The signature detection process is a crucial and compulsory step to resolve ownership conflict. The inputs required to detect triple-phase watermark are: (a) decoded vendor signature, (b) application, and (c) watermarked IP core in the form of controller and datapath HDL. The triple-phase watermark can be achieved in three steps and each step verifies the presence of watermarking constraints of each phase. In the signature detection and verification process of phase 1 watermark, the control steps of modified operations are extracted from the decoded signature which is then compared with the controller HDL of the watermarked IP. To detect and verify the phase 2 watermark, the allocated hardware of the watermarked operations are extracted from the decoded signature which is then identified with the help of original application and its corresponding inputs. Then, the watermarked hardware information fetched from the decoded watermark is compared with the datapath HDL of the watermarked IP. Similarly, to detect and verify the phase 3 watermark, the shared inputs of each multiplexer should be fetched from the datapath HDL of the watermarked IP. It is then compared with the 3rd phase watermarking constraints extracted from the decoded signature. If all the constraints of decode signature are available in the watermarked IP core then the vendor who provided the decoded signature is awarded as the original owner of that IP core. The complete signature detection process of triple phase watermark is shown in Figure 4.26.

4.3.3.4 Didactic example of triple-phase watermarking process

In this sub-section, we demonstrate an end-to-end triple-phase IP core watermark embedding process through a representative example. The DFG of discrete wavelet transformation (DWT) benchmark shown in Figure 4.27 is taken as input and then scheduled using user given hardware configuration, i.e., three adders and three multipliers (according to step A.1). After that, the functional unit allocation of each operation and the register allocation of each storage variable (V0–V21) are performed (according to step A.2). In the triple-phase watermarking approach, two distinctive IP core vendors are employed to achieve better security. For example, in this case, out of three adders, two are acquired from vendor type 1 (A1) and one is acquired from vendor type 2 (A2), similarly, out of three multipliers, two are obtained from vendor type 1 (M1) and one is obtained from vendor type 2 (M2). The scheduled DFG after performing functional unit re-allocation and register re-allocation (before watermarking) is shown in Figure 4.28. The IP core design before embedding watermarking constraints uses list scheduling algorithm and random functional unit allocation. Register allocation for the same design (before watermark) is performed based on CIG (shown in Figure 4.29). A CIG is constructed with 22 nodes, i.e., V0–V21 and five registers, i.e., register red (R), register green (G), register blue (B), register yellow (Y), and register purple (P). The timing table for ‘non-critical operations,’ ‘functional unit allocation’ table, and ‘register allocation’ table of the non-watermarked design are generated as shown in Tables 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8, respectively (according to step A.3). All the operations are sorted control step wise in ascending order (according to step A.4). As an example, a 12-digits vendor signature: ‘ɣ ɣ ɑ β ɑ β β i I IT !’ is selected which is a combination of seven aforementioned signature variables (according to step A.5). All the pre-processing steps to embed single-phase watermark is complete now. The vendor’s signatures and its corresponding decoded meaning are shown in Table 4.9. In the 1st phase of the triple-phase watermark, all the ‘γ’ digits should be embedded. According to the encoding rule of ‘γ’, the first ‘γ’ digit of vendor’s signature moves operation (opn.) two from control step (cs) 1 to cs 2. For next ‘γ’ digit, the next operation which satisfies all the rules of B.1 is opn.9, because operations 3, 4, and 5 do not satisfy the rule mentioned in B.1(i), and opn.7 does not satisfy the rule mentioned in B.1(ii). Because between operations 8 and 9, opn.9 has higher mobility value, hence it is moved from cs 3 to cs 4. The modified timing table for ‘non-critical operations’ and its corresponding scheduled DFG is shown in Table 4.10 and Figure 4.30 (according to step B.2). In the 2nd phase of the triple-phase watermark, all the ‘α’ and ‘β’ digits should be embedded on the top of 1st phase watermarked design (according to step C.1). According to the encoding rule of ‘α’, the third digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.1 from M2 (multiplier obtained from vendor type 2) to M1 (multiplier obtained from vendor type 1). Similarly, according to the encoding rule of ‘β’, the sixth digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.4 from M2 to M1. (Note: no modification of hardware assignment is required for the fourth and fifth digit of the signature.) Similarly, the seventh digit of the signature modifies the hardware assignment of opn.5 from M1 to M2. The modified ‘functional unit allocation’ table and its corresponding scheduled DFG is shown in Table 4.11 and Figure 4.31 (according to step C.3). In the 3rd phase of the triple-phase watermark, hall the ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ digits should be embedded on the top of 1st and 2nd phase watermarked design (according to step D.1). According to the decoded signature shown in Table 4.9, the list of additional edges includes edges between nodes (V2 and V3), (V2 and V4), (V2 and V6), (V1 and V2), and (V0 and V1). Among these five edges except the edge between nodes (V2 and V6), all are already present in the constructed CIG. It can be observed that edge between node (V2 and V6) forces storage variable V2 and V6 to be executed through distinct register, therefore node color of V2 and V6 must be different which is blue (B) now (see Figure 4.29 and Table 4.8 marked in bold). Hence to accommodate this constraint, the allocated register for storage variable V6 (Reg_B) needs to be swapped with another storage variable in same control step. Swapping V6 with V5 does not violate any constraints; therefore, storage variable V6 is now allocated to Reg_R (previously allocated to Reg_B) and storage variable V5 is now allocated to Reg_B (previously allocated to Reg_R). After embedding the additional edges in the CIG, the final modified graph is shown in Figure 4.32. The modified register allocation table and its corresponding modified scheduled DFG containing watermark information is shown in Table 4.12 and Figure 4.33.

4.3.4 Desired properties of IP core watermark

Every ideal IP core watermark should satisfy following properties:

  •   (i) Low-design overhead: Embedding additional design constraints in the form of watermark may incur design overhead. However, an ideal IP core watermarking process should incur minimal design overhead as possible. The design overhead of both single- and triple-phase watermark discussed in this chapter in terms of design area and design latency is significantly low.

  •  (ii) Strong resiliency: An ideal IP core watermark should be resilient against removal attack. Therefore, the watermarking constraints should be implanted as a core part of an IP core design. Both single- and triple-phase watermarks contain multi-variable encoding rules where the watermarking constraints are dispersed all over the design (especially in triple-phase watermarking process). Therefore, complete removal of watermarking constraints from the entire IP core design is enormously difficult for an attacker. Thus, substantial resiliency against removal attack is achieved in both watermarking processes.

  • (iii) Strong tamper tolerance: An ideal IP core watermark should have strong tamper tolerance ability, i.e., partial removal should not impact the proof of ownership of an IP core. The watermarking constraints of single- and triple-phase presented in this chapter are distributed using multiple encoding variables. Moreover, in triple-phase watermarking process, watermark constraints are embedded in three different phases of HLS. Additionally, as mentioned earlier, 1st and 3rd phase of triple-phase watermark is independent of other two phases. Thus, strong tamper tolerance ability is achieved in both watermarking process.

  • (iv) Low-signature embedding and detection time: A robust signature may incur complex signature decoding and high-embedding time; therefore, the total runtime to generate a watermarked IP core may increase massively. An ideal IP core watermark should be embedded with lower embedding time. Additionally, signature detection process for a genuine vendor (who has the thorough information of encoding rule and the signature) should be quick. Due to unobvious encoding rules and robust signature embedding process, the embedding time of both single- and triple-phase watermark phase presented in this chapter is low. Furthermore, signature detection time for a genuine entity is also straightforward and speedy.

  •  (v) Correct functionality: In the process of embedding watermarking constraints, the correct functionality of an IP core must be preserved. Both single- and triple-phase watermarking processes phase presented in this chapter do not perform any alteration of IP core functionality while embedding watermarking constraints. Thus, functionality of an IP core does not get affected at all.

4.3.5 Possible cases of dishonest claim of IP core/hardware ownership and its resolution

This section presents the possible threat scenarios of the false claim of IP core ownership and its resolution using watermarking process presented in this chapter. Let us assume ‘Alice’ is an IP vendor, designed a watermarked IP core with her signature and sold it to ‘Bob.’ In that case, Bob can claim his IP core ownership using any three possible scenarios as discussed below (Koushanfar et al., 2005):

  •   (i) Claiming any arbitrary design information as the signature: After purchasing the watermarked IP core, Bob can reverse engineer the IP core and extract the complete information of the IP core design. Then, he may claim any random design information as his watermarking constraints, thus may claim his ownership of that IP core. Bob’s claim may valid for a single design, but will invalid for other watermarked design. Thus, Bob’s claim is not strong enough to prove his ownership. On the other hand, Alice’s watermarking constraints will be more meaningful and consistent for all watermarked design. In such scenario, the entity having more meaningful and consistent watermark will be awarded to the original owner of the IP core. The presented watermarking in this chapter is capable to resolve this threat.

  •  (ii) Inserting illegal signature: Bob can embed his own signature on the top of the watermarked design purchased from Alice and then claim for his IP ownership. In such scenario, Alice can prove her ownership easily because the watermarked design coming from Alice contents only Alice’s watermark; however, the watermarked design coming from Bob contains both Alice’s and Bob’s watermark. The presented watermarking in this chapter is also capable to resolve this threat.

  • (iii) Tampering/partial removing of original watermark: Though it is recommended that watermarking constraints should be an integral part of the design, still sometime it may be possible to identify some design information as the watermarking constraints of the design. In such case, Bob may perform some modification/alteration in the design to remove those watermarks. In such scenario, if the watermarking constraints are independent of each other and distributed throughout the design removal of the complete watermark is extremely difficult. Therefore, ownership of Alice can be proved. Additionally, sometimes tampering of embedded watermarking constraints may force to perform all the pre-synthesis steps from the beginning, which is a costly and time-consuming process. The presented watermarking in this chapter is also capable to resolve this threat.

4.4 Analysis on case studies

In this section, we discuss the triple-phase watermarking process (Sengupta et al., 2018) on case studies/test cases and compare it with a multiple-variable single-phase watermarking process (Sengupta et al., 2016) and a dual-variable single-phase watermarking process (Koushanfar et al., 2005). This section is divided into three sub-sections: (i) system setup, (ii) security analysis of triple-phase watermark, and (iii) design cost analysis of triple-phase watermark.

The baseline (original non-watermarked) design, dual-variable single-phase watermark design (Koushanfar et al., 2005), multi-variable single-phase watermark design (Sengupta et al., 2016), and triple-phase watermark design (Sengupta et al., 2018) were all implemented in Java 8 and executed on Windows platform with 4 GB DDR3 primary memory with processor frequency of 3.20 GHz 15-nm NanGate based technology scales (NanGate Open Cell Library, 2018) is employed to assess both watermarked design area and design latency. While calculating the design cost, equal weightage is provided to both design area and design latency.

4.4.1 Security analysis of triple-phase watermark for DSP IP cores

The possibility of generating the same solution before and after embedding watermark is calculated based on the probability of coincidence (Pc) metric. Lower Pc value indicates a higher strength of watermark. The metric partially adopted from Koushanfar et al. (2005) can be expressed below:

where, ‘w’ is the watermark strength/size, N(Ri) is the number of functional unit of type i, ‘D’ indicates the type of functional unit, and ‘c’ is the number of colors used in CIG before embedding watermark. Table 4.13 reports the comparative study of the probability of coincidence between triple-phase watermarking (Sengupta et al., 2016, 2018; Koushanfar et al., 2005) for signature size 80. It can be observed from Table 4.13 that the triple-phase approach achieves 1.4 × 1027 times lower Pc value in average compared with Sengupta et al. (2016) and Koushanfar et al. (2005) which indicates the higher robustness of watermark. Low Pc value is desirable which is achievable by incrementing the watermark size. However, too bigger size of watermarking constraints may result in register overhead, thereby increasing the design cost. According to Sengupta et al. (2016), the desirable maximum range of signature size should be 80.

Table 4.13 Comparison of probability of coincidence between, triple-phase (Sengupta et al., 2016), dual-variable (Koushanfar et al., 2005), and multi-variable (Sengupta et al., 2016) for W = 80

A watermark has higher tamper tolerance (Tt) ability if finding the correct signature from a watermarked design is highly complex and time-consuming. If the total number of possible signature combination is large then identifying the exact watermark for an attacker through brute-force search is time consuming and cost expending process. The total number of possible signature combinations for ‘v’ variable encoding and ‘w’ digits watermark can be calculated by the following expression:

It can be observed from Table 4.14 that the triple-phase approach achieves higher Tt value for all watermark size compared with Sengupta et al. (2016) and Koushanfar et al. 4.5 Conclusion

This chapter discussed in details about hardware watermarking of DSP application based IP cores used in CE devices. Several selected state-of-the-art watermarking approaches at different abstraction levels were reviewed. Two watermarking approaches used for DSP cores have been presented with greater details. These approaches implant watermark signature digits before RTL synthesis (during high-level synthesis). Embedding watermarking before RTL synthesis enables watermarking constraints to propagate to the lower levels of design. For example, how gate level design of a DSP core reflects the watermarking constraints that is embedded at its higher design level is explained and demonstrated with examples in this chapter. This chapter also lucidly explains the design flow of designing a watermarked DSP core with some industry standard examples of FIR filter, IIR low-pass Butterworth filter, etc. Details on security metrics were also presented and analyzed. We also demonstrate why hardware watermarking is an extremely useful tool for combating false claim of ownership, IP piracy, forgery, and other attacks.

Chapter 5
Symmetrical protection of DSP IP core and integrated circuits using fingerprinting and watermarking

This chapter discusses the use of watermarking and fingerprinting for symmetrical protection of DSP IP cores and integrated circuits. Symmetrical IP core protection is a mechanism in which both seller and buyers of an IP can have signature for double-proof of ownership and whereas significantly reducing false ownership claims. The chapter is structured as follows: Section 5.2 discusses the fundamentals of IP core protection with emphasis on symmetrical IP core protection techniques for DSP cores; Section 5.3 discusses the low-cost DSP core IP core protection; Section 5.4 explained that methodology with a motivational example. Section 5.5 discusses the results of that approach. The conclusion of this chapter is provided in Section 5.6.

5.1 Introduction

The designs of integrated circuits have evolved into greater sophistication than ever before with the revolution of implementation and application technology in consumer electronics industry. The usage of digital signal processing (DSP) intellectual property (IP) cores (Castillo et al., 2007) generated using architectural synthesis not only maintains a proper balance between time-to-market pressure and design productivity but additionally help in design cost reduction. High-level synthesis (HLS) (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011, 2013) is an automated design process that transforms an algorithmic/behavioral description of a digital circuit or IP into its corresponding register transfer level (RTL) digital hardware through numerous sub-processes like scheduling, hardware and register allocation, and binding (Mohanty, 2015). In the process of manufacturing an IP core, two entities are involved, viz. seller and buyer. An IP seller also known as IP vendor is the creator of an IP, whereas an IP buyer also known as IP user is the purchaser of an IP. However, to maintain a viable application of IP cores in composite SoC-based designs, protection of both the entities against threats is extremely crucial. Let us now discuss on the protection aspect of IP buyer and IP seller. In an IP core, an IP buyer may claim buyer privilege as a buyer so that the same IP copy should not be usable/accessible to his competitors in the market. This is possible when customized specifications of an IP core are obtained by an IP seller from an IP buyer, thus creating an exclusive one-to-one mapping between both parties. Embedding a unique buyer’s signature (known as buyer fingerprint) into an IP core design facilitates detection of unlawfully redistributed/resold duplicates of an IP core by a deceitful seller (Gang and Potkonjak, 2007). Likewise, an IP seller must protect his design from piracy and false claim of ownership before selling it to an IP buyer. Embedding a unique seller’s signature (known as seller watermark) into an IP core design protects an IP core from ownership abuse (Alkabani et al., 2007; Sengupta and Kundu, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2017, 2018; Kougianos et al., 2009; Maltoni et al., 2009; Roy et al., 2008; Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2008; Sengupta, 2016, 2017; Sengupta and Roy, 2017).

Therefore, symmetrical protection of DSP IP cores provides user right as well as nullifies IP ownership abuse. A thematic summary is highlighted in Figure 5.1. Significant investments are required in terms of man-power, time and cost to design, and verify an IP core; however, it can be cloned, modified, or resold easily by a rough entity. Therefore, both seller and buyer of IP designs want to nullify the possibilities of false claiming and illegal reselling of an IP core. Symmetrical protection can be achieved by implanting dual entity signature scheme in a DSP IP core during any of the design abstraction level. Standard IP protection methods (Yuan et al., 2006) such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, etc., are distributed, restricted in capacities, and insufficient in securing IP cores from buyer and seller viewpoint. Additionally, several signature embedding schemes in different multimedia applications, like image, text, video, and audio are also not appropriate to protect an IP core as it does not preserve the functionality and precision of a design in signature insertion. Thus, from the perspective of IP core protection, necessary action needs be taken to preserve the functionality and correctness of the design while embedding any signature.

Figure 5.1 Thematic overview of symmetrical IP core protection

5.1.1 Background on watermark and fingerprint

Watermark and fingerprint represents the signature of two distinct entities of a DSP reusable IP core to protect their corresponding ownership right. While fingerprint conveys the signature of an IP buyer, watermark is intended for an IP seller. An ideal signature for both cases must meet the below features:

  • It must be implanted as vital part of an IP design so that it must not be perceptible through traditional scanning.

  • It must be inimitable in nature so that the proof of ownership can be established easily.

  • For manifold signature implanting mechanism, each signature must be self-governing of each other.

  • It should be tamper tolerant so that partial removal of signature should not impact on the proof on ownership.

  • It should be resilient against attacks like reverse engineering.

  • Low embedding runtime.

  • Nominal latency and hardware overhead after implanting signatures.

  • Seamless signature detection process for an authentic owner with comprehensive cognizance of encoding rules (Koushanfar et al., 2005; Cox et al., 2007).

  • Must uphold logic correctness of an IP core post-implanting signatures.

5.1.2 Threat model

The ultimate goals of IP core security are:

  1. Buyer’s standpoint: detect unlawfully redistributed/resold copies in the market by a deceitful IP seller (Gang and Potkonjak, 2007).

  2. Seller’s standpoint: security against ownership exploitation (Yu and Zhu, 2011).

5.1.3 Benefits of protection at higher abstraction

Although DSP IP core protection can be provided in any of the design abstraction level, however, embedding buyer fingerprint and seller watermark architecture level (Mohanty et al., 2002, 2014) are beneficial as the signature constraints embedded in higher design abstraction level will automatically propagate in the lower design abstraction level; thus, it will protect the higher level as well as the lower level of the design. Additionally, symmetrical protection in higher level can be achieved in lesser signature embedding complexity while incurring lower design overhead. Roy and Sengupta (2017) presented a multi-variable fingerprinting and watermarking-based symmetrical IP core protection mechanism during multiple sub-steps of architectural synthesis/HLS process. Additionally, the approach incurs minimal design overhead while incorporating both signature constraints.

5.2 Fundamentals of IP core protection

This chapter discusses fundamentals of different reusable IP core protection mechanisms (shown in Figure 5.2) with emphasis on higher design abstraction level-based IP core protections that are available in the literature and how they are different when compared with symmetrical IP core protection. Reusable IP core protection mechanism can be classified into two parts: (a) non-symmetric approach and (b) symmetric approach.

Figure 5.2 Classification and corresponding works on IP core protection

5.2.1 Overview on non-symmetric IP core protection techniques

According to the literature, non-symmetric IP core protection techniques mainly provide protection from a seller’s perspective. It can be performed in three different techniques: (i) hardware obfuscation, (ii) computational forensic engineering (CFE), and (iii) watermark.

  1. Hardware obfuscation: Obfuscation is the process of transforming an original application or design into its functionally equivalent form to make the reverse engineering process significantly more challenging (Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009). It can protect an IP core either by obscuring the IP design/code, known as structural obfuscation (Hada, 2000; Sengupta et al., 2017) or by generating a locked netlist (Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009). A person who has the proper knowledge of the design of the correct key combination can only use it. In other words, structural obfuscation hides the functionality of an IP core whereas functional obfuscation hides the implementation of an IP core.

  2. Computational forensic engineering: Computational forensic engineering (CFE) is a signature-free driven process which can be performed in three steps, feature collection, feature extraction, and IP validation (Sengupta and Kachave, 2018). It tries to identify a list of features that can be used to identify an IP core uniquely (Wong et al., 2004). In case of ownership conflict, these features can be used to recognize the real owner of the IP core.

  3. Watermark: IP protection of a single entity (for IP seller only) can be achieved by embedding a seller watermark in to the IP core design. Watermark can be inserted either at lower design abstraction level (Ziener and Teich, 2006, 2008; Nie et al., 2013) or at higher design abstraction level (Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016; Koushanfar et al., 2005; Hong and Potkonjak, 1999; Le Gal and Bossuet, 2012; Sengupta et al., 2016). Watermark at lower design level can be detected from the power supply pins of field programmable gate array (FPGA) (Ziener and Teich, 2006), or from the bit-stream of the IP core design (Nie et al., 2013), or by tracing the voltage (Ziener and Teich, 2008), etc. On the other hand, watermark at higher design level be identified from the datapath and/or the control path of the IP design.

5.2.2 Overview on symmetric IP core protection techniques

The main goal of symmetrical IP core protection is to generating unique one to one mapped IP core between IP user and IP seller. From the seller side, it will not only protect the ownership of the IP seller but also he can identify the traitors among the list of IP buyers. If all the buyers get identical IP from the seller and one of them may unlawfully redistribute it identifying the actual dishonest buyer will become insurmountable (Gang and Potkonjak, 2007). There are only two approaches in the literature which have presented symmetrical IP core protection techniques. In the approach presented in Lach et al. (2001), a hidden encrypted mark is embedded into the physical layout of a digital circuit when it is placed and routed onto the FPGA. This mark uniquely identifies both the source of the circuit and original recipient of the circuit, which is also difficult to remove. Thus, the approach provides protection for both the entities (IP buyer and IP seller) but in lower design abstraction level, i.e. layout level, not in higher design abstraction level. On the other hand, the approach presented in Roy and Sengupta (2017) provides symmetrical protection during HLS. This approach embeds hidden buyer’s and seller’s signature constraints as multi-variable fingerprint and watermark during register allocation and scheduling stages of architectural synthesis. Signature embedding process is not time consuming and less complex; additionally, overhead generated due to additional constraints is significantly low. Furthermore, detail explanation of this approach is discussed in the next section.

5.3 Symmetrical IP core protection for DSP core

The symmetrical protection approach presented in Roy and Sengupta (2017) covertly inserts fingerprinting and watermarking constraints to protect the IP buyer as well as the IP seller during HLS. Based on the signature constraints provided by a buyer, an IP seller inserts buyer fingerprint with his own watermark; thus, safeguards the privileges of seller and buyer against popular IP threats like IP piracy, IP cloning, false claim of ownership, etc. (discussed in Section 5.1). Both buyer fingerprint and seller watermark taken as input from the respective entities are decoded to obtain the corresponding signature constraints. Firstly, the fingerprinting constraints are embedded in scheduling and register allocation phase within HLS (shown in Figure 5.3). Once the fingerprint implanted design is obtained; then, lastly the watermarking constraints are implanted in register allocation phase. Thus, a DSP IP core design has both fingerprinted and watermarked constraints, in addition to its normal design constraints (i.e. module library, resource configurations, etc.). The multiplexing process for each resource is generated to identify the resource interconnectivity, multiplexer size, and inputs/outputs of the watermarked and fingerprinted design. Using generated multiplexing scheme of each resource, the complete datapath and timing description of the control unit of the DSP IP core are developed. Thus, the final output of a symmetrically protected RTL design of an IP core is created as datapath and controller where each component is designed using hardware description language (HDL).

Figure 5.3 Symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores

Thereafter, these HDL files are fed into computer-aided design (CAD) software for RTL synthesis. It produces optimal gate level description of the respective design. This is then subsequently verified and transformed to corresponding bitstreams for the validation on a programmable hardware. After being validated, it is then fed into CAD tools for physical designing. Lastly, the GDS design file generated is sent to the fab.

5.3.1 Problem formulation

To determine an optimal symmetrically protected design solution for a particular data flow graph (DFG) within user specified area-delay constraints. It may be expressed as:

Minimize: Embedding cost (Atotal, Ltotal) for an optimal design solution (Xi), where (Xi) = N(R1), N(R2),…, N(RD); and N(RD) is the number of resource type RD.

Subject to: Atotal ≤ Acons and Ltotal ≤ Lcons to symmetrically protect an IP core, where Atotal and Ltotal are total area and latency of the symmetrically protected design and Acons and Lcons are user provided area and latency constraints respectively.

Total design area (Atotal) consumed by a symmetrically protected reusable IP core is formulated by the following model (Roy and Sengupta, 2017):

Total design area is evaluated by adding total area of hardware resource units (like adder, subtractor, multiplier, etc.), interconnecting units (such as multiplexer and de-multiplexer), and storage units (such as register). The total design area is evaluated for module library of 15-nm NanGate-based technology (NanGate, 2017).

The design cost is assessed by following metric (Roy and Sengupta, 2017):

5.3.5 Encoding rules of buyer fingerprint and seller watermark for DSP IP cores

Signatures for both parties can be embedded into the design during HLS as encoded additional constraints. Roy and Sengupta (2017) encoded fingerprinting and watermarking constraints are implanted covertly in scheduling and register allocation phases of DSP core design methodology (using HLS as backbone). More specifically, buyer fingerprint constraints in scheduling step are performed by forcing particular operations in a particular CS while resolving scheduling conflict. It is a very intelligent process of embedding buyer fingerprint, as it will incur zero hardware and may incur nominal latency overhead. Additionally, during register allocation, the fingerprinting and watermarking constraints are inserted with the notion of colored interval graph (CIG), where each node of the graph indicates storage variables of the design and the connecting edges indicates execution-time overlapping between conforming storage variables.

More explicitly, if there is execution-time overlap between two storage variables, then there will be an edge between those corresponding nodes. Therefore, injecting extra edges as encoded signature constraints will force storage variables of a CIG to implement using distinctive registers. Corresponding illustration of the approach devised in Roy and Sengupta (2017) is shown is Figure 5.4.

Figure 5.4 Design flow of symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores using fingerprint and watermark

Fingerprint encoding rules: The fingerprint encoding process devised in Roy and Sengupta (2017) embeds additional constraints in both scheduling and register allocation phases of DSP core design to enhance the signature strength. The definition of fingerprint encoding rule for each variable devised in Roy and Sengupta (2017) is as follows:

  • A = While resolving scheduling conflict force even operation in odd CS in scheduling phase.

  • B = While resolving scheduling conflict force odd operation in even CS in scheduling phase.

  • C = Add additional edge between node pair number (odd, odd) in the CIG.

The operations need to be sorted initially based on their operation number to apply the encoded fingerprinting constraints for ‘A’ and ‘B.’ Similarly, the storage variables need to be sorted before applying encoded fingerprinting constraints for ‘C’ (note: this encoded fingerprint embedding approach is demonstrated using a working application in the upcoming section). The robustness of buyer fingerprint is directly proportional with the signature strength. Roy and Sengupta (2017) are capable to accept and embed any big size fingerprint. As seen, this fingerprint embedding process includes of three different variables and each variable carries a distinctive encoding rule which un-invites significant overhead to the design with respect to area and latency while preserving robustness.

It is recommended that while selecting buyer fingerprint, the signature should have higher number of ‘A’ and ‘B’ digits than ‘C’ digits. The reason is that, the encoding of ‘A’ and ‘B’ digit are formulated in a way that it incurs nil hardware area and trivial latency overhead. This is conceivable as both the digits are injected while resolving operation scheduling conflict, i.e. fingerprint encoding rule acts as conflict resolver. On the contrary, too many ‘C’ digits in the signature may yield hardware overhead. Nonetheless, it is a key digit as it augments additional security layer by implanting the fingerprint constraint in another phase of HLS.

Watermark encoding rules: The watermark encoding mechanism used in Roy and Sengupta (2017) is adopted from (Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016). In (Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016), supplementary constraints for watermark are implanted in the register allocation by injecting the extra edges between the nodes of a CIG. Inserting extra edges mandates storage variables of a CIG to be implemented in distinctive registers. This methodology is flexible for injecting any number of extra edges in the register allocation step. The robustness of the watermark surges with the number of extra edges (i.e. signature magnitude) implanted. Although strength upsurges by increment in size of watermark signature, a bulky signature invites major design overhead. Consequently, it becomes obligatory to use a strong watermarking that delivers extensive protection with marginal design cost burden. As mentioned earlier, (Roy and Sengupta 2017) use a multi-variable watermark process from (Sengupta and Bhadauria 2016). The watermark generation mechanism in Sengupta and Bhadauria (2016) consist of four different variables. The seller can generate unique watermark through an arbitrary blend of these four variables. Each variable depicts a unique encoding rule injects an extra edge between two specific nodes. More explicitly, choice of node pair from CIG to insert an extra edge is well explained in the encoding scheme. The explanation of the encoding scheme has been described below:

  • i = Add additional edge between node pair number (prime, prime) in the CIG.

  • I = Add additional edge between node pair number (even, even) in the CIG.

  • T = Add additional edge between node pair number (odd, even) in the CIG.

  • ! = Add additional edge between node pair number (0, any integer) in the CIG.

Although ‘C’ digit of fingerprint and ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ digits of watermark, implant signature constraints in register allocation phase through CIG, nevertheless as their encoding rules are distinctive; therefore, the ensuing constraints will be totally dissimilar.

5.3.6 Multi-variable signature embedding process

The steps to achieve symmetrical IP protection by implanting fingerprint and watermark process are described in the rest of the section.

Process of implanting fingerprint

Broad steps:

  1. Choose buyer signature.

  2. Decode the signature to obtain equivalent fingerprinting constraints.

  3. Resolve operation conflict during scheduling to embed fingerprinting constraints.

  4. Construct the CIG based on assigning storage variables into register.

  5. Perform re-allocation of register if necessary while inserting additional edges in CIG based on fingerprinting constraints.

Detailed steps:

  1. Receive a preferred signature as random mixture of: ‘A,’ ‘B,’ and ‘C’ digits from buyer.

  2. Construct a sorted list of operations of the DFG in increasing order based on their operation number.

  3. Decode fingerprinting constraint corresponding to digits ‘A’ and ‘B’ that will help to resolve operation conflict during scheduling phase.

  4. Initiate DFG scheduling based on the given resource configuration.

  5. In case of operation conflict during scheduling, apply decoded fingerprint constraints (in step 3) to resolve the conflict. Note: When there are no fingerprinting constraints available, conflict is broken based on sorted ordering.

  6. Allocate storage variables in the partially fingerprinting constraints embedded scheduling and construct a CIG to identify the least number of registers compulsory for assignment.

  7. Sort the allocated storage variables in increasing order based on their number.

  8. Construct a timing table for register allocation based on the generated CIG.

  9. Generate a list of extra edge pairs conforming to ‘C’ digit(s) by traversing the sorted storage variables in step 7.

  10. Inject the extra edges in the CIG based on decoded fingerprint constraints and perform re-allocation of register if necessary.

After executing the aforesaid steps, a buyer fingerprint implanted IP design is produced. This buyer fingerprint implanted IP design acts as an input for implanting the seller watermark next.

Process of implanting watermark

Broad steps:

  1. Choose seller signature.

  2. Decode the signature to obtain equivalent watermarking constraints.

  3. Construct the CIG from the fingerprint constraints embedded scheduling.

  4. Perform re-allocation of register if necessary while inserting extra edges in CIG based on watermarking constraints.

Detailed steps:

  1. Accept fingerprint constraints implanted IP design as an input.

  2. Sort the allocated storage variables in increasing order based on their number.

  3. Admit a chosen signature as random blend of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’, and ‘!’ from seller where each character carries a unique value of additional edges to be inserted.

  4. Create a list of additional edge pairs corresponding to its encoded values by scanning the sorted nodes.

  5. Inject the extra edges in the CIG of fingerprint implanted design as watermark constraints.

  6. Alter the timing table design of register allocation based on generated watermark.

Post-execution of the aforesaid steps, an IP design with seller watermark is also produced. Therefore, the IP design contains signature of the dual entities.

5.3.7 Signature detection process

This process is obligatory for any encoded signature embedding scheme. As evident, in this phase, the implanted signature constraints are detected from an IP core. It is a crucial process to resolve ownership conflict. Signature detection presented in Roy and Sengupta (2017) is a two-step process:

  • Design inspection: Design inspection step collects the pertinent evidence in terms of specification, structural feature, etc., from a signature implanted IP core design. The objective is to rebuild the controller and the datapath.

  • Signature verification: Signature verification step performs validation of the signatures in the received IP core. The existences of signature constraints are corroborated in the controller and datapath design to determine the seller’s and buyer’s right.

5.3.8 Desirable properties of signature

The signatures embedded into the symmetrically protected IP core design contain the properties below:

  • Lower embedding cost: An ideal signature should incur marginal design overhead with respect to hardware area and latency. In Roy and Sengupta (2017), both fingerprint and watermark imposes low design overhead.

  • Resiliency against attacks: An ideal signature must be so strong and robust that it cannot be removed or tampered easily by an attacker. In Roy and Sengupta (2017), both fingerprint and watermark are equipped with strong protection. In the absence of comprehensive information of both encoding rules, it is extremely challenging to eliminate or meddle the fingerprint and watermark. Additionally, it is also difficult to identify in which HLS step the signatures are embedded. Besides, the signatures’ constraints are distributed all over the IP design which renders it more resistant against attacks.

  • Fault tolerance ability: An ideal signature must be distributed enough throughout the design so that partial removal of the signature constraints does not prevent the proof of ownership. As in Roy and Sengupta (2017), the signature scheme dispenses the constraints all over the design; therefore, ownership remains intact even after fractional elimination of the signature constraints.

  • Adaptability to modern CAD tool: An ideal signature must be easily adaptable into any modern CAD tool. In the approach (Roy and Sengupta, 2017), both the signature inserting procedure is well-suited to any CAD software. It can be incorporated effortlessly.

  • Lower time: An ideal signature creation process must not be very composite to generate a signature. In Roy and Sengupta (2017), the signature creation time for both fingerprint and watermark are significantly low. Additionally, for an authentic entity (who has the comprehensive cognizance of encoding rules), the signature detection methodology is straightforward.

5.4 Case study of symmetrical IP core protection

This section is divided into two subsections: the first subsection demonstrates the fingerprint formation and embedding process while next portion demonstrates the watermark formation and embedding scheme of Roy and Sengupta (2017). As stated earlier, fingerprint constraints of ‘A’ and ‘B’ have been implanted during scheduling phase by allocating particular operations to particular CS, during schedule conflict resolution mechanism. On the other hand, variable ‘C’ injects extra edges in register allocation phase by forcing specific storage variables to implement in distinctive registers. On the contrary, watermarking constraints (as a mix of ‘i’, ‘I’, ‘T’ and ‘!’) are implanted in the register allocation step by forcing specific storage variables to implement in diverse registers.

5.4.1 Demonstration of fingerprinting constraints embedding process

DFG of MESA benchmark is taken for demonstration purpose. Additionally, two adders and three multipliers are provided as resource configuration. The scheduled DFG of MESA benchmark using aforesaid resource configuration is shown in Figure 5.5. No signature constraint is embedded in that design. Corresponding tabular representation of the same scheduling is shown in Table 5.1. Now let us assume that a 7-digit buyer signature is provided as: ‘AAABACC’. The signature provided by the buyer is then deciphered. The signature and its respective deciphered constraints are depicted in Table 5.2. Deciphered constraints are attained using the fingerprint encoding rules described in Section 5.3.E. Now, the DFG of MESA benchmark needs is subjected to scheduling based on the resource configuration with fingerprinting constraints. In cs 1, four multiplication operations, viz., opn 1, opn 2, opn 3, and opn 4, are ready to be scheduled but only three multiplier units are present. This creates schedule operation conflict situation. This conflict can be resolved by inserting decoded fingerprint constraints in the scheduling phase. For instance, first digit ‘A’ forces even multiplication operation, i.e. opn 2 into odd CS, i.e. cs 1 while resolving scheduling conflict. Likewise, the next digit ‘A’ forces multiplication opn 4 in odd cs 1, while resolving the scheduling conflict. In case of the third digit ‘A’, no even operation is available to schedule; therefore, next multiplication is scheduled in cs 1 by merely picking the first operation from the sorted list. Hence, opn 1 is chosen and scheduled in cs 1. Similarly, for fourth digit ‘B’ odd operation, i.e. opn 5 is scheduled in even cs 2, while resolving scheduling conflict. Further even operation, i.e. opn 6 is scheduled in odd cs 3 for fingerprint encoding of digit ‘A’. This fingerprint constraint implanting mechanism in scheduling will operate up until all operation conflicts resolutions are done. The final schedule after embedding buyer fingerprint is shown in Table 5.3. It can be observed from Table 5.1 (no constraints embedded) and Table 5.3 (with fingerprint constraints) that both the scheduled design has same number of CS and same resource configuration. Consequently, the buyer fingerprint is implanted in the design with completely nil area and nil latency overhead, without changing the functionality.

Figure 5.5 Scheduled DFG of MESA benchmark using two adders and three multipliers without embedding any constraints

Table 5.2 Fingerprint and watermark and its corresponding decoded constraints

Table 5.3 Tabular representation of scheduled MESA benchmark using two adders and three multipliers post implanting fingerprint constraints

Subsequently, the storage variables (S1–S17) are allocated in the fingerprint embedded scheduling and its equivalent CIG is generated (shown in Figure 5.6). In the CIG of Figures 5.6 and 5.7, red node is indicated by R, yellow node by Y, blue node by B, and green node by G. Similar convention is applicable for Tables 5.4 and 5.5. The timing table of register allocation of the same CIG is shown in Table 5.4. Corresponding to two ‘C’ digits, two additional edges need to be inserted in the generated CIG as fingerprint constraints. Although two extra edges have to be inserted, but fortuitously an edge between S1, S3 is previously present in the CIG. Therefore, only one new edge between S1, S5 needs to be added. This indicates storage variable S1 and S5 must be executed through distinct register. According to Table 5.4, both S1 and S5 are executed through same register (Green), which indicates that modification in register allocation process is required. The revised timing table of register allocation is evident in Table 5.5, where S1 is executed through register green and S5 is executed through register red.

Figure 5.6 Colored interval graph before embedding any constraints as additional edge

Figure 5.7 Modified colored interval graph after embedding fingerprint and watermark constraints as extra edges

5.4.2 Demonstration of watermarking constraints embedding process

After implanting buyer fingerprinting constraints in the design, the fingerprint embedded design is now fed into the block for watermark insertion. For demo purpose, a 7-digit seller signature is chosen as: ‘i i i I I T !’. The signature and its equivalent deciphered constraints as extra edge between nodes in CIG are shown in Table 5.2. It can be observed using the CIG shown in Figure 5.6, only two extra edges ((S2, S7) and (S1, S4)) as constraints requires implanting in the CIG, because rest of the five edges are previously existing. Because of an extra edge injected between S1 and S4, both are forced to execute in distinctive registers. S2 and S7 are by default implemented using distinctive registers as apparent in Table 5.5. The final revised CIG is shown in Figure 5.7, and Table 5.6 depicts its corresponding timing table for register allocation. In Figure 5.7, dotted edge between S1 and S5 indicates fingerprint constraints and dotted edge between S2 and S7 indicates watermark constraints. It is evident that nil area and latency overhead are obtained after implanting watermark. Therefore, in case of MESA application, implanting both fingerprint and watermark attains completely nil area and latency design.

5.5 Analysis of case studies for DSP cores

Symmetrical IP core protection mechanism in Roy and Sengupta (2017) generates a low overhead strongly secured DSP IP core design. To validate the robustness and low overhead, following metrics are used by Roy and Sengupta (2017):

  • Implanting cost for both signatures in a design indicating design quality.

  • Area overhead with respect to resources and extra register needed while implanting fingerprint and watermark.

  • Time consumed to generate signature.

  • Strength of signature in terms of probability of coincidence.

  • Influence of large size fingerprint and watermark on design area, design delay, and implanting cost.

  • Scalability to deal with bigger size applications.

Therefore, the analysis/case study section is divided as follows: (i) result of symmetrical IP core protection approach (Roy et al., 2008) in context of design latency, design area, embedding cost, and strength of signature, and (ii) comparative study between Roy et al. (2008) and unsymmetrical IP core protection approach (Koushanfar et al., 2005). (Note: as no approach for symmetrical IP core protection exists for DSP core.)

The analysis of design latency, design area, and implanting cost of DSP cores for both fingerprint strength (F) and watermark strength (W) equal to 30 is shown in Table 5.7. For instance, for JPEG, the resultant latency, area, and embedding cost are 14.24 ps, 724.30 μm2, and 0.7349, respectively. (Note: module library includes resources corresponding to 15-nm technology scale extracted from NanGate (2017).) The cost of each solution is calculated based on Eq. (3).

It can be observed from Table 5.9 that for most of the benchmarks, the increment of design area is zero with the increment of fingerprint size. Cost overhead of Roy and Sengupta (2017) is maximum for ARF benchmark (which includes least possible number of parallel operations), while it is minimal for JPEG benchmark (which includes maximum number of parallel operations). The reason of the following: Roy and Sengupta (2017) embed fingerprint constraints, while resolving operation scheduling conflict which happens frequently for larger size benchmarks (having huge amount of parallel operations) operating within a given/explored resource constraint. Thus, Roy and Sengupta (2017) attain almost insignificant overhead for large size benchmarks, thus satisfying the scalability property.

5.6 Conclusion

This chapter presents a symmetrical IP core protection mechanism for DSP cores. This approach incurs very low overhead in the context of design latency, design area, and embedding cost compared with baseline design. Furthermore, the fingerprint and watermark encoding mechanisms discussed in this chapter are very strong in terms of security. In addition to producing marginal overhead and providing strong robustness, this approach has fault tolerance ability, lower signature embedding time, and adaptability to any CAD tool. The robustness of the symmetrical protection discussed in chapter can be improved by embedding signature constraints in other steps of HLS like resource binding, hardware allocation, etc. This would allow executing a relative investigative study between distinctive HLS phases to explore the well-matched step for signature implanting. Additionally, robustness can also be improved by adding more variables in the signature encoding process.
