Chapter 8
Functional obfuscation of DSP cores used in CE devices

The previous chapter detailed many approaches for structural obfuscation but we now move forward to another class of obfuscation called “functional obfuscation.” The use of either of the techniques is the choice of design engineers. This chapter presents several methods to thwart IP piracy and RE attacks through functional obfuscation. More specifically, we will discuss IP functional locking blocks (ILBs)-based logic obfuscation for DSP cores used in CE devices as hardware hardening technique (Sengupta et al., 2018). Moreover, a PSO-based DSE is performed to generate a low-overhead, functionally obfuscated (FO) design solution for DSP cores (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011, 2013). The rest of the chapter is organized as follows: Section 8.2 discusses different attack scenarios and threat model. Section 8.3 explains selected functional obfuscation techniques that are available in the literature. Section 8.4 discusses the design process of functional obfuscation for DSP IP cores used in CE devices. Section 8.5 presents the security analysis of functional obfuscation methodology for DSP IP core design. Section 8.6 discusses PSO-based optimization for FO design. Section 8.7 presents analysis on case studies/test cases.

8.1 Introduction

In the current IC supply chain model, multiple parties are involved to handle the increasing design complexity and cost. To avoid establishing and maintaining charge of a foundry with advanced fabrication facility, fabless semiconductor companies export their designed ICs (such as DSP cores) to another company having fabrication facility. Additionally, sometimes system integrator while designing a SoC, imports DSP IP cores from 3PIP vendors to meet the time-to-market requirement (Castillo et al., 2007). Thus, in this globalized business model for DSP cores, different countries and companies have different IP regulation policies and models. Therefore, in this scenario, chip designing process is susceptible to many serious IP security threats such as piracy, overbuilding, counterfeiting, RE, and insertion of hardware Trojan (Sengupta and Kundu, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2018b; Wong et al., 2004; Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007). This necessitates improvement in the chip-designing process to thwart these threats.

IP piracy is a process of illegal usage or selling of IP cores. An untrusted foundry, present in the design flow of an IP core, can steal a design, clone it illegally, and then resell it to an other entity. Thus, it can bypass a substantial amount of research and development process, workforce, money, and time invested by an original IP designer. Moreover, he/she can claim the ownership of that IP core (Koushanfar, 2012; Roy and Sengupta, 2017; Sengupta and Roy, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2018b). Similarly, an untrusted foundry may insert malicious logic in the form of hardware Trojan into the design to introduce malfunctioning of DSP IP cores (Sengupta et al., 2017b). Insertion of hardware Trojan can serve many benefits to the adversary based on its type. It can leak crucial information of a DSP IP core used in the defense system, damage the reputation of a well-established company, or degrade the performance of an IP core, etc. According to The Economic Impacts of Counterfeiting and Piracy (2017), the total fiscal revenue loss due to piracy and counterfeiting in 2013 for G20 nations was $96–130 billion which may rise to $199–270 billion in 2022. It is identified that 10% of the globally sold electronics products are counterfeited (Guajardo et al., 2008; Lao and Parhi, 2015).

RE of a DSP/IP core is a process of gaining the complete understanding of its functionality, design, and structure (Vijayakumar et al., 2017; Torrance and James, 2009; Sengupta et al., 2017a). Therefore, people can use RE process for both honest and fraudulent intentions. People can also use RE as a tool for education, research and development, and analysis and evaluation purpose of an existing product. In many countries, RE with honest intentions is considered as a legal process until it violates any design copyrights and patents issues (Biggerstaff, 1989). However, RE can also be used for dishonest intentions such as overbuilding, piracy, or counterfeiting a DSP/IP core design or inserting a hardware Trojan, which may lead to huge profit for an adversary. Therefore, RE for dishonest intentions incubates or invites these aforementioned potential threats. The possibility of RE attack during various stages of IC design, based on Rajendran et al. (2015), is shown in Figure 8.1.

Figure 8.1 Possibility of RE attack during various stages of IC design

One popular hardware hardening technique to counteract RE attack for DSP IP core is functional/logic obfuscation. Functional obfuscation (also known as logic encryption) inserts additional logic components known as key-components into the design to hide its functionality and implementation. These additional logic components accept key bits as input and produce the output based on these key values. Therefore, applying correct key combination will produce correct result while applying wrong keys will lead to exhibit an incorrect functionality of the design. Thus functional obfuscation thwarts RE process for fraudulent intentions.

8.2 Attack scenarios and threat model

This section discusses the possible attack scenarios and threat model of functional obfuscation.

8.2.1 Possible attack scenarios

To generate a locked netlist, key components or key-gates can be inserted anywhere in the circuit. However, incorrect placement of key components may invite several attacks. In this subsection, we discuss about the attacks related to placements of key components as well as other attacks.

  1. Isolated key-gates-based key-sensitization attack: A key-gate in an locked netlist is considered as isolated if there is no path between that key-gate and any other key-gates (Yasin et al., 2016). An attacker can easily sensitize the key value of an isolated key-gate. For example in Figure 8.2(a), there is no path between key-gates K1 and K2. Therefore, K1 and K2 are isolated key-gates. An attacker can sensitize the value of K1 as 0 to the output 1 (O1) by applying “100XXX” i/p pattern.

    Figure 8.2 (a) Isolated key gates K1 and K2; (b) run of key gates K1 and K2; and (c) concurrently mutable key gates K1 and K2

  2. Run of key-gates-based key-sensitization attack: A set of key-gates in an locked netlist is considered as run of key-gates if they are connected in a back-to-back fashion (Yasin et al., 2016). Few run of key-gate structures are vulnerable for locked netlist as it reduces the effort of an attacker to identify the correct key by increasing the possible correct key combinations. The reason is that some run of key-gate structure may be replaceable with a single key-gate, thus, diminishing security strength. For example, in Figure 8.2(b), K1 and K2 are connected back to back, thus forming a run of key-gates. In this case both “01” and “10” are correct key values. Moreover, K1 and K2 can be replaced by a single key-gate (XOR) with “1” as the correct key value.

  3. Mutable key-gates-based key-sensitization attack: If two or more key-gates converge but have no common path between them, sensitization may still occur (Yasin et al., 2016). Therefore, if key-gates K1 and K2 converge to another gate so that a specific key-bit can be obtained by muting the other, then both key-gates are called concurrently mutable key-gates. In this type of scenario, an attacker can easily trace the key value of K1 by muting K2. For example, in Figure 8.2(c), K1 and K2 converge at the gate G. The value of K1 can be sensitized to O1 by muting the effect of K2. Applying I6 = 0 in the input pattern will mute K2. Similarly, the value of K2 can be sensitized to O1 by muting the effect of K1. Applying I1 = 1 in the input pattern will mute K1.

  4. IP piracy and Trojan attack: If somehow the correct key combination of a locked netlist is identified by an attacker, he/she can easily discover the correct functionality of that netlist. This may enhance the possibility of IP piracy/counterfeit and Trojan insertion attacks. An attacker can either resell/redistribute the IP core illegally to make a profit or can insert a Trojan logic at safe places to introduce malfunctioning of an IP core.

  5. SAT attack: This attack is based on the following model:

    • An attacker may be present in an untrusted foundry whose objective is to identify the correct key value of the locked netlist.

    • The attacker has access to the GDSII (graphic data system) layout file of the locked netlist. He/she will try to perform RE to extract the locked netlist from the GDSII file. This is because fabrication is performed at the foundry containing layout details provided by the designer.

    • Attacker also has an activated functional IC bought from the open market, which can be used to identify the correct key value by providing a set of input patterns and inspecting their corresponding correct output as black box.

    The core of the SAT attack algorithm works iteratively by finding distinguishing input patterns (DIPs) that identify a subset of wrong key combinations that produce incorrect output, until the correct input output pair is obtained (Subramanyan et al., 2015; Xie and Srivastava, 2018). First, the SAT attack algorithm formulates a SAT formula and then the SAT solver generates an assignment to input variable (which is the distinguishing input pattern). Once the distinguishing input pattern is formed, it is then fed to the activated functional IC and correct output is observed. This distinguishing input/output pair can be used to eliminate the wrong key combinations, till no new one is found.

  6. Removal attack: In this attack, an adversary tries to remove all the key component from the locked netlist to generate an unlocked circuit. Removal attack identifies all the key components from a locked netlist and removes them. An attacker can then resell/redistribute the IP core illegally to make a profit or can insert a Trojan logic at safe places to introduce malfunctioning of the unlocked netlist.

8.2.2 Threat model

The functional obfuscation approach aims to protect an IC/IP core (such as a DSP core or combinational/sequential circuit) by generating a locked netlist of it, in order to enhance the complexity of RE attack. In this threat model, it is assumed that an adversary may be present in an untrusted foundry.

8.3 Selected functional obfuscation approaches

This section discusses few selected functional obfuscation-based IC/IP core protection mechanisms with emphasis on the functional obfuscation of DSP cores.

As mentioned earlier, functional obfuscation hides the implementation and functionality of a design by inserting key-components into it. The original circuit integrated with key-components is known as locked design. These key-components could be designed using FSM (Chakraborty and Bhunia, 2009), XOR/XNOR gates (Roy et al., 2008; Rajendran et al., 2015), AND/OR gates (Dupuis et al., 2014), lookup table (LUT) (Baumgarten et al., 2010), muxes (Wang et al., 2016; Zhang, 2016), ILBs (Sengupta et al., 2018), or a combination of these elements (Lee and Touba, 2015). All these key-components are inserted into the design in such a way that the correct functionality of the circuit will only depend on the correct key value.

Authors in Sengupta et al. (2018) propose ILBs to generate FO DSP cores. Among other functional obfuscation techniques available in the literature, this approach targets to generate a locked design for DSP cores. This approach inserts 8-bit key value-based ILB on each bit of output data. It can generate several different structures of ILBs (of similar area/delay) based on the key value. The ILBs are designed using various combinations of AND, NAND, NOT, XOR, and XNOR gates. Each ILB structure produces correct output for a unique key value. Moreover, these ILBs are capable to provide multi pair-wise security feature against sensitization attack and defense against SAT attack through a light-weight custom AES block integrated with the key bits. Thus, this approach ensures strong counter against the RE attack. Additionally, a PSO-driven DSE process is performed to explore optimal design architecture for obfuscated DSP cores. Therefore, it is capable to generate a low-cost, low-power, and secured FO netlist for DSP IP core. Further detailed explanation of this approach is discussed in the next section. Other popular functional obfuscation techniques (except Lao and Parhi (2015) which partially uses functional locking) available in the literature mostly target to generate a locked netlist for sequential or combination circuits but not DSP cores. Authors in Lao and Parhi (2015) perform both structural and functional obfuscations. Structural obfuscation is performed through folding-based transformation technique and functional obfuscation is achieved by using the correct initialization key. Incorrect initialization key value fails to enable the reconfigurator, resulting in activating either a meaningful but nonfunctional mode or a non-meaningful mode.

Authors in Chakraborty and Bhunia (2009) insert dummy states as key-components within the original states of the FSM of a design. FSM enters into an invalid state (obfuscation mode) with incorrect key value and will reach a valid state (normal mode) with correct key value. Desai et al. (2013) generated a locked design based on Code-Word, which is similar to an internally generated key sequence based on a specific state transition function. For incorrect key value, the FSM will deviate from the correct transition path and will resume normal transition with the correct key value. Both these approaches generate a locked design for sequential circuits.

In the combinational circuits, Roy et al. (2008) proposed the framework for generating locked design using XOR/XNOR gates for the first time. However, in this approach, key-components are inserted at random locations of the design which becomes vulnerable to key-sensitization and removal attacks. Additionally, random insertion of key-component may not always guarantee to produce incorrect output for the locked design on applying incorrect key value. Yasin et al. (2016) proposed selection algorithm for the key-component location which will maximize the Hamming distance between incorrect and correct output. Additionally, this approach provides pairwise security through prohibiting isolated key-gates, runs of key-gates, and mutable convergent key-gates to prevent key-sensitization attack. For example, in Figure 8.3(a), both the key-gates K1 and K2 are pairwise secure. Therefore, sensitizing K1 in the output bit is not possible without controlling the K2, and vice versa. This mandates to apply brute force on the key bits.

Figure 8.3 (a) Sensitization attack on K1 and K2 is not possible as K1 and K2 are pairwise secured and (b) ORF circuit based countermeasure against SAT based attack

One-way random functions (ORF) circuit based countermeasure against SAT based attack is shown in Figure 8.3(b) (Yasin et al., 2016). In this approach, a public AES has been used as ORF to defend SAT attack instead of PUF because PUF has following drawbacks: (1) it cannot add a significant number of clauses as it has a small circuit; and (2) it is susceptible to modeling attacks (Pappu et al., 2002). Removal attack on AES is handled by synthesizing the public AES along with the locked netlist, such that it changes the complete structure of the public AES. Therefore, it becomes difficult for an attacker to identify the AES block separately from the locked design.

Lee and Touba (2015) proposed key-components as a combination of XOR/XNOR gates and multiplexers to enhance the HD between incorrect and correct output. Baumgarten et al. (2010) used LUT as key-component to achieve the locked design. In this functional obfuscation approach, the complete design is subdivided into multiple fixed and reconfigurable parts, and then the LUTs are only used to implement reconfigurable parts. After fabrication, once the design is returned from the foundry, these key-controlled LUTs are changed to a different logic. Thus, misuse of a design by an untrusted foundry can be prevented.

Functional obfuscation is vulnerable to many attacks, such as key-component removal attack, key-sensitization attack (Yasin et al., 2016), Boolean SAT attack and hill-climbing search-based attack (Subramanyan et al., 2015), an approximate deobfuscation algorithm-based SAT attack (Kaveh et al., 2017), etc. Moreover, inserting additional key-components into a design incur power and area overhead resulting in a higher design cost.

8.4 Design of functionally obfuscated DSP core

As mentioned earlier, Sengupta et al.’s approach (2018) is the only one which protects a DSP IP core completely through functional obfuscation. To achieve the FO design, this approach inserts different ILBs as key-component in the netlist design of a DSP core. Additionally, to explore optimal design architecture, PSO-driven DSE is integrated with the functional obfuscation approach. In this section, we discuss formulation and low-cost functional obfuscation approach for DSP core (Sengupta et al., 2018).

8.4.1 Formulation

To generate a low-cost, low-power FO netlist for a DSP application (given in the form of a C-code or CDFG), which accepts module library and PSO control parameters as inputs.

8.4.2 Low-cost obfuscation method for DSP core

The design process of low-cost functional obfuscation for DSP core consists of two major phases, i.e., (1) designing functionally locked DSP core and (2) exploring low-cost design configuration through the PSO-DSE process. Both these phases perform iteratively until a globally optimal design configuration is explored. Figure 8.4 shows the two major phases, their corresponding steps, and the primary inputs to perform low-cost functional obfuscation. As shown in Figure 8.4, the primary inputs are a DSP application in the form of a C-code/CDFG, ILB design (based on each 8-bit key value), module library, and PSO control parameters (such as acceleration coefficient, inertia weight, swarm size, terminating criteria). In the process of PSO-DSE in HLS (detailed PSO-DSE framework is explained in Section 8.6), each iteration explores a design configuration and ILB structure, as a particle in the swarm. Based on this design configuration, a gate-level datapath structure (post-processing through standard HLS framework) of the input CDFG application is generated, which is then locked using ILB (where structures of some ILBs are decided on encrypted output from AES block and remaining without encryption. More details are provided in VC). This generates an FO design of the input DSP core. Then the total power and delay of the locked design are calculated to evaluate the design cost through a fitness function. Subsequently, particle positions are updated to explore a new fitter particle, and the complete process is repeated till the termination condition is met. Thus, the final particle position after meeting the terminating condition is used to generate a low-cost obfuscated design of a DSP core. Therefore, the final design architecture not only optimizes the total power, delay, and implementation cost but also minimizes the total gate count of the complete locked netlist, which includes total number of functional units, registers/latches, muxes/demuxes, and ILBs.

Figure 8.4 Framework for functional obfuscation of DSP cores

Lack of an optimization framework, for generating a locked netlist of DSP IP core, results in huge design overhead. This is because DSP cores are generally large in size and can be designed using multiple alternative hardware design solutions. Any random selection of design solution will lead to higher design overhead. In this approach (Sengupta et al., 2018), particles are encoded with both hardware resource configuration and ILB block insertion procedure to obtain the optimal locked design. Thus, the optimal obfuscated design solution in terms of the number of gate count, power consumption, and execution delay of the locked netlist is achieved through a PSO-DSE process. In the next three subsections, we discuss the overviews of ILBs, its security features, and insertion technique, respectively.

  1. Overview: IP core-locking blocks: This subsection explains a brief overview of IP core-locking block. ILBs are key components inserted into a nonobfuscated design to generate a FO design. Each ILB consists of 8-bit key value inserted into each bit of output data. ILBs are designed using the different combination of AND, NAND, NOT, XOR, and XNOR gates. However, structures of ILB depend on the key values. Innumerable different structures of ILBs with the same area are possible. Each of these ILBs generates correct output if a correct key value is provided. In Sengupta et al. (2018), a subset of key-bits are fed as input to an AES block and based on the encrypted output the ILB structures are configured. However, rest of the key-bits are fed directly to the ILBs. This is because it can help prevent SAT attack for DSP core (which is not possible now but as a proactive countermeasure for future). The ILBs are designed using various combination of AND, NAND, NOT, XOR, and XNOR gates and with multiple features (explained in the next subsection) to handle different attacks.

  2. Features: IP core-locking blocks: This subsection discusses the major security features of ILB design. As mentioned earlier, the ILBs are inserted in each output data bit of the gate structure of DSP IP core to generate a locked netlist. These ILB structures are designed mainly to avoid key-sensitization and removal attacks. Key-sensitization attack is a process of identifying the key value by applying different input patterns and checking their corresponding outputs (Yasin et al., 2016). Therefore, multiple features are considered while designing the ILBs to avoid any possible scenario of key-sensitization and removal attacks.

    Multi pair-wise security: All key-bits in a locked netlist are considered as multi pair-wise secure if an attacker cannot sensitize anyone of them to the output data bit without controlling or knowing the remaining all other key-bit values (Yasin et al., 2016). In a locked netlist, key-bits are inaccessible to an attacker, therefore, he/she cannot feed input to it. Thus, in multi pair-wise secure key-bits, identifying one key value of a key-bit depends on the key value of all remaining key-bits, therefore an attacker cannot crack any key value of the locked design. Different sample ILB structures of Sengupta et al. (2018) are shown in Figure 8.5. According to Figure 8.5, all the ILBs have 8 key-bits and all are multi pair-wise secure. In other words, to sensitize any key-bit of an ILB to the output, an attacker has to know or control the correct value of other seven key-bits. Therefore, to identify the correct value of other seven key-bits, an attacker has to apply brute-force attack. For example, to sensitize key-bit K1 of the ILB shown in Figure 8.5(a) to the output bit, an attacker has to control the other seven key-bits’ value, i.e., “0110000” which is challenging. Thus, multi pair-wise security feature enhances key-sensitization attack for the ILBs.

    Prohibiting key-gate isolation: To avoid key-sensitization attack, a locked netlist design should be prohibited from isolated key-gate. Different ILBs structures (shown in Figure 8.5) designed in Sengupta et al. (2018) consist of eight intertwined key-gates dependent on each other. This ensures no isolated key-gate is present in the ILBs. Thus, prohibiting isolated key-gate from the locked netlist enhances key-sensitization attack for the ILBs.

    Protection against run of key-gates: In Sengupta et al. (2018), the key-gates of ILBs are interlaced among each other, therefore, replacing all key-gates (eight input key-gates) with a single one is highly difficult.

    Nonmutable convergent key-gates: If two key-gates converge at some other gate in such a way that none of the key-bits can be muted, we can call these key-gates as nonmutable convergent key-gates (Yasin et al., 2016). As in Sengupta et al. (2018), all the ILBs consist of eight nonmutable key-bits, therefore, to sensitize one key-bit to the output remaining seven key-bits need to be muted, which is a complicated process. Thus, nonmutable key-gate placement in the locked netlist enhances key-sensitization attack for the ILBs.

    Figure 8.5 Different sample ILB structures designed based on key values (coming either from AES block or directly)

  3. Insertion: IP core-locking blocks: In the process of inserting ILBs, the first step is to generate a random integer number “μ” (through PSO-DSE process) such that:

    where TILB indicates the total number of ILB structures/templates available to insert in the design (e.g., Sengupta et al. (2018) used TILB = 4). Post HLS, after obtaining gate-level datapath structures, ILBs are inserted in each output data bit of functional unit based on the “μ” value to generate a locked netlist. In this process, same ILB is inserted “μ” times into the design and then after “μ” repetition next ILB from TILB is selected. This process will continue until all the output data bits of functional units are connected to ILBs. For instance, a gate-level structure of FIR benchmark (Mohanty, 2015), designed using 1 adder and 1 multiplier, is functionally obfuscated through “μ” = 2. The complete gate structure of FO (through ILBs) design is shown in Figure 8.6. As “μ” = 2 is used while inserting ILBs, ILB1 (shown in Figure 8.5(a)) is inserted for the first two output data bit of adder, and then ILB2 (shown in Figure 8.5(b)) is inserted for the next two output data bit, and so on until all the output data bit of adder and multiplier are locked through ILBs. Insertion of ILBs in the design can be performed randomly also to lock the design, but according to Sengupta et al. (2018), this may incur huge power and cost overhead with compromised security. On the contrary, in this approach different “μ” values are explored through power-delay trade-off, thus optimizing the overheads. Additionally, no output data bit remains unobfuscated (unlocked) in this approach, thus ensuring strong security.

    Figure 8.6 Obfuscated gate structure of 4-bit FIR designed using (1A, 1M, μ = 2), locked with 64-bit keys (I53–I84, I25–I52, I17–I20)

8.5 Security of functionally obfuscated DSP core design

In this section, we discuss different aspects of security for FO DSP core design. In the first subsection, we discuss about total possible key-space for a locked netlist through ILBs. In the second subsection, we discuss about the security analysis of designed ILBs from an attacker’s perspective. In the last subsection, we discuss about different possible attack scenarios and how the designed ILBs thwart them.

8.5.1 Keyspace

The number of possible key-space (Ks) for a locked netlist through ILBs can be represented using the following equation:

where “Ks” provides a measure of “Strength of Obfuscation,” “b” is the number of key-bits per ILB, “m” is the output bit-width of each functional unit, and “f” is the number of functional units used to design the datapath. For example, as shown in Figure 8.6, a 4-bit FIR is designed using one adder and one multiplier, which is locked using an 8-bit key-based ILBs. Thus, for this example, b = 8, m = 4, and f = 2. Therefore, using (8.2), the possible key-space of this locked netlist is determined as 2(8*4*2) = 1.8 * 1019.

8.5.2 Security analysis

In the security analysis of the locked netlist, it is assumed that an attacker has access to following three things:

  •   (i) A FO netlist

  •  (ii) Activated functional circuit (brought from the market)

  • (iii) Advance RE facility

In this scenario, through RE, an attacker can determine the total number of input key bits, he/she then searches in the key-space to identify the combination of key values. For instance, as shown in Figure 8.6, an attacker can determine that the design contains 64 numbers of input key-bits. He/she can perform brute force attack to identify a correct combination of 64 key values, which require testing of total 264 different combinations. During brute force attack, if we assume that 1 billion (109) keys can be applied per second to the locked netlist, it will take approximately 585 years to identify the correct key value.

8.5.3 Countermeasures against attacks

With the same assumptions that an attacker has access to three aforementioned things, in this section we will discuss countermeasures against key-sensitization attacks (Yasin et al., 2016), IP piracy attacks (Sengupta, 2016; Castillo et al., 2007), Trojan insertion (Sengupta, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2017b), SAT attacks (Subramanyan et al., 2015; Xie and Srivastava, 2018), and their countermeasures.

(1) Key-sensitization attack: In this attack, the attacker tries to determine/sensitize the correct key value by applying multiple input patterns. Key-sensitization attack will be easy for an attacker if key-gates are isolated, not pairwise secured, mutable, and connected in a back-to-back fashion. An attacker can apply a particular input pattern on the functional IC brought from the market and observe its corresponding, then apply the same input in the locked netlist with different key values to determine the correct one. Therefore, to prevent the key-sensitization attack placement of key-component is very important. Key-gates should be placed in a locked netlist in such a fashion that there is a dependency between key-gates. This ensures “prohibition of key isolation” and “multi pair-wise security” features (discussed in Section 8.2).

Multiple key-gates should not be connected in such a fashion that it can be replaceable using a single key-gate, which increases the number of valid keys in the key-space. This ensures “prohibition of run of key-gates.” Additionally, sensitization attack can also be performed if key-gates can be muted (discussed in Section 8.2.1). The ILBs are designed in such a way (with intertwining among gate structures for eight key inputs) that key-gates are multi pair-wise secure, no isolated key-gates are available in an ILB, no key-gates can be muted and enhances attack complexity to determine and replace run of key-gates using a single key. Thus, Sengupta et al.’s (2018) approach provides resilience against key-sensitization attacks.

(2) IP piracy and Trojan attack: The ILB-based functional obfuscation methodology hinders an attacker’s effort (as key-gates structures are heavily intertwined among themselves for 8-bit key inputs) to detect the correct key through RE. Only a valid combination of key-value can actuate the locked netlist.

(3) SAT attack: SAT solver is not scalable for multiplier circuit (Subramanyan et al., 2015; Finke, 2015; Chakraborty et al., 2017). Even for a small-size 3-bit multiplier, the equivalent CNF has 20 clauses (Finke, 2015). Generally, a DSP core comprises several large bit-size multipliers as an integral part. Therefore, DSP IP core designs are SAT-attack-resistant. However, authors in Sengupta et al. (2018) provide a proactive countermeasure (assuming efficient SAT attacks may be formulated for DSP cores in future), solution motivated from Yasin et al. (2016), where the subset of the key-bits are encrypted through a custom lightweight. AES block (not public design) with fixed secret key. Based on the encrypted key-bits, subset of ILBs are designed and inserted in the obfuscated netlist. This prevents an attacker from determining the correct key value if he/she does not have the key of AES block (shown in Figure 8.7). Sengupta et al. (2018) designed their own custom lightweight AES architecture comprising 429 logic elements. This AES block utilizes <1% of final design logic elements while implementation using Altera Quartus (2018) 13.0 version in Cyclone II FPGA (2018) after integration with the obfuscated netlist of the DSP core. Top-level design of custom AES block-integrated obfuscated 4-bit FIR and its corresponding gate structure implemented in Altera Quartus are shown in Figures 8.8 and 8.9, respectively. A partially extracted portion of AES-integrated obfuscated netlist file is shown in Figure 8.10, which demonstrates that individual logic components are indistinguishable. The simulation result of the FO FIR design is shown in Figure 8.11. Some examples of lightweight AES architectures available in the literature are Hamalainen et al. (2006) and Morioka and Satoh (2002). Post-synthesis result for FIR DSP core after integrating custom AES block is shown in Table 8.1. It is computationally infeasible to determine the inputs of AES from its output when the key is unknown. To prevent SAT attack, following steps are performed:

  •   (i) Designer synthesizes an AES block with a fixed secret key.

  •  (ii) Subsets of keys of functional obfuscation are encrypted through the AES block.

  • (iii) The outputs of the AES block (encrypted keys) are connected to few ILBs in the locked netlist depending on the number of keys are encrypted through AES.

  •  (iv) Based on the fixed secret key of the AES block and the input to AES, a designer can identify the output of AES and configures the ILBs accordingly by re-organizing the internal gate structure of ILB. (Note: The internal reorganization of the gate within ILB does not add any extra gate but only changes its configuration and connectivity.)

Therefore, the total area of ILB and design cost remain almost similar. For example, based on an encrypted output of key bits (first 8-bits, viz., 11001101) through AES block, a reconfigured ILB can be designed as shown in Figure 8.12. As a custom AES block is designed in Sengupta et al. (2018), its structure is unknown to an outsider. Therefore, distinguishing and removing AES block from the post-synthesized functionally locked gate design is not feasible. However, it is important to note that more the number of key inputs of functional obfuscation fed into the AES block, more is the number of available exhaustive options for reconfigurable ILBs. For example, if the number of key inputs of functional obfuscation fed through AES block is 8 bit, then the exhaustive reconfigurations possible is 28; while if it is 16 bits, the exhaustive reconfigurations possible is 216 = 65,536 (which is large). Further, the attack time grows exponentially which enhances the difficulty for an attacker in determining the correct key value. However, instead of using custom lightweight AES block, alternative lightweight solutions such as anti-SAT block (Xie and Srivastava, 2018) may also be used to prevent SAT attack. However, as mentioned in Yasin et al. (2017), detection and removal of the anti-SAT block could be possible through “signal probability skew (SPS)” attack.

Figure 8.12 Example of a reconfigured ILB based on a sample encrypted output (11001101….) from AES circuit. Shows only the first encrypted 8 keys acting as actual keys inputs to a ILB in design netlist

(4) ILB and AES removal attack: The removal of ILBs and AES from the locked netlist is difficult because:

  •  (i) The ILBs along with AES block inserted into the design for locking is resynthesized. This synthesis makes each component of the AES circuit along with the ILB-based locked netlist indistinguishable, which is not feasible to remove by an attacker. This is because of two reasons: (1) first, as mentioned earlier, the subset of ILB structures inserted in the netlist is reconfigured by the designer based on the AES-encrypted output corresponding to the secret key. Therefore, no fixed template of ILBs are available, the configuration of ILB depends on AES output which in turn depends on the secret key and input of the AES, resulting into several possible structures. Moreover, the number of possibilities also increase with the number of key-inputs fed to ILBs through AES. Therefore, knowing the structures of all the possible ILBs for an attacker is not practical in this scenario. (2) Second, since Sengupta et al. (2018) have designed their own custom lightweight AES architecture which is not publicly available, component of AES structure after post-synthesis become indistinguishable from the locked netlist of DSP core.

  • (ii) The sequencing of ILBs to generate a locked netlist of DSP core depends on the “μ” variable explored through PSO-DSE process. Therefore, identifying ILB configuration cannot be determined in advance.

8.6 Optimization engine for functional obfuscation of DSP cores

The ILB-based functional obfuscation approach for DSP cores (Sengupta et al., 2018) uses the PSO-DSE framework to achieve low-cost obfuscated netlist for DSP IP cores. The PSO-DSE process used in this approach comprises three subprocesses, viz., encoding and initialization of particle, evaluating the fitness of a particle, and generating fitter particle position.

8.6.1 Particle encoding

To optimize the obfuscated design cost, each particle is encoded through the array of available resource types and “μ” value. For example, ith encoded particle (Pi) in the particle population can be represented as Pi = {n(R1), n(R2), …, n(Rd), μ}, where n(Rd) indicates the number of resources of type Rd; and “d” is the total number of resource types available; “μ” is defined in (8.1). Based on the aforementioned encoding template, the first three particles (P1, P2, and P3) of the PSO-DSE process are initialized with the minimum, maximum, and mid-resource values, respectively, which can be represented as follows:

If the initial number of population is more than three, rest of the particles are initialized as follows:

In the above expression, “α” indicates a random integer number within the range of maximum and minimum resource values of resource type Rd.

8.6.2 Particle fitness

After performing particle encoding and particle initialization, the next process is to calculate the fitness of each particle to determine the fittest one. To calculate the fitness of each particle, a FO gate structure is generated based on that particle position. Then the total area/power consumption and delay of that obfuscated design are determined, based on which, the fitness of that particle is calculated using the following equation:

where Cf(Pi) indicates normalized weighted cost/fitness of a particle Pi, Ø1, and Ø2 denote user-provided weightage factor for area/power and delay components, respectively. The total power consumption and execution delay of a FO design are indicated through PFO and DFO, respectively. PmaxFO and DmaxFO indicate the maximum possible power (estimated as power consumption of maximum number of hardware resources available in the module library) and DmaxFO maximum possible delay (estimated as delay utilizing minimum number of hardware resources) of FO design, respectively.

8.6.3 Updating particle

After calculating the fitness of each particle of the swarm, the fittest particle (having the lowest cost value) till the current iteration known as “local best” is updated. Further, the global best is updated among all the local best particle positions. Based on the local and global best, each dimension (d) of a particle velocity () can be updated using following equation:

where and are the new and current velocity of ith particle in the dth dimension, respectively; is resource value of ith particle in dth dimension; is the local best position of ith particle in dth dimension; and is the global best of dth dimension; ω is the inertia weight, b1 and b2 are social and cognitive factors, respectively; r1 and r2 are random numbers between 0 and 1. The new particle position is generated based on the following expression:

where is the updated resource value of ith particle in dth dimension.

All the aforementioned three sub-processes of PSO-DSE execute iteratively to search for a low-cost obfuscated solution until any one of the following terminating criteria is met:

  •  (i) The global best is not updated for 10 consecutive iterations.

  • (ii) The number of iteration reached the user-defined maximum number of iteration limits.

After reaching the termination criteria, the current global best design solution is the final low-cost solution for functional obfuscated design among all the possible design solutions.

8.7 Analysis of case studies

As discussed earlier, excluding (Sengupta et al., 2018) robust functional obfuscation (RF-Ob), other approaches do not perform functional obfuscation for DSP IP cores. Thus, Sengupta et al. (2018) had re-implemented the functional obfuscation technique of Yasin et al. (2016)—robust functional locking (RFL)—and tested for DSP IP cores followed by performing comparative analysis in terms of security and design overhead. However, in Yasin et al. (2016), the target applications are the sequential and combinational circuits, available in ISCAS-85 benchmark circuits (Hansen et al., 1999). On the other hand, RF-Ob (Sengupta et al., 2018) target DSP cores, available in EXPRESS benchmark suites (DSP Benchmark Suite, 2017). A 15nm NanGate-based technology scales (Open Cell Library, 2017) was used to evaluate both power consumption and execution delay of a FO DSP IP core. The design cost is calculated using (8.3).

The analysis of case studies/test cases of DSP cores discussed in this chapter is divided into three sub-sections: (1) security analysis, (2) design overhead analysis, and (3) comparative analysis between Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016).

8.7.1 Security analysis

The term “strength of obfuscation (SoO)” is used as a metric of security to determine how difficult it is to reverse engineer an FO DSP IP design for an attacker. The SoO is calculated based on (8.2). The time required to determine the correct key combination is determined with the assumption of 1 billion key combinations were applied per second. The SoOs of both Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) for DSP cores are reported in Table 8.2. For example, in FIR benchmark, total 2.13 × 1096 different input combinations of key value are possible according to Sengupta et al. (2018) approach to decipher the FO netlist through the brute-force attack. Similarly, in Yasin et al. (2016) approach, total 2.23 × 1043 different combinations of key values are possible. Therefore, Sengupta et al. (2018) approach enhances SoO by a factor of 9.57 × 1052 compared to Yasin et al.’s (2016). The comparison of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) in terms of SoO is shown in Figure 8.13.

Table 8.2 Comparison of SoO and attack time between RF-Ob (Sengupta et al., 2018) and RFL (Yasin et al., 2016) for DSP cores

Figure 8.13 Comparison of strength of obfuscation for DSP cores

Table 8.2 also reports the time required to determine the correct key combination from a locked netlist of DSP IP core. For example, for the same benchmark (FIR benchmark), in Sengupta et al. (2018) approach, total 6.75 × 1079 years are required to identify the correct key combination through the brute-force attack. Similarly, in Yasin et al.’s (2016) approach, total 7.07 × 1026 years are required to identify the correct key combination. Therefore, Sengupta et al. (2018) approach enhances attack time by a factor of 9.57 × 1052 compared to Yasin et al.’s (2016) approach. The comparison of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. Further, AES block conjunction with ILBs is capable of increasing the SAT attack time exponentially for DSP IP cores. As mentioned in Sengupta et al. (2018), if the number of key inputs fed onto AES block increases linearly, the SAT attack time increases exponentially.

8.7.2 Overhead analysis

In this sub-section, we analyze the design overhead of RF-Ob (Sengupta et al., 2018) and RFL (Yasin et al., 2016) in terms of leakage power and cost due to the insertion of key components, compared to its equivalent nonobfuscated (baseline) design. The nonobfuscated design, also known as baseline design, indicates an unsecured, unlocked DSP IP core design where no key components are inserted. Table 8.3 reports the power consumption comparison of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) with baseline design and their corresponding overhead percentage. The power overhead occurs for both the functional obfuscation techniques due to insertion of key components. However, the overhead is comparatively lesser for Sengupta et al. (2018) than that of Yasin et al. (2016) because low-cost optimal DSP core design solution is explored for Sengupta et al. (2018) through PSO-DSE framework (Sengupta et al., 2017b). More explicitly, Yasin et al. (2016) incur higher power overhead due to the lack of a DSP architecture optimization framework. In Sengupta et al. (2018), not only power overhead is optimized through PSO-DSE process but also the total gate count after inserting ILBs, total execution delay, and the overhead design cost of the locked netlist are additionally optimized. Lack of an architecture optimization framework while generating an obfuscated DSP IP core incurs huge design overhead cost. The reason is because mostly DSP cores are huge in size and can be designed using various alternative design architectures. Selecting low-cost design architectural solution from a pool of alternatives necessitates integration of an optimization framework. In Sengupta et al. (2018), the low-cost design solution that optimizes the overall gate count of locked netlist (including the ILB blocks) is explored through PSO-DSE (discussed in detail earlier in Section 8.6).

Table 8.3 Comparison of power of RF-Ob (Sengupta et al., 2018) and RFL (Yasin et al., 2016) w.r.t. baseline for DSP cores

The average power overheads of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) for DSP core benchmarks are 31.30% and 48.08%, respectively, compared to a baseline design. Table 8.4 reports the design cost comparison of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) with baseline design and their corresponding overhead percentage. The average design cost overheads of Sengupta et al. (2018) and Yasin et al. (2016) for DSP benchmarks are 11.82% and 23.28%, respectively, compared to a baseline design. For both the cases, the reason for achieving lesser overhead is the same, as discussed before.

8.8 Conclusion

This chapter presents a low-cost, functional obfuscation mechanism for DSP IP core. This mechanism inserts reconfigured ILBs to lock a netlist of DSP IP core. Moreover, it integrates AES block to prevent SAT attack as a proactive countermeasure. Moreover, it was observed that Sengupta et al. (2018) yielded power reduction, design cost reduction, and SoO enhancement over other similar approaches. The research on functional obfuscation is still an open area and more research needs to be conducted for the protection of other hardware circuits such as combinational/sequential circuit benchmarks against SAT attacks. There are new attacks such as approximate SAT and signal probability skew that are being launched to nullify the effect of anti-SAT blocks used in conjunction with combinational/sequential circuit benchmarks. There is significant scope of work in the future in this direction.

Chapter 9
Obfuscation of JPEG CODEC IP core for CE devices

Joint Picture Export Group (JPEG) is the most commonly used image compression standard in the world. One cannot comprehend a CE system that does not process a JPEG. Without JPEG there is no smartphone photography, no social media. So, authors feel strongly that this important multimedia core “JPEG” needs to give well-deserving credit in terms of securing it when security/protection of “DSP core” has been a major focus of all the discussions in this book so far. The chapter is organized as follows: Section 9.2 provides an overview of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression process. Section 9.3 explains the design process of generating structurally obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core; Section 9.4 provides a detailed insight on the implementation process of obfuscated JPEG codec IP core in a CAD synthesis tool. Section 9.5 provides implementation and analysis of JPEG CODEC IP core as well as compressed images through the devised JPEG CODEC IP core.

9.1 Introduction

Most of the modern CE device comprises a dedicated lens or camera to capture and/or display digital images such as smartphone, tablets, scanner, laptop, smartwatch (Thavalengal and Corcoran, 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Corcoran and Andrae, 2014; Tang et al., 2016). Due to the enhancement of camera lenses, recording components, and displaying components, current digital imaging systems are capable of capturing and displaying high-resolution images (Corcoran et al., 2001; Andorko et al., 2011). As high-resolution images contain too much detailed information, they are large in size. Storing or transmitting these large size images is a critical issue for storage space and transmission bandwidth, respectively. Reducing the size of an image while storing and/or transferring is one of the popular and commercially successful techniques to address this crisis. JPEG standard formed in 1992 proposed DCT-based image compression. Image compressions are of two types: (1) lossy and (2) lossless. In lossy image compression, less important information of an image is discarded permanently (Mohanty et al., 2003; Mohanty, 1999). Camera (Corcoran et al., 2001; Andorko et al., 2011) in a smartphone, tablets, laptop, smartwatch, etc. uses lossy image compression (Hnesh and Demirel, 2016). In lossless image compression, no loss of information occurs. Camera in medical imaging (Bilgin and Marcellin, 1998), satellite imaging, forensic imaging, etc. uses lossless image compression (Li et al., 2017; Scarmana and McDougall, 2015).

DCT-based JPEG image compression is lossy by nature (Obukhov and Kharlamov, 2008). DCT segregates an image into multiple subparts or blocks based on the visual quality of the image and then converts each block to the frequency domain from spatial domain. It discards small high-frequency components; therefore, DCT-based JPEG image compression method is lossy.

Image compression and decompression (CODEC) is a major data-intensive/power-intensive computational process in the SoC of almost all smart CE devices. Therefore, in these CE products, JPEG-based CODEC is a vital function implemented through a dedicated IP core to perform the data-intensive/power-intensive computational process for image compression and decompression (Roy and Sengupta, 2018). The use of JPEG CODEC in the form of an IP core not only balances the trade-off between hardware area and processing speed but also enhances the design productivity. For these aforementioned advantages, JPEG CODEC IP core may face several threats such as IP piracy (Sengupta et al., 2018a), IP infringement (Sengupta and Roy, 2017a; Roy and Sengupta, 2017; Wong et al., 2004; Alkabani and Koushanfar, 2007), malicious Trojan insertion (Sengupta et al., 2017a), RE (Sengupta and Roy, 2017b; Lao and Parhi, 2015; Vijayakumar et al., 2017; Sengupta et al., 2017b), which therefore demands its protection (Sengupta, 2017). The motivation for designing a protected JPEG CODEC IP core is explained in the rest of the section.

Motivation: Standard JPEG CODEC design process is not capable (also does not aim) to obscure the functionality from an adversary by transforming the architecture. This does not deter RE process for an adversary. Successful RE attack enables an adversary (in the foundry) to identify the functionality of the design to counterfeit the netlist of the design and make several copies of it without the knowledge of the IP vendor/owner. Further, if an adversary is able to identify the functionality of the design from its functional structure, he/she can make a malicious modification (i.e., insert Trojan) into the design and create malfunctioning. Both these threats can be avoided if RE process is made harder for an adversary. This is possible by structurally obfuscating the JPEG CODEC design such that the functionality of it becomes unobvious to an adversary, i.e., architecture designed to be hidden to an adversary. This strongly hinders the RE process, thus thwarting the threats. Therefore, a JPEG CODEC is considered secure, if its architecture is not obvious, i.e., its functionality is not easily discoverable by inspecting its structure (Sengupta et al., 2018b). A thematic attack scenario of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core is shown in Figure 9.1.

Figure 9.1. A pictorial representation of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core use in different camera-based CE devices

JPEG CODEC is selected as a case study in this chapter because it is a very vital core widely used in several CE applications. Keeping in view the recent surge of IP counterfeits and hardware Trojan, it is essential to secure JPEG CODEC IP cores against RE threats as failing to do so may lead to serious functional failures (due to Trojan) and/or significant loss to CE industry (due to IP counterfeit). There has not been much discussion to addresses this concern; therefore, this chapter provides a detailed discussion on this crucial aspect.

9.2 Overview of JPEG compression and decompression

Typically, JPEG is a lossy image compression technique based on DCT. DCT is a Fourier-like transformation technique proposed by Ahmed et al. (1974). However, unlike Fourier transformation which represents a signal as a mixture of sine and cosine expansion, DCT represents a signal in only cosine expansion. Based on the image’s visual quality, DCT segregates it into multiple parts or spectral sub-bands. It converts an input image from the spatial domain to the frequency domain. The DCT is known for its high “energy compaction” property, meaning that the transformed signal can be easily analyzed using few low-frequency components. In simpler terms, DCT discards small high-frequency components, i.e., sharp transitions in intensity for grayscale images. Therefore, DCT-based image compression method is lossy, where less important information of an image is discarded. The process of discarding less important information is known as quantization. Image compression ratio with image quality can be controlled through quantization factor. The output bitstream is generated from the quantized coefficients through different encoding mechanisms and is then stored into a storage device. Reconstruction of the compressed image starts with decoding the bitstream data. De-quantization and inverse DCT (IDCT) is applied back to back on the decoded data to generate the decompressed image. The complete end-to-end flow of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression is shown in Figure 9.2 (Mohanty et al., 2003; Mohanty, 1999). Each step of JPEG image compression and decompression process is discussed in the rest of the section.

Figure 9.2. End-to-end flow of DCT-based JPEG compression and decompression process

9.2.1 DCT-based JPEG image compression process

9.2.1.1 Processing of the input image

In an 8-bit grayscale image, the pixel intensity ranges from [0–255], where 0 indicates pure black and 255 indicates pure white. Therefore, each grayscale image is represented using 256 shades of gray. To reduce the dynamic range (required in DCT processing), the midpoint of this range, i.e., 128 is subtracted from each pixel value of the image. Therefore, the modified data range, i.e., [−128, 127] is centered on zero. The generic 2D-DCT coefficient matrix (T) for a sample of N×N can be expressed as follows (DCT matrix, 2018):

where “N” is the size of the DCT matrix, “i” and “j” is the ith row, jth column component of the 2D-DCT matrix. In standard JPEG process, “N” is equal to 8 and i and j vary from 0 to 7. The 2D-DCT coefficient matrix for an 8 × 8 block is shown in Figure 9.3 (also explained in Chapter 3). According to Figure 9.3, all elements of the first row (i = 0) are equal to 1/√8 according to (9.1). As “T” is an orthogonal matrix, the inverse of “T” (i.e., T−1) is equal to the transpose of “T” (i.e., Ttrans).

Figure 9.3. 2D-DCT coefficient matrix

9.2.1.2 Perform DCT on input image

To perform DCT on the input image, the image should be subdivided into multiple nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks. Each block can be processed independently, therefore block-wise parallelism is possible for transformation, which is the key feature of 8 × 8 DCT. A generic 8 × 8 block “M” of input image matrix is shown in Figure 9.4, where mij express pixel intensity of ith row, jth column component of the “M” block. The DCT on the “M” block can be performed through following matrix multiplications:

Figure 9.4. Generic 8×8 block of input image

In the above expression, D is calculated as follows:

The “D” matrix (d11, d12, …, d88) transforms the rows of the “M” block. Further, “X” matrix (X11, X12, …, X88) transforms the columns of the “D” matrix. Thus, transforms both rows and columns of the “M” block. Therefore, “X” is the DCT block of “M” block.

9.2.1.3 Perform quantization

The transformed block “X” is now ready to compress through quantization. As human eye is not good in distinguishing the high-frequency brightness deviation in an image, a large amount of information reduction is possible from the high-frequency components of an image. This is achieved by dividing each element of transformed block “X” by the corresponding element of the quantization matrix (Q) and then rounding to the nearest integer. As a result, most of the high-frequency components are rounded to zero, which indicates discarding less important high-frequency components. Additionally, many of the remaining components become small positive or negative numbers, which take fewer bits to represent. The quantization matrix is designed in such a way that it provides more resolution to higher perceivable frequency components over lower perceivable frequency components. The designing process of standard quantization matrix (Q50) involves subjective experiment of human visual system. In the range of 1 to 100, standard quantization matrix provides quality level as 50. It thus provides a balance between image compression ratio and image quality. The standard quantization matrix is shown in Figure 9.5. However, image quality and compression ratio can vary by changing the quantization matrix. To obtain a quantization matrix with quality level greater than Q50, each element of Q50 should be multiplied with (100−quality level)/50 and then rounding to the nearest integer. Similarly, to obtain a quantization matrix with quality level lower than Q50, each element of Q50 should be multiplied with 50/quality level and then rounding to the nearest integer.

Figure 9.5. Standard quantization matrix (Q50)

9.2.1.4 Data encoding

The 2D quantized 8 × 8 block (X′) is now ready to be compressed through encoding. The block is converted to a 1D array through “zigzag” scanning. Thereafter, employing run-length encoding (RLE), enables grouping similar frequencies together. The encoded data is then converted into binary to generate a bitstream. Finally, the bitstream data of the compressed image is stored into a storage device.

9.2.2 DCT-based JPEG image decompression process

9.2.2.1 Data decoding

Image reconstruction process starts with data decoding. The stored data is first fetched from the storage device and decoded through RLE. The quantized 2D 8 × 8 block (X′) is reconstructed through “inverse zigzag” scanning from the 1D array.

9.2.2.2 Perform inverse quantization

The reconstructed X′ is now ready to be decompressed through inverse quantization. Decompression is achieved by multiplying each element of reconstructed block by the corresponding element of quantization matrix, to obtain block (X″).

9.2.2.3 Perform IDCT on decompressed image

Similar to applying DCT on the input block in the JPEG compression process, IDCT is applied on the decompressed block (X″). The IDCT on the X″ block can be performed through following matrix multiplications:

In the above expression, E is calculated as follows:

The “E” matrix (e11, e12, …, e88) transforms the rows of the X″ block. Further, “O” matrix (o11, o12, …, o88) transforms the columns of the “E” matrix. Thus the above transformations, transform both the rows and columns of the X″ block. Therefore, “O” is the IDCT block of X″ block. After applying IDCT on the decompressed block, each element is rounded to the nearest integer.

9.2.2.4 Reconstruct the decompressed image

To reconstruct the decompressed image from the inversely transformed decompressed block, 128 is added to each of the element of the decompressed block to keep the range of output image pixel between [0, 255] instead of [−128, 127].

9.3 Design process of structurally obfuscated JPEG IP core

9.3.1 Threat model, problem formulation, and optimization framework

9.3.1.1 Threat model

To protect a JPEG CODEC IP core from RE and Trojan insertion through structural obfuscation. In order to maximize protection ability, impede the correct functionality of the application by generating a functionally equivalent but structurally nonobvious architecture of JPEG CODEC IP Core. (Note: Motivation of using structural obfuscation to guard against RE was thoroughly explained in Chapter 7).

9.3.1.2 Problem formulation

In order to protect a JPEG CODEC IP core from RE threat, design a structurally obfuscated, low-cost hardware. The hardware design cost is evaluated by calculating the total hardware area and total design latency. The hardware design cost adopted from Sengupta et al. (2018b) is formulated as:

where Cf(Xi) is the hardware design cost for design solution Xi; LtotalJPEG and AtotalJPEG represent the total design latency and total hardware area of the obfuscated JPEG IP core, respectively; LmaxJPEG and AmaxJPEG indicate the maximum possible design latency and hardware area, respectively, using the specified module library; weightage factor of two design parameters (latency-area) is controlled via w1 and w2.

9.3.1.3 Optimization framework

To obtain a low-cost hardware for JPEG IP core, PSO-driven DSE framework is used. This particle-based heuristic approach iteratively searches for a new global optima based on local minima and current global optima. Detailed explanation of the PSO-DSE process and formulation models is provided in Chapter 3 and in Sengupta et al. (2017a). Benefits of the PSO-DSE process are as follows:

  •   (i) Capable of obtaining global optima while bypassing local minima

  •  (ii) Capable of incorporating stochasticity during exploration process

  • (iii) Capable of preserving a proper balance between exploitation and exploration throughout the iterations

9.3.2 Constructing non-obfuscated DFG for JPEG compression

The generic steps to design a structurally obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core are shown in Figure 9.6. In this section, we discuss how to construct a standard (non-obfuscated) DFG from the matrix expression of JPEG compression. Equations (9.2) and (9.3) represent the function of applying 2D-DCT on the input image block M. (Note: Detailed explanation of generating DCT matrix and its corresponding graph is given in Chapter 3.) This function is expanded and modeled as a mathematical expression to design an equivalent DFG. Further, this DFG is fed to an HLS engine to obtain a JPEG compression IP core. Based on (9.2), the corresponding mathematical expression for the first pixel (X11) of the transformed block is modeled as:

whereas based on (9.3), d11, d12, …, d18 are modeled as:

Similarly,

Figure 9.6. Steps to design a low-cost obfuscated JPEG IP core

Similarly, mathematical expression for the rest of the pixels of the transformed block can also be modeled, where the pixel values (m11–m88) and DCT coefficient will change depending on the pixel coordinate of the transformed block. However, the overall pattern of operations of the expression will be same. Based on this pattern, a DFG is generated where different pixel values and DCT coefficients are fed as the input. As in (9.7), we have modeled the mathematical expression for the first pixel (X11) of the transformed block, and the corresponding DFG is shown in Figure 9.7. In the process of computing X11 through the complete DFG, termed as macro IP, each dij (represented through (9.8–9.10)) is computed through a sub-DFG termed as micro-IP. For example, micro-IP8, represented through blue node executes d18. The zoom in representation of micro-IP8 is also shown in Figure 9.7. Totally 16 nodes (node no. 113–128) are part of micro-IP, where darker nodes indicate multiplication operation and lighter nodes indicate addition operation. Similarly, micro-IP1-7 executes d11–d17. The macro IP contains total 136 nodes; among these, the output of node number 135 produces the transformed pixel intensity of X11. As mentioned earlier, quantization is applied on the each pixel of the transformed block, where each element of the transformed block is divided with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix. In this DFG, the output of node number 135 is multiplied with the inverse value of corresponding number (i.e., instead of division, multiplication is performed with the inverse of the number) of the quantization matrix (Q). This q value is fed as another input of the DFG based on the quality level of the compressed image. For higher quality level, the q value will be less and vice versa while calculating the same pixel. Subsequently, the output of node number 136 produces the compressed pixel intensities (X11′) as the final output. This standard structure of JPEG DFG is common for most of the applications; therefore, identifying functionality from its structure is easy for an attacker. This invites threats such as RE, insertion of Trojan logic, counterfeits as fraudulent means of designing/maligning JPEG IP Core. This can be shielded to a certain extent by hiding functionality of the design. In the next subsections, we first discuss how to design a structurally obfuscated DFG for JPEG compression, followed up with its obfuscated hardware design.

Figure 9.7. Non-obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression for calculating first compressed image pixel (X′ 11)

9.3.3 Generating structurally obfuscated JPEG compression IP core

Structural obfuscation hinders the RE process by transforming the standard architecture of JPEG hardware to an unobvious design. Therefore, identifying the original functionality of the structurally obfuscated design is harder for an attacker. THT-based structural obfuscation is applied to the standard structure of JPEG DFG (Sengupta et al., 2017b). It is a compiler-driven optimization technique which parallelizes the dependent critical path operations by dividing it into temporary sub-computations. However, this technique has not been used to generate a structurally obfuscated DFG for JPEG. The standard structure of JPEG DFG shown in Figure 9.7 is structurally obfuscated through THT. The transformed structure of JPEG DFG is shown in Figure 9.8. The zoom-in representation of obfuscated micro-IP8 is also shown in the figure. Due to this transformation, each micro-IP, as well as macro-IP, is modified. For example, in micro-IP8, 12 nodes among 16 nodes are affected. They are node no. 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120, 122, 123, 124, 125, 126, and 127. Therefore, in the eight micro-IPs, 96 nodes are affected. Additionally in the macro IP, six nodes are affected which include 130, 131, 132, 133, 134, and 135. A node is considered affected if its parents or child is changed or the operation type of that node is changed compared to the original one. These changes produce a different structure of datapath, interconnectivity logic, multiplexers/demultiplexers, and controller logic, once processed through high-level synthesis.

Figure 9.8. Obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression for calculating first compressed image pixel (X′11)

The design process of obfuscated, low-cost JPEG compression IP core is shown in Figure 9.9. As shown in this figure, the primary input is the non-obfuscated (standard) DFG of JPEG compression (designed in the previous section). Then it is structurally obfuscated through THT (explained initially in this section). A low-cost hardware configuration for obfuscated JPEG DFG is explored through PSO-DSE which is used to design a JPEG compression IP core in HLS framework (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011; Coussy et al., 2009). In order to perform this process, PSO-DSE accepts additional inputs such as resource constraints, module library, and control parameters. For a detailed explanation of the PSO-DSE process, see Chapter 3 and Sengupta et al. (2017a). Finally, a dedicated IP core for JPEG compression is developed which is structurally obfuscated and low cost by nature. This IP core accepts leveled-off pixel intensity, 2D-DCT coefficient, and quantization matrix as inputs and produces transformed compressed pixel intensity as output.

Figure 9.9. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG compression

9.3.4 Generating structurally obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core

In this section, we discuss how to construct an obfuscated DFG from the matrix expression of JPEG decompression. The compressed block X′ is decompressed through inverse quantization. In this process, each element of X′ is multiplied with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix of the same quality level, to obtain decompressed block X″. Then 2D-IDCT is performed on the decompressed block X″. Equations (9.4) and (9.5) represent the function of applying 2D-IDCT on the decompressed block X″. Similar to JPEG compression process, this function is expanded and modeled as a mathematical expression to design an equivalent DFG. Further, this DFG is fed to a HLS engine to obtain a JPEG decompression IP core. Based on (9.4), the corresponding mathematical expression for the first pixel (o11) of the inversely transformed block is modeled as follows:

In the above expression, e11, e12, …, e18 can be expressed as :

Similarly,

Similarly, the mathematical expression for rest of the pixels of the inversely transformed block can be modeled, where the pixel values of X″11–X″88 and IDCT coefficients will change depending on the pixel coordinate of the inversely transformed block. Since the overall pattern of operations of the expression is same as DCT-based JPEG compression process, we can conclude that the DFG of JPEG DCT and IDCT are almost same except for few things. For example, in case of compression we assumed that each element of the compressed block is multiplied with the corresponding element (q) of the quantization matrix, to perform quantization (through node number 136). However, quantization through node number 136 is not required in DFG of JPEG IDCT. Instead, the last node (node 136) can be used to perform de-levelization by adding 128 to the pixel intensity of the decompressed block. Thus, the total number of nodes in the DFG for both JPEG compression and decompression remains the same. Therefore, THT-based structurally obfuscated DFG can be similarly generated for the JPEG decompression also.

The design process of obfuscated, low-cost JPEG decompression IP core is almost similar to JPEG compression IP core. The obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is shown in Figure 9.10. As shown, the decompression IP core accepts processed (i.e., after multiplying each element of compressed block with the corresponding element of the quantization matrix) compressed pixel intensity and 2D-DCT coefficient as inputs and produces inversely transformed decompressed pixel intensity as output.

Figure 9.10. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG decompression

9.4 Implementation of JPEG CODEC IP core

9.4.1 Designing obfuscated JPEG compression IP core

The complete design flow of JPEG compression process using devised low-cost, obfuscated JPEG compression IP core is shown in Figure 9.11. In this complete design flow, partial steps are performed through hardware and the remaining steps are performed through software. More specifically, 2D-DCT transformation and quantization steps are performed through devised JPEG compression IP core and leveling of input image pixel intensity and data encoding is performed through software. Each 8 × 8 block leveled-off pixel intensity, stored in a hardware queue, is provided as input to the devised JPEG compression IP core, along with quantization matrix and 2D-DCT coefficient matrix. In this section, we emphasize the implementation of hardware portion of JPEG compression IP core design process. The JPEG compression IP core is designed using HLS framework (Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011; Coussy et al., 2009), where the obfuscated DFG of JPEG compression (shown in Figure 9.8) is first scheduled based on a resource configuration. As mentioned earlier, the resource configuration which generates a low-cost design is explored through PSO-DSE process. Here, the DFG is scheduled based on the list-scheduling algorithm with three adders (Adder_A1, Adder_A2, and Adder_A3) and three multipliers (Multiplier_M1, Multiplier_M2, and Multiplier_M3). This indicates, based on the dependency, each CS of the scheduled DFG can have maximum three additions and three multiplication operations out of 136 operations available in the DFG. In each CS, every scheduled operation is assigned to its corresponding hardware and operations assigned to a same hardware are bound (shared) together. Table 9.1 represents all the 136 operations, their CS, and corresponding assigned hardware. Total 30 CS are required to schedule all the operations. Both adders and multipliers are designed in IEEE 754 half precision floating-point format. Therefore, all the operators have bit-width 16 bits. The implemented JPEG compression IP core consists of two units: data path unit and controller unit. The data path unit represents the required number of resources and their interconnections while the controller unit synchronizes those resources by changing their signals (e.g., enables, selectors, strobes). In other words, controller unit is responsible for controlling the data flow through the data path by activating and deactivating different components of data path in different clock cycle, thus synchronizing each component to generate an error-free output. The generic block diagram representation of data path unit of low-cost obfuscated JPEG IP is shown in Figure 9.12. As shown in this figure, the data-path consist of three adders and multipliers, ten multiplexer of type 32:1, two multiplexer of type 16:1, five demultiplexer of type 1:32, one demultiplexer of type 1:16, forty registers of 16-bits and 18 latches. The primary inputs are represented through A1,…A8,…Q1,…Q8 and the dependent inputs are represented through i1, i2, …, i135, while i136 represents the output. The implemented schematic representation of the data path unit and the complete IP core are shown in Figures 9.13 and 9.14, respectively, and the complete controller unit signal description is available in the “Appendix.” Both data path and controller is implemented using Quartus CAD tool in Intel Cyclone II (Cyclone II FPGA, 2018) FPGA.

Figure 9.11. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG decompression
