Figure 9.12. Block diagram representation of data-path unit of devised low-cost obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core

Figure 9.13. Schematic representation of data-path unit of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core

Figure 9.14. Schematic representation of complete obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core

9.4.2 Designing obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core

The complete design flow of JPEG decompression process using devised low-cost obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is shown in Figure 9.15. Similar to the JPEG compression design flow, few steps are performed through software and rest is performed through hardware. More specifically, data decoding and inverse quantization are performed through software and 2D-IDCT transformation and leveling of output image pixel intensity are performed through devised JPEG decompression IP. Finally, each 8 × 8 block with leveled-off decompressed pixel intensity is stored in an output hardware queue.

Figure 9.15. Obfuscated low-cost IP core for JPEG decompression

Similar to JPEG compression, during DFG scheduling, same resource configuration is used. The same number of components, i.e., three adders and multipliers of 16-bits, ten multiplexers of type 32:1, two multiplexers of type 16:1, five demultiplexers of type 1:32, one demultiplexer of type 1:16, Forty registers of 16-bits and 18 latches are used in the data path unit. Similar to the JPEG compression IP core, both data-path and controller of JPEG decompression IP core are also implemented using Quartus CAD tool in Intel Cyclone II (Cyclone II FPGA, 2018) FPGA.

9.4.3 End-to-end JPEG CODEC through designed hardware/IP core

In this section, we discuss the end-to-end JPEG CODEC process through the devised JPEG IP core. This discussion has three segments. In the first segment, we discuss about each step of image compression starting from an input image to generating a quantized image through an illustrative example. In the second segment, we present about data encoding and decoding process through RLE algorithm using an illustrative example. In the last segment, we discuss about each step of image decompression starting from a de-quantized image to generate the post-compression reconstructed image pixel through another illustrative example.

A grayscale image of 512 × 512 taken from “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” (Standard dataset, 2018) is selected as an input image. The input image is shown in Figure 9.16(a). To perform DCT on the input image, multiple leveled-off, nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks of the image pixel are formed from the input image. Out of multiple nonoverlapping 8 × 8 blocks, a randomly selected block for the input image is shown in Figure 9.16(b). This block (containing 64-pixel values) is provided as one of the primary inputs to the devised obfuscated JPEG compression IP core (shown in Figure 9.16(c)). The designing process of obfuscated JPEG compression IP core is discussed in Section 9.4.1. The designed IP core performs DCT and quantization on the input block and produces transformed and quantized image as output. In this example, we have performed compression based on quality level 90, i.e., using quantization matrix Q90. This process is repeated until all the 8 × 8 blocks of the input image is transformed and quantized. The generated transformed and quantized image is shown in Figure 9.16(d).

Figure 9.16. Motivational example of JPEG compression through compression IP core

Data encoding, which is a form of lossless data compression, is performed on each quantized block, before storing the pixel data into a storage device. It involves arranging the data of the quantized block in “zigzag” fashion then employing RLE algorithm on it. Figure 9.17(a) shows the quantized block corresponding to input image block (shown in Figure 9.16(b)). Zigzag scanning (the format of zigzag scanning is shown in Figure 9.17(b)) is performed on the quantized block and the output is shown in Figure 9.17(c). The quantized data sequenced in zigzag fashion is encoded through RLE algorithm. RLE replaces each nonzero AC coefficient value with a pair (RUNLENGTH, AMPLITUDE), where “RUNLENGTH” is the number of zeroes that came before that nonzero AC coefficient and “AMPLITUDE” is the value of that particular nonzero coefficient. The encoded version of the quantized data using RLE is shown in Figure 9.17(d), where (0, 0) always indicates the end of the block. The remaining elements (from the 64 available slots) of the 1D array in RLE encoded data are not stored, as they are all zeroes. (Note: The first value of the matrix, i.e., 16 is the DC coefficient; it is not encoded through RLE.) Each of these encoded values is converted to its equivalent binary form to generate the corresponding bitstream of the block and then stored in a storage device. To regenerate the quantized block from the bitstream data, decoding needs to be performed. To achieve the decoding of data, all the aforementioned steps have to be performed in reverse order. Thus while obtaining (decoding) 1D array from RLE encoded data, the vacant slots from the 64 elements (of 8 × 8 block) are filled up with zeroes. The inverse zig-zagging is performed to obtain 2D array of 8 × 8 block of quantized block.

Figure 9.17. Demonstrative example of data encoding through RLE algorithm

To reconstruct the image from its transformed and quantized form, each block is de-quantized using the same quantization matrix used for compression. As in this example, we have performed compression using quantization matrix Q90, the de-quantization (inverse quantization) is performed based on quantization matrix Q90 only. The generated de-quantized image is shown in Figure 9.18(a). The 8 × 8 de-quantized block (containing 64-pixel values) is provided as one of the primary input to the devised obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core (shown in Figure 9.18(b)). The designing process of obfuscated JPEG decompression IP core is discussed in Section 9.4.2. The designed IP core performs IDCT and leveling-off of the de-quantized block and produces 8 × 8 decompressed image pixel intensity values as output. The corresponding decompressed image pixel intensity of the same 8 × 8 block (shown in Figure 9.16(b)) is shown in Figure 9.18(c). Again, this process is repeated until all the 8 × 8 de-quantized blocks are inversely transformed and leveled off. Finally, the post-compression reconstructed image is generated by combining all the 8 × 8 inversely transformed and leveled-off blocks. The reconstructed image of the corresponding input image (shown in Figure 9.16(a)) is shown in Figure 9.18(d).

Figure 9.18. Informative example of JPEG decompression through devised JPEG decompression IP core

9.5 Analysis on case studies

To verify the devised IP cores for JPEG compression and decompression, images (bit depth equal to 4 bits) provided as input are taken from two different image datasets. They are “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” (Standard dataset, 2018) and “NASA images” (NASA images, 2018). Both the devised IP cores are designed, implemented, and simulated in Intel Quartus (Intel Quartus, 2018) v7.2 software with respect to Cyclone II family (Cyclone II FPGA, 2018), device no. EP2C35F672C6 at 50-MHz clock frequency. However, it can be emulated in any FPGA device. Table 9.2 reports the device utilization summary of devised JPEG compression IP core for the aforementioned target device. The devised JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated and low-cost in nature is compared with another JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated but not optimized in nature indicating the design configuration of the obfuscated IP core is not explored through any optimization framework/engine. Therefore, deficiency of any low-cost DSE framework results in higher design cost overhead. Table 9.3 reports the comparative analysis between these two aforementioned IP cores in terms of design area, latency, and cost. A 15 nm technology scale based on NanGate library (Open Cell Library, 2018) is used to evaluate the design area and the design latency of both IP cores, where area is in μm2 and latency is calculated in picoseconds. Based on the weighted normalized design area and design latency of the obfuscated JPEG IP core, design cost is calculated using (9.6).

Table 9.2 Device utilization summary of devised JPEG CODEC IP cores w.r.t. Intel Cyclone II FPGA

Table 9.3 Comparison of low-cost obfuscated IP core with nonoptimized obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core in terms of area, latency, and cost

Therefore, design cost of the obfuscated JPEG IP core is unitless. According to the results shown in Table 9.3, the devised JPEG CODEC IP core design achieves more than 5% lower design cost than the non-optimized obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design. The reason for achieving lower design cost is due to the involvement of PSO-DSE engine, which explores the low-cost design configuration. Therefore, it is referred as “low-cost” JPEG CODEC IP core.

The devised JPEG CODEC IP core which is structurally obfuscated and low-cost in nature is also compared with another JPEG CODEC IP core which is not structurally obfuscated indicating that no structural transformation technique is performed in the DFG of JPEG CODEC to hide its structural identity. Therefore, deficiency of any structural transformation technique results in nonsecured design which is vulnerable to RE attack. Table 9.4 reports the comparative analysis between these two aforementioned IP cores in terms of design area, latency, cost, and SoO. The SoO of JPEG CODEC IP core is measured through a metric, which is partially adopted from Sengupta et al. (2018b), expressed as follows:

where aJPEG indicates that the number of nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC is altered due to structural transformation; aJPEGTotal indicates the total available nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC before applying THT technique. The robustness of obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core is measured through SoO metric, a higher SoO value indicates stronger robustness in the range of [0, 1]. In other words, SoO metric indicates how much the structure of an obfuscated IP core differs from its original structure. The more a design differs from its original structure the harder it will be for an attacker to identify the application through RE. Therefore, insertion of any malicious logic in the IP design or performing IP piracy is extremely difficult without knowing the actual functionality of the application. According to the results shown in Table 9.4, the devised obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design achieves more than 76% SoO than a non-obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core design. The structural obfuscation is obtained using THT which is responsible for obfuscating the original design of JPEG CODEC by transforming the height of the data flow graph representing the JPEG CODEC, thus modifying the nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC. Modification of a node in a DFG indicates whether, (1) the source/parents of a node is changed; (2) the child of a node is changed; or (3) operation type of a node is changed, compared to the original. The effect of modification of nodes is also reflected in the gate structure/netlist of the design. According to the results shown in Table 9.4, more than 10,000 gates are affected due to the modification of nodes in the DFG of the JPEG CODEC. This is achieved due to the transformation in gate-level architecture of functional resources, multiplexers, demultiplexers, and registers. This enormous transformation in gate-level architecture of the complete JPEG CODEC IP core makes it an unobvious structure. Therefore, identifying the correct functionality of this unobvious structure is extremely complex and tedious for an attacker. Figure 9.19(a)–(c) shows the comparison between devised, non-obfuscated, and nonoptimized JPEG CODEC IP core in terms of area, latency, and cost, respectively.

Table 9.4 Comparison of low-cost obfuscated IP core with non-obfuscated JPEG CODEC IP core in terms of area, latency, cost, SoO

To compress standard input images using devised JPEG CODEC IP core, totally six images are chosen from “dataset of standard 512 × 512 grayscale test images” (Standard dataset, 2018) and “NASA images” (NASA images, 2018) datasets. The compression is performed for two different quality levels, i.e., quality level 90 (Q90) and 70 (Q70). Additionally, the mean square error (MSE) and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the corresponding compressed images obtained through devised JPEG CODEC IP core design are also calculated. 9.6 Conclusion

This chapter discussed a case study of structural obfuscation using JPEG CODEC IP core which is available in almost every CE devices. The design mechanism and implementation process of low-cost obfuscated on-chip IP core design for 2D-DCT-based JPEG image compression and decompression are explained here. This structural obfuscation hides an application and its implementation from an adversary by transforming its standard architecture to a non-obvious one. In this process, THT is used to structurally obfuscate the design and low-cost hardware configuration is explored through PSO-DSE engine. The devised IP core is synthesized and simulated through Intel Quartus Cyclone II FPGA. The designed IP core can be used as a dedicated IP core in any camera-based CE devices to perform image CODEC. Further, the robustness of the structurally obfuscated design is measured through SoO metric, which indicates that more than 76% SoO is achieved compared to a standard non-obfuscated JPEG CODEC design. Additionally, as structural obfuscation does not incur any design overhead, therefore, it is an extremely useful method of protection for Trojan insertion, IP piracy/counterfeit. The SoO of the devised JPEG CODEC IP core discussed in this chapter can be enhanced by performing multiple transformation techniques on the DFG of the JPEG CODEC IP core as a part of future work. Additionally, combination of functional obfuscation technique with structural obfuscation can also enhance the robustness for DSP applications. This would enable to hide an application and its implementation from an adversary.

Chapter 10
Advanced encryption standard (AES) and its hardware watermarking for ownership protection

In this era of consumer electronics, cyber security is one of the key challenges. Any security, privacy, or protection methods that are deployed rely on cryptography. Advance encryption standard (AES) is one of the heavily used cryptography algorithms for its advantages. This chapter is dedicated to the process of AES and its hardware design in the form of IP core. Several hardware security techniques rely on AES IP core as an important block. Additionally, since this is such an important core, its self-protection against forgery/piracy is also crucial. Thus, this chapter will also discuss about AES IP core protection using watermarking.

10.1 Introduction

Cryptography is very widely used in everyday life, ranging from established applications such as wireless local area network, procuring items with a credit or debit card, installing a software update, smart cards, banking application, voice of internet protocol (VOIP) to emergent domains, such as electronic health system, internet of things security, smart city security, and hardware security (Paar and Pelzl, 2009; Bhunia and Tehranipoor, 2018; Sengupta, 2013, 2015, 2017; Sengupta et al., 2017; Sengupta and Bhadauria, 2016; Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2011; Mishra et al., 2017; Sengupta and Sedaghat, 2013; Sengupta and Roy, 2017a, 2017b). Cryptography comprises cryptographic algorithms that are symmetrical by nature. There is tremendous usage of symmetric ciphers, especially for the encryption of data and integrity check of messages. Furthermore, cryptographic protocol deals with the application of cryptographic algorithms. An example of cryptographic protocol is transport layer security (TLS) scheme, widely employed in browser advanced encryption standard (AES) is a very popular symmetric cipher used today. The AES, also known by its original name Rijndael, is a specification for the encryption of electronic data recognized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). In the context of AES (Rijndael family), three members were designated by NIST, each with a block size of 128 bits, but dissimilar key lengths: 128, 192, and 256 bits. It is a mandatory standard in several industry/commercial systems and US government applications such as Wi-Fi encryption standard IEEE 802.11i, TLS, and VOIP (Paar and Pelzl, 2009).

In this chapter, we focus on the following aspects: (a) AES algorithm—description of each step and its flow diagram, (b) corresponding hardware mapping of AES block cipher—overview of how each step can be mapped to a specific hardware sub-block, (c) key scheduler—description of each step, (d) corresponding hardware mapping of key scheduler used in AES, (e) watermarking encoding of AES hardware—protecting an AES hardware against threats such as false claim of ownership and piracy, (f) design of watermarked AES hardware—description of the watermark embedding process, and (g) impact of several different watermark signature types on AES hardware and its implementation on FPGA—to highlight the overhead due to watermark.

10.2 AES algorithm

10.2.1 Overview of AES

AES algorithm has three different variations of key sizes, i.e., 128 bits or 192 bits or 256 bits. The input data size is 128 bits and the output encrypted data is also 128 bits. The input data is called the plain text and the output encrypted data is called cypher text. Figure 10.1 shows the AES input/output parameters. The core structure of AES comprises the following components: (i) byte substitution layer, (ii) diffusion layer, (iii) key addition layer, and (iv) key schedule (Kosaraju et al., 2006; Mohanty et al., 2007). Three key lengths are supported in AES. The number of internal rounds of the cipher depends on the key length. For example, in case of 128 bit key length, the number of internal rounds (nr) is 10, while for 192 bit key length, the number of internal rounds is 12, and finally for 256 bit key length, the value of nr is 14, respectively.

Figure 10.1 AES block cipher

10.2.2 AES algorithm—description and custom hardware design

The first major phase of AES algorithm is ‘byte substitution layer (S-box)’ which is responsible for non-linear transformation using lookup tables for each element of the state. The main significance of this step is to add ‘confusion’ to the data elements. In other words, the transformation achieved in individual state bits is rapidly propagated into the datapath. The second major phase is called ‘Diffusion’ which consists of two sub-layers, viz. ‘ShiftRows’ that permutes the data at the byte level and ‘MixColumn’ is a matrix based operation that is responsible for mixing of blocks of four bytes of data. The significance of ‘Diffusion’ is to introduce diffusion property to the data element. The third major phase is ‘key addition’ layer which is responsible for XOR-ing the 128 bit key (or its derived key) to the state of each element obtained after performing ‘MixColumn’ operation. Finally, the ‘key schedule’ calculates round keys or subkeys (k0, k1,…,knr) from the original AES key. Figure 10.2 shows the major steps of the AES algorithm in terms of design flow highlighting each block responsible for performing specific operation. As an example, we use key length of 128 bits for demonstration (Paar and Pelzl, 2009).

Figure 10.2 Round ‘i’ (1–10) of AES algorithm for 128 bit key and 128 bit I/O

10.2.2.1 Byte substitution (S-box) layer

S-box is the non-linear component of AES which is accountable for bit manipulation. It consists of 16 S-boxes all of which are identical to each other. All 256 possible input elements have a unique mapping to one output element. S-box is shown in Figure 10.3 and is adopted from Paar and Pelzl (2009). For example, if input byte to the S-box is (B2)hex, then based on the mapping available in S-box, the output byte is (37)hex. In other words, S((B2)hex) → (37)hex → S(10110010) → 00110111. This clearly shows how bit manipulation is achieved using byte substitution layer of AES. As shown in Figure 10.2, bytes X0, X1, X2,…,X15 are substituted with Y0, Y1, Y3,…,Y15 using S-box. Every four bytes of data X0, X1, X2, X3 gets transformed into Y0, Y1, Y2, Y3. Similarly, for next four bytes X4, X5, X6, X7 gets transformed into Y4, Y5, Y6, Y7. Further similarly, next four bytes X8, X9, X10, X11 gets transformed into Y8, Y9, Y10, Y11. Finally, last four bytes X12, X13, X14, X15 gets transformed into Y12, Y13, Y14, Y15.

Figure 10.3 S-box (Paar and Pelzl, 2009)

10.2.2.2 Row-shifting diffusion layer

The significance of the ShiftRows transformation is to upsurge the diffusion process of AES. This transformation works as follows:

  1. First row is retained unaffected.

  2. Second row is cyclically moved three bytes to the right.

  3. Third row is cyclically moved two bytes to the right.

  4. Fourth row is cyclically moved one byte to the right.

The output of byte substitution layer is fed as an input to the ShiftRows diffusion layer as shown below. Let us assume the output of byte substitution layer is Y0, Y1, Y2, Y3,…,Y15. It is arranged in matrix form as shown below in Table 10.1. The transformation applied on each row is indicated through notes on the top of the arrow. The outputs for every four input byte are indicated in each column. For example, corresponding to the input four bytes Y0, Y1, Y2, Y3, the transformed output four bytes are Y0, Y5, Y10, Y15 as shown in Table 10.2. Similarly, the outputs are obtained for the remaining four bytes in each column.

10.2.2.3 MixColumn diffusion layer

This step is a major diffusion process in AES since each every input byte impacts four output bytes. It is responsible for mixing each column of the state matrix. The input to the MixColumn diffusion layer is the output of ShiftRows diffusion layer. In order to perform MixColumn diffusion each 4-byte column is assumed as a vector and multiplied by a fixed 4 × 4 matrix. The matrix comprises of some constant values. The main important thing to note is that the matrix addition and multiplication is performed in Galois Field (GF) arithmetic (not integer arithmetic). The first four output bytes of ShiftRows diffusion acting as input to MixColumn diffusion are Y0, Y5, Y10, Y15 which is assumed as a vector and multiplied by a fixed 4 × 4 matrix as shown below. Similarly, the next four bytes of ShiftRows diffusion acting as input to MixColumn diffusion are Y4, Y9, Y14, Y3. Furthermore, the next four bytes of ShiftRows diffusion acting as input to MixColumn diffusion are Y8, Y13, Y2, Y7. Finally, the last four bytes of ShiftRows diffusion acting as input to MixColumn diffusion are Y12, Y1, Y6, Y11. The respective outputs are Z0, Z1, Z2, Z3; Z4, Z5, Z6, Z7; Z8, Z9, Z10, Z11; Z12, Z13, Z14, Z15.

After performing matrix multiplication, the following equations are obtained on which GF arithmetic is performed.

Similarly, the rest of the equations can be derived from matrix multiplications, followed by GF arithmetic computation. Note: in GF arithmetic, the additions are simple bitwise XORs of the respective bytes. Multiplication by 01 is multiplication by the identity and does not include any specific operation. Multiplication by 02 can be realized as a multiplication by x, which is a left shift by one bit, and a modular reduction with P(x) = (x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1) for 8 bit data or (x4 + x + 1) for 4 bit data. Note: In AES, 4-bit product is not possible after multiplication, thus P(x) = (x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1) → (100011011) is used. Similarly, multiplication by 03, which represents the polynomial (x + 1), can be realized by a left shift by one bit and addition of the original value, subsequently by performing modular reduction with P(x).

For instance, let us consider eqn. (10.1) above as: Z0 = (02 · Y0) + (03 · Y5) + (01 · Y10) + (01 · Y15).

Furthermore, let us consider the state of input to MixColumn diffusion as: (Y0, Y5, Y10, Y15) = (25, 25, 25, 25).

Now converting (25)hex in hexadecimal format to binary is: 00100101. This is also equivalent to polynomial: x5 + x2 + 1. Now inserting the binary of (25)hex = 00100101 in eqn. (10.1) we get:

(Note: Multiplying by 01 is same value; multiplying by 02 is left shift by 1 bit; multiplying by 03 is left shift by 1 bit and addition of the original value followed by a modular reduction with P(x) if required. The addition is achieved by XOR the bytes.)

The above value is equivalent to x5 + x2 + 1. Since the order of power is less than 8, thus modular reduction is not required. Similarly, the rest of the values (Z1, Z2,…,Z15) can be computed.

10.2.2.4 Key addition layer

The inputs to the key addition layer are the output of MixColumn diffusion layer (current 16-byte state matrix) and a subkey which also comprises of 16 bytes. Bitwise XOR is performed on the two inputs to yield the output O0–O15 for the next round (see Figure 10.2). This output is used as an input for byte substitution layer in next round. The example below illustrates the process in Tables 10.3 and 10.4. As seen below, keys (K0–K3) are bitwise XOR-ed with state matrix element (Z0–Z3) to obtain outputs (O0–O3) which is fed as an input for the next round. Similarly for the remaining elements of the state matrix, the output is computed (see Figure 10.2).

10.2.2.5 Key scheduler for 128-bit AES

The main role of key scheduler in AES is to accept the original 128 bit key and derive the subkeys for the next rounds of AES. The number of subkeys needed is obtained by adding one to the number of rounds. Hence, for key length of 128 bits, the number of rounds is nr = 10, and there are 11 subkeys, each of 128 bits. The AES with a 192-bit key requires 13 subkeys of length 128 bits, and AES with a 256-bit key has 15 subkeys. The AES subkeys are calculated recursively, i.e., in order to derive subkey ki, subkey ki−1 must be known. We will discuss the process of key scheduler in more details a little later. But now since all major phases of AES algorithm has been discussed, thus let us have a look at the hardware mapping process of AES in Figure 10.4. This is the generic hardware mapping process that is used to develop a custom hardware-based AES block. We will look into the hardware block of diffusion layer 2 (MixColumn) from the context of optimization now and digital watermarking later. The MixColumn hardware block can be designed as shown in Figure 10.5. However, in order to achieve delay and resource optimization, the hardware structure in Figure 10.5 can be re-designed/re-configured as shown in Figure 10.6.

Figure 10.4 Hardware mapping of 128 bit AES algorithm

Figure 10.5 MixColumn (diffusion layer 2) hardware before optimization

Figure 10.6 MixColumn (diffusion layer 2) hardware after optimization

The AES key schedule is word-oriented, where 1 word = 32 bits. Subkeys are stored in a key expansion array M that comprises of words. Figure 10.7 shows the key scheduler process for round ‘i’. Similarly, how the keys for round 1 have been generated, and the keys for next rounds using key scheduler are obtained. The g-function in the key scheduler process is responsible for non-linearity in the key scheduling. It accepts a four-byte input and produces a four-byte output. The sub-steps inside g-function are following: left rotation (e.g., V0, V1, V2, V3 changes to V1, V2, V3, V0), byte substitution using S-box, and adding round coefficient (RC). The RC is an element of the GF (28), i.e., an 8-bit value. It is only added to the leftmost byte in the function g. The RC value varies round to round and is added as per the following rule based on eqn. (10.5) in Paar and Pelzl (2009):

Figure 10.7 AES key schedule for 128-bit key size for round ‘i’

But we know GF(28) = x8 + x4 + x3 + x + 1 = 100011011.

Thus, for example when we compute RC[9] = x8 using eqn. (10.5):

Furthermore, RC[10] = x9 = 2 × x8 which is equivalent to left shifting the value RC[9], i.e., (000011011)2 → (00110110)2.

The respective hardware mapping of key scheduler process is shown in Figure 10.8, which indicates the hardware structures necessary for rotation, S-box implementation, RC, as well as the others units.

10.3 AES digital watermarking

We have learnt about the motivation of embedding watermark in an IP core or hardware. Similarly, in order to provide protection (provide deterrent) against false claim of ownership, piracy, forgery, digital watermark needs to be implanted in AES hardware design. In the chapter, we show how to implant watermark in a certain portion of AES hardware structure. The selected portion of AES structure where watermarking is embedded in ‘MixColumn diffusion layer 2 hardware block’ (shown in Figures 10.4 and 10.5, respectively).

This portion of AES hardware is selected for watermarking because of following desirable properties:

  1. Option of embedding watermark without much design overhead.

  2. Ease of implementation.

  3. Seamless signature detection.

  4. No chance of hardware functionality being affected.

  5. Maximal opportunity of adding several signature digits corresponding to a watermark.

10.3.1 AES watermark encoding

In this chapter, we present a new encoding scheme for embedding signature digits ‘α’ and ‘β’ into the AES diffusion layer to design structure. The formal definition of digits ‘α’ and ‘β’ are as follows:

For example, Figure 10.9a represents the portion of MixColumn structure responsible for computing Z0 (refer Figure 10.5). Embedding of ‘α’ indicates double sharing of two consecutive XOR blocks (indicated in Figure 10.9a), while embedding of ‘β’ indicates triple sharing of three consecutive XOR blocks (also indicated in Figure 10.9a). Figure 10.9b shows the resultant structure after embedding a ‘α’ digit in the original AES MixColumn structure. The resultant structure now contains two extra 2:1 multiplexers and one 1:2 demultiplexer (and storage registers) with a minimization of one XOR block. On the other hand, if a ‘β’ digit is implanted in the original AES MixColumn structure, then the resultant structure is shown in Figure 10.9c. The resultant structure now contains two extra 4:1 multiplexers and one 1:4 demultiplexer (and storage registers) with a minimization of two XOR block. Thus, evident different area-delay tradeoff is possible due to choice of different watermark signature digits. Moreover, the design overhead would also vary depending on the choice of the signature digits. We further present the portion of original MixColumn structure (with no watermark) responsible for computing Z1, Z2, and Z3, along with its corresponding watermarked design in Figures 10.10, 10.11, and 10.12, respectively.

Figure 10.9 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z0 MixColumn structure of AES

Figure 10.10 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z1 MixColumn structure of AES

Figure 10.11 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z2 MixColumn structure of AES

Figure 10.12 Embedding watermark for ‘α’ and ‘β’ digit in Z3 MixColumn structure of AE

10.3.2 Process of embedding watermark in AES

  1. Sort the output variables of MixColumn hardware structure in ascending order, i.e., Z0, Z1, Z2,…,Z15 and store in list L[k].

  2. Create a desired 16 digit watermark signature using random combinations of α and β digits.

  3. For each occurrence of α or β digits, apply design changes (reconfiguration) to the MixColumn hardware structure corresponding to sorted output variables. Example, first α or β digit in a signature will affect the hardware structure corresponding to first sorted variable Z0 (as it first in the sorted list L[k]), followed by next α or β digit affects the hardware structure corresponding to next sorted variable Z1 and so on.

  4. Insert registers after each multiplexer and demultiplexer in the modified MixColumn hardware structure.

10.3.3 Signature detection

Signature detection is performed through the following two phases:

  1. Inspection of the datapath of AES MixColumn structure to collect relevant hardware information.

  2. Signature verification is performed to authenticate the existence of vendor’s signature in the AES IP core design. Firstly, the encoded signature is decoded through the cognizance of the encoding rules. Subsequently, the presence of extra constraints as watermark is verified in the MixColumn hardware structure.

10.4 Case study of a watermarked AES hardware

The AES design was implemented in VHDL in Altera Quartus v.13 and run on AMD A8-4500M with 4 GB DDR3. The target hardware platform selected was Cyclone II—Device EP2C70F896C6.

For the sake of analysis, two different watermark signature sizes were chosen, viz. 8-digit and 16-digit for embedding into the AES hardware design. Three types of experiments were conducted: (a) variation of different 8-digit signature combinations and its impact on synthesis results of AES hardware, (b) variation of different 16-digit signature combinations and its impact on synthesis results of AES hardware, and (c) overhead obtained due to 8-digit signature and 16-digit signature compared to non-watermarked AES. Following parameters were observed and analyzed: total logic elements, total combinational functions, dedicated logic registers, total registers, and total pins. Results of implementation of AES for 8-digit and 16-digit watermark signature as well as non-watermark AES hardware is reported in Tables 10.5 and 10.6, respectively. A portion of watermarked AES hardware corresponding to signature ααββααββ is shown in Figure 10.13. Figure 10.14 shows the comparison of non-watermarked AES128 design with three different combinations of 8-digit watermarked design in terms of logic elements. Figures 10.14 and 10.15 shows comparison of non-watermarked AES128 hardware with different combinations of 8-digit and 16-digit watermarked AES.

10.5 Conclusion

This chapter presented the following novel and interesting aspects: (a) AES algorithm—description of each step and its flow diagram, (b) corresponding hardware mapping of AES block cipher—overview of how each step can be mapped to a specific hardware sub-block, (c) key scheduler—description of each step, (d) corresponding hardware mapping of key scheduler used in AES, (e) watermarking encoding of AES hardware—protecting an AES hardware against threats such as false claim of ownership and piracy, (f) design of watermarked AES hardware—description of the watermark embedding process, and (g) impact of several different watermark signature types on AES hardware and its implementation on FPGA—to highlight the overhead due to watermark. There is no chapter that deals with the design flow of AES algorithm, its hardware design perspective as well as its digital watermarking process for different signature digits. Finally, it provides a lucid comparative study of watermarked AES hardware with a non-watermarked AES hardware. The content of this chapter is useful in understanding the details of AES described in conjunction with functional obfuscation of digital signal processing cores presented in Chapter 08.

Chapter 11
Hardware approaches for media and information protection and authentication

Technology scaling has allowed us to design high-performance devices with a low-power consumption. The advent of IoT has increased the versatility of data collection and there are many different ways of collecting and transferring data over the Internet. The data that is being collected is also in different forms, that is, text, images, videos, and audios. When they are shared, for a legit use, attackers can break the security and use them for illegible purposes or claim ownership to sell them commercially. This has been the trend lately where many counterfeit products are appearing in the market. This section discusses the digital watermarking, different schemes of digital watermarking, and how a media object can be secured using a watermark. They are also not completely resistant to attacks and measures need to be taken to secure the content that is being watermarked. The chapter also presents different issues with the watermark implementations, attacks and countermeasures to those attacks on watermarking. Section 11.1 presents a broad overview of the IP protection. Section 11.2 discusses the generic overview and components of any watermark system. Section 11.3 summarizes various types of watermarks. Section 11.4 discusses various applications of watermarking. Section 11.5 presents desired characteristics of watermarks. Sections 11.6 discusses the technical challenges of the watermarking. Section 11.7 discusses hardware-based watermarking systems available in the current literature. Section 11.8 discusses about watermarking in smart vehicles. Section 11.9 discusses about medical signal authentication. Section 11.10 highlights side-channel information leakage and its countermeasures. Section 11.11 outlines various forms of attacks on watermarks and watermarking systems. Section 11.12 presents the difficulties involved in making use of them in practice.

11.1 IP Protection—a broad overview

With the advent of new technology, new devices are being introduced into the world and high-performance applications are being designed. With better systems coming out every day, there is also a problem that they are used for various malicious applications like counterfeiting, which is a major problem in hardware and in media also. Many people nowadays are producing content and sharing it with the world (Krishnamurthy, 2018; Mohanty, 2015). But the content that they own is being illegally used by many commercially, without paying royalties to the owner and in some cases, the content is being misused also. This raises many problems pertaining to the IPR and their protection. Figure 11.1 shows a broad overview on the area of counterfeiting. An image can be produced by the owner and watermarked but an attacker can attack, tamper, or remove the watermark from the image and can claim ownership. This creates many issues on the copyrights and ownership rights.

Figure 11.1 Broad overview of IP protection (Mohanty, 2009; Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018)

11.1.1 Digital rights management

Figure 11.2 shows different media and threat levels which are vulnerable to attacks. A cinema will have a high privacy, whereas a broadcast content will have low security. This has become a major issue lately where the content of the owner is being reproduced without paying royalties to him/her.

Figure 11.2 Multimedia video overview (Mohanty, 2009; Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018)

In such cases, the owner will have copyrights violated and misses out on the royalties that are entitled legally. When a content media like a digital video disc (DVD) or Blu-ray is produced with a video content, it is considered to be secured with the watermarks embedded in it. But there are also many attacks available that can remove or tamper the watermark on the content. Figure 11.3 shows different types of multimedia that are available on the Internet. Many of the audio services provide audio to the user at a monthly cost. But tampering with the audio that is broadcast over the Internet is not difficult with the technological advancements that are present at a current date. Digital rights management (DRM) is a major issue that many different areas of research are concentrating on. Watermarking the audio files, video files, images, and also text is a solution.

Figure 11.3 Multimedia music overview (Mohanty, 2009; Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018)

11.1.2 Copyright protection of multimedia—a brief history

There are several advantages to digital media over the analog world. Higher quality, ease of processing, and editing are some of them. The most common forms of digital media are compact disc (CD), DVD, TV broadcast, and computers. But there are also many disadvantages to the digital media. Digital media counterfeiting has been a very big problem lately. It can easily be duplicated, which has raised the need for more secure and effective DRM tools (Devillier, 2017; Kougianos et al., 2009; Lah and Lewis, 2016; Ma, 2017; Ma et al., 2016). Watermarking is one of the ways of securing the digital media such as audios, photographs, and videos. There are different kinds of watermarking like visible or invisible and can be inserted into different domains like spatial or frequency. There are various software implementations of digital watermarking but very few hardware implementations (Liu et al., 2017; Sarreshtedari et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015). When designing a hardware implementation of watermarking, various issues are to be considered such as low-power consumption, high-performance, ease of integration, and reliability.

Emil Hembrooke invented electronic watermarking in 1954 (Cox and Miller, 2002). Since then there has been extensive research carried on by various experts from different domains, such as cryptography, computer science, communications, and signal processing. Digital watermarking was proposed to provide robust protection along with encryption and scrambling. Many of the following questions were raised by the community (Cox and Miller, 2002; Zhao et al., 1999; Yeung, 1998):

  1. What is digital watermarking and what are its properties?

  2. What is the process of implementing digital watermarking?

  3. What are its disadvantages?

Digital watermarking is the process of embedding information into digital media and generating a watermarked media (Liu et al., 2017; Sarreshtedari et al., 2015; Sequeira and Kundur, 2001; Zhao et al., 2015) which evolved from steganography techniques. A difference between steganography and cryptography is shown in Figure 11.4. In the case of cryptography, a key is used to encrypt the message and convert into a cipher text and when it is decrypted, the original message will be exposed and will not be protected. In the case of steganography, the message is hidden in the plain text, and the Data is embedded with the original message (Mathivanan and Ganesh, 2017; Vijayan and Sreedivya, 2017). The way and intent of using the method differs between steganography and digital watermarking. A watermark can be perceived as an attribute of the carrier (cover). The information that will be watermarked into the media can be anything, including, and not limited to, tracking, license, authorship, copyright, and so on.

Figure 11.4 (a) Steganography versus (b) cryptography (Kahn, 1996; Pfitzmann, 1996)

Digital watermarking has been around for a very long time and many applications are being developed that use the watermarking for security (Cox and Miller, 2002; Kamaruddin et al., 2018; Kirovski and Malvar, 2001; Loan et al., 2018; Memon and Wong, 1998; Mintzer et al., 1997; Barnett, 1999), such as fingerprinting, ownership evidence, and authentication. No single watermarking technique can be universally used for all the applications, which makes the research and development of new techniques in watermarking more difficult and challenging. The watermarking technique depends on various factors including the type of application and deployment (Kamaruddin et al., 2018). There are different attacks that can be launched on a media and its watermark, and the security resistance against such attacks and performance determines the success of watermarking scheme (Vellaisamy and Ramesh, 2014; Wang et al., 2017b; Xiang et al., 2014). The two major conflicting factors of watermarking are the performance of the embedded watermark and fulfilling the desired characteristics. Various benchmarks are available for watermarking techniques (Kaur et al., 2012; Voloshynovskiy et al., 2001).

There are three different parts of a watermark (Memon and Wong, 1998; Mohanty, 1999):

  • The encoder

  • The watermark

  • The decoder

Algorithm that is used for marking will embed the watermark into the media object and the verification algorithm will authenticate if the object is watermarked. Spatial or frequency domain can be used to embed a watermark into the media, which can be visible or invisible. A visible watermark will be a translucent mark that the original media is overlaid on and is visible only to the consumer on careful observation. An invisible watermark cannot be seen even with careful observation and needs to be retrieved from the pixels where it is embedded into. To increase the robustness, multiple watermarks can be embedded into a single media object (Hua et al., 2001; Mohanty et al., 1999), which can be used for content authentication or copyright protection.

Before a watermarking scheme is used in a consumer market, different technical, legal, and social issues need to be addressed. Watermarking schemes have been already in use for a very long time. IBM visible watermarking techniques have been used in Vatican library project (Mintzer et al., 1996). In order to develop a robust watermarking scheme or an algorithm, various properties need to be met. For example, application-specific watermarking algorithms need to be developed, which will require a formal body to be involved (ASCAP, 2018; Cox and Miller, 2002; Mintzer et al., 1998; Broadcast Music Inc., 2018; Motion Picture Licensing Corporation, 2018). Copy Protection Technical Working Group (CPTWG) is a group that focuses on sharing knowledge and information on copyright protection (CPTWG, 2018). There has been extensive research in this area and many algorithms were proposed for watermarking. Hardware integration of watermarking has also been explored for better robustness and performance. Figure 11.5 shows a hardware watermarking chip integrated into a camera (Mohanty, 2009; Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018). The watermarks in the camera will be embedded in the spatial or DCT domain. The watermarking can be performed for either images or videos. An example of encoder in spatial and DCT domain modules for JPEG compression is presented in Figure 11.6.

Figure 11.5 System architecture for a digital camera with DRM hardware components (Mohanty, 2009; Mohanty et al., 2004, 2005b, 2018)

Figure 11.6 JPEG encoder with watermarking modules: (a) spatial domain and (b) DCT domain (Mohanty et al., 2003)

11.1.3 Hardware versus media protection

Many questions arise when it comes to the copyright protection. There is a major issue of counterfeiting which should be protected against. Many different agencies are trying to protect the copyrights of the owners. But there are always attackers who illegally claim ownership by attacking the watermark protection of the original image or tampering with it. There is media protection and hardware protection when it comes to the Copyright Safeguarding and DRMs. Compared to media, hardware watermarking schemes are better. This is because they can be optimized for a better performance with a low-power consumption. The chip area of the watermarking module can also be optimized so that the overall cost of production is lower. Media protection in some cases is protecting the media on which the copy of original content is reproduced on. For example, DVD will have an information on the discs such that they will not be able to play the content outside the region of distribution. A disc produced in an area and region locked cannot be played outside that region in another drive. The contents of the disc will not be visible for reading. The hardware watermarking can be used for copyright protection and ownership authentication of the owner.

11.2 General framework for copyright protection

Primary use of watermark is to embed it into a digital media using different algorithms and extract it at a later time for authentication of ownership and so on. The digital media can be an image, a video, or an audio. For example, a watermark on media can be considered as a “seal” that is on an image to identify the ownership, the quality of media, and in some cases, the identity of purchaser (Wang et al., 2018). Figure 11.7 shows the big picture of encoding and decoding techniques which consists of various parts such as encoder, comparator, and decoder (Memon and Wong, 1998; Mohanty, 1999). In case of a visible watermarking technique, the watermark used will be an image. But in case of an invisible watermarking technique, the watermark can be an image, a random, or a pseudo random number. The owner may have a unique watermark of his/her own and can also embed different watermarks in different media objects. When needed, the watermark can be extracted for authentication.

Figure 11.7 General framework for watermarking: (a) the encoder and (b) the decoder (Craver et al., 1998; Memon and Wong, 1998; Mohanty, 1999)

11.2.1 The encoder

Figure 11.7(a) shows the process of embedding a watermark into an original image. The block “E” in the figure represents an encoder. The original image (I) is fed to the encoder along with the watermark. The encoder is designed based on the watermark insertion algorithm that the owner wishes to use to secure the original image. Depending on the algorithm used, the original image is watermarked with the one that is given as an input to the encoder.

For example, let the original image input is denoted by I and watermark input is denoted by . The output watermarked image is denoted by . The encoder function is denoted by E and the inputs to the encoder for the original and watermark images are denoted as I and W, respectively. The output is given as:

The input watermark image W depends on various factors like size of I, its features, and identity.

11.2.2 The decoder

When the watermarked image is needed to be authenticated, it should sent through a decoder. Figure 11.6 shows the big picture of the decoding process. The decoding process will depend on various factors, including the process of inserting a watermark into the original image and nature of watermarking algorithm. The watermark extraction process is where the entire watermark is extracted from the image. But in some cases, only a specific watermark signal can be detected in the media, and this process is called a watermark detection. Watermark extraction can prove the authenticity of ownership on the media, but only detection can verify the ownership. The input to the decoder D is an image, that is watermarked, nonwatermarked, or even corrupted, denoted as J, which needs to be challenged for ownership. The decoder will recover the watermark . In this process, an additional image I can also be included, which is often the original and nonwatermarked version of J.

11.2.3 The comparator

After the watermark is extracted, it needs to be compared to the original watermarked image. The extracted watermark image from the decoder is sent to the comparator. The comparator is also given the original watermark as the input as shown in Figure 11.7(b). The comparator compares the extracted watermark and the original watermark W. The output of the comparator will be in binary, “1” if both the and W match and “0” if they do not.
