11.8 Dynamic watermarking in smart car or UAV

IoT has become a major focus of research nowadays. With all the new technologies coming out everyday, designing new THINGS has been possible and sensor integration into various devices has become an important task in every applications. Smart transportation and UAV technology have developed significantly since their advent (Mohanty, 2015). Autonomous vehicles and UAVs are being used for various purposes. Self-driving cars are not so far ahead in the future. With all these coming into picture, security is one of the main concerns that is bothering the research community. Both UAV and smart car will have video-recording capabilities. Watermarking that video will help in determining if the video that is recorded in the camera is tampered or not.

The video that is recorded in the vehicles is in some cases processed real time and in some cases, stored in the memory to be analyzed at a later time. Both these cases are important when it comes to a smart car and UAV. When the video is recorded, the cars and UAV might be subject to different kinds of attacks that let the attacker to tamper with the video surveillance footage of the vehicle. So, the watermark that is introduced in the vehicle should be tamper resistant (Fallahpour et al., 2014). Many video editing software lets the user to tamper with the video and make the stream unreliable which defeats the purpose of the recording (Su et al., 2011). So, detection and distinguishing of the tampered video is also necessary in such scenarios.

Hence the watermark should be able to provide transparency, robustness, and higher capacity so that it can be embedded into different kinds of video footage. A fragile watermarking is used in most cases for detecting the tampering of a video (Fridrich et al., 2000). The attacker will try to change the watermarked video or object in the case of tampering but without touching the watermark itself. This poses a huge threat as distinguishing the original untampered video will become difficult. A fragile watermarking will be able to protect the footage against such tampering attacks. In case of a fragile watermarking algorithm, the video footage will become highly sensitive to the modifications and this will make it difficult to perform any kinds of modifications to the video like re-compression. A semi-fragile scheme was also proposed by Sang and Alam (2008).

11.9 Medical signals authentication

As mentioned in the previous sections, the advancements of technology have allowed us to explore high-bandwidth communications which led to transmitting data globally (Singh et al., 2017). There has become no bounds for devices used for transmission, especially for medical use, such as the Internet, mobiles phones, wireless communications, and so on. There are different kinds of threats that are posed on the communication networks of such kind. The information that is being shared is also highly sensitive, which contains medical records of patients. This demands for higher levels of confidentiality and security. Medical image watermarking can provide a better service which can address these issues (Acharya et al., 2001; Coatrieux et al., 2006). There have been few implementations of such security initiatives. For example, the use of watermarking in tele-medical applications in order to enhance the security of the transmitted sensitive medical data has been implemented. Tele-medicine watermarking will demand more care when the data is encrypted within the medical images as the information itself and its quality cannot be affected. The reliability, confidentiality, and availability are the major concerns of the security in the electronic patient record (EPR) exchange. Modern telecommunication infrastructure supports the possibility of delivering quality health care without the physical presence of medical experts. The integrity of biomedical signals being transmitted through communication channels must be established before their utilization. Investigations have been performed where digital watermarking techniques for signal integrity verification in an electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring application were performed.

A digital watermark which uses both the ECG and the patient demographic text as two-level watermarks was proposed by Annadurai et al. (2012). In the insertion process, DWT is applied to the object, and it is decomposed into three sub-bands. After that the texture matrix will be calculated for each of the sub-bands. The wavelet coefficients are then selected for the watermarks which are used as threshold values. Authenticating the watermarked object is the main goal of this watermarking scheme. A wavelet spread-spectrum watermarking mechanism for both text and image is presented by Singh et al. (2015). The watermark size is varied and the gain factor is obtained in this scenario for the experimental results. BCH codes are used for an increased robustness.

Researchers across the globe are using the hybrid watermarking schemes to improve the performance of the watermarking systems (Fatima and Tuptewar, 2016; Vo et al., 2017). DCT and DWT can be used to embed the watermark into an image and the watermark can be selected at random. After a third level of decomposition, a DCT can be applied on them. A watermark with a zero mean and one variance is inserted in this process. The extraction process does not require the original image to be present in the memory.

Machine learning can also be used for the watermarking techniques. There are many variants of watermarking techniques that use machine learning and offer more imperceptibility and security compared to the other but demand high computational power. A blind watermarking technique which uses the multiwavelet and support vector machine (SVM) is presented by Peng et al. (2010). Initially the multiwavelet is performed on the each of the blocks of image. After this stage is complete, the lowest frequency sub-band is selected and the watermark is embedded into that using modulation. The watermark information contains a reference to the owner and the signature of binary logo image. The reference information of the owner will be helpful in training the SVM when extracting the watermark.

11.10 Side-channel information leakage attacks and countermeasures

Watermarking and cryptography hardware modules have an advantage of the low-power consumption along with a high performance and throughput. They can also be designed at a low cost per module and are integrated into different applications with ease. Besides these advantages, there are also some disadvantages to the hardware modules. They are made out of CMOS technology and are susceptible to various kinds of attacks such as side-channel attacks. The side-channel attacks collect the information from the hardware modules like the hardware watermarking chip directly unlike the software attacks.

During World War II, an engineer observed that the oscilloscope signal had a spike in it when a key was pressed in the secure typewriter Model 131-B2 at Bell Labs in 1943 (Mohanty, 2015). Based on that the first publicly known side-channel attack was reported in 1965. Any attack that uses the physical implementation of cryptosystem and gains information is called a side-channel attack. There are two types of attacks that are possible on a crypto system: nondestructive and destructive. The target of the first type is analyzing the target module and gain information from it without destroying or tampering the device itself. Side-channel attacks are included in this category of attacks. Different side-channel attacks are presented in Figure 11.24 (Parameswaran, 2018). This section discusses in detail the CPA and DPA attacks on the modules. There are also fault attacks, acoustic noise attacks, elapsed time attacks, EM radiation attacks, and so on, which exploit the advantages of different components of a device, like the time taken to complete a process, injecting faults into the device algorithms, and so on.

Figure 11.24 Different side-channel attacks (Parameswaran, 2018)

11.10.1 An encryption hardware

Figure 11.25 shows the process of AES encryption. AES is widely used for encryption and decryption in communication between two devices or nodes. It is considered to be the most secure cipher as the variable data block is supported by this standard with a variable key size (Mohanty et al., 2018). The key size and the block size can be chosen as any multiple of 32 and between 128 and 256. AES has no practical attacks against it and is more secure. Brute-forcing an AES encryption is highly difficult and requires high computational power. Fundamental algebraic transformations are present in AES like shift row, mix column, round key, and substitution. They are present for each of the standard round but there is an exception of the least standard round.

Figure 11.25 Advanced encryption standard (AES)

11.10.2 Side-channel analysis attacks

Two major side-channel analysis attacks are considered in this section, CPA and DPA (Jayasinghe et al., 2015). CPA is the analysis of relationship between the cipher-text and the plain-text and it’s correlation as well as the instantaneous power consumption of the cryptographic device. When compared to DPA, CPA is a more effective attacking method. DPA uses the relation between the power and the data. Using that DPA will try to look at the difference of the category averages for all the keys. As it uses the averages, more power correlation data is needed for successfully launching this attack. So it consumes more time and is less efficient compared to the CPA. Figure 11.26 presents a big picture of DPA and CPA (Zhang and Shi, 2011).

Figure 11.26 DPA and CPA on HMAC: (a) oscilloscope and (b) detector (Zhang and Shi, 2011)

A DPA attack is a side-channel attack which statistically analyzes the consumed power by the respective module in a cryptosystem. The module can be a watermarking chip or a cryptographic processor which performs encryption and decryption. Figure 11.27 shows the overall process of DPA (Parameswaran, 2018). The biases varying power consumption is taken. Here, the microcontroller is monitored and the power analysis is performed when various operations are performed on the chip, which involve the secret keys. Signal processing and error correction properties are necessary for performing DPA, which are used for the extraction of secrets from the power consumption measurements. There is also noise that comes with the measurements so it must be filtered before the analysis is performed. A secret key can be obtained by the attacker by analyzing the power from the cryptographic operations on the chip using DPA.

Figure 11.27 Differential power analysis: (a) differential power analysis big picture and (b) differential power analysis attack overview (Parameswaran, 2018)

A CPA uses the relation between the data and the power as mentioned before. Figure 11.28 shows the overall picture of the CPA (Parameswaran, 2018). This uses a correlation between the guesses of the keys. Hence, low power is required compared to the DPA. CPA is used to find a key that is stored in memory of the victim device. Launching a CPA attack involves the following four steps.

  • The power consumption model of the victim device should be noted.

  • The victim should encrypt different files of plain text.

  • Record the trace of the power consumption on the victim device.

  • Attack the small parts of the secret key from the observed power analysis.

Figure 11.28 Correlation power analysis: (a) correlation power analysis big picture and (b) correlation power analysis attack overview (Parameswaran, 2018)

Every possible combination for the subkey should be considered. When each guess is performed, it is compared to the power that is analyzed on the main board. Repeating this process will give a guess of the subkey which will equal to the main key and power of the key used on the plain text will match the power observed from the module.

11.10.3 Side-channel attack countermeasures

Side-channel attacks are highly efficient in stealing information from the microcontroller or memory. The attacker can use various kinds of attacks such as CPA, DPA, timing analysis, and so on on the hardware to get the information stored on it. Many techniques are available to mitigate the issues of power analysis attacks (Ambrose et al., 2015; Jayasinghe et al., 2015). There are many ways to avoid the side-channel attacks on the hardware modules. Figures 11.29 and 11.30 show different ways of safeguarding the hardware modules from CPA and DPA attacks.

Figure 11.29 Differential power analysis attacks countermeasures

Figure 11.30 Correlation power analysis attacks countermeasures

One of the main drawbacks of the power analysis attacks is that the hardware should be powered on during the time of the attacks in most of the cases. So, if the power supply to the module is turned off, the attacker cannot perform the attack anymore. Introducing some interrupts to the power can also mitigate the security threats to some extent. Power supply to the module can be detached when unused but this will only apply when the module is not solely in the hands of the attacker. During the execution process, there can be a nondeterministic execution which will not give out the exact power statistics of the device during the processing of secret keys. These are some of the hardware solutions that can be implemented. De-synchronization, software balancing, random masking, and so on are the software countermeasures to the DPA attacks on the security modules.

11.11 Attacks on watermarks and watermarking systems

When a watermark is embedded into a media object, there is a great chance that it might be subjected to manipulative attacks before the media reaches the receiver. Some of the manipulations are analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversions, resampling, quantization, dithering, low-pass and high-pass filtering, and so on. The media can be printed and rescanned in some cases intended to remove the watermark from the media. Any processing of the watermarked image that is intended to remove or tamper the watermark and fail the detection process is an attack on the watermark (Cox and Linnartz, 1998; Mintzer et al., 1998; Sequeira and Kundur, 2001; Swanson et al., 1998; Voloshynovskiy et al., 2001). The characteristics of the watermark and its performance against the attacks which are mutually conflicting FoM. Comparing metrics for different algorithms is needed to come to a decision in selecting a suitable watermarking scheme for a particular application. Benchmarks of the watermark are different attacks in a unified framework which allow the owner to check the scheme for applicability.

This section discusses different attacks that are possible on a watermarked image. There are different types of attacks on a watermarked image to remove the watermark. They are classified into four different types (Liu et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2001; Vellaisamy and Ramesh, 2014; Voloshynovskiy et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017a, 2017b; Xiang et al., 2014) as shown in Figure 11.31:

  • Geometric attacks

  • Removal and interference attacks

  • Cryptographic attacks

  • Protocol attacks

Figure 11.31 Attacks on watermarks (Pereira et al., 2001; Voloshynovskiy et al., 2001)

11.11.1 Removal and interference attacks

Removal attack on the watermark is targeted to remove the watermark from the object. A watermark is the noise that is added to the original image and this is taken as an advantage by the attacker to remove the watermark. Interference attacks target the watermark by adding more noise to the watermarked image. Quantization, lossy compression, collusion, remodulation, denoise, averaging, and noise storm are the examples of such kinds of attacks. JPEG, MPEG, and so on are the lossy compression styles that can degrade the quality of watermark that is embedded in the media object. When many legit owners of the watermarked copy of the media come together to create a nonwatermarked image, it is called a collude attack. This can be achieved by averaging different objects in the media that is already watermarked.

11.11.2 Geometric attacks

The geometric attacks are more targeted toward the watermarked images and videos. These kinds of attacks do not remove the watermark present in the media but will manipulate the watermarked media so that the detector will not be able to extract or retrieve the watermark. Affine transformations such as translation, rotation, and scaling are used to successfully launch this attack. Line removal, wrapping, and cropping can also be done to remove the watermark from the media object. Mosaic attack is another example of this category (Koubaa et al., 2007). In such attacks, the media object is divided into different parts and again rearranged into one using HTML, which makes the watermark difficult to be detected by the detector.

11.11.3 Cryptographic attacks

The two attacks that are discussed above will not be able to breach the algorithm security. A cryptographic attack is the one that precisely attacks the security of the watermarking algorithm and cracks it. When the watermark is secured with a secret key, as discussed in the previous sections, a brute-force attack can be performed and broken, which can be considered as a cryptographic attack. Oracle attack is another kind of cryptographic attack which uses a public watermark detector to create a nonwatermarked media object.

11.11.4 Protocol attacks

This kind of attacks takes advantage of the loopholes that are present in the watermarking algorithm (Craver et al., 1996, 1998; Wang, 2009; Zhang and Liu, 2017). This kind of attack is also known as inversion, deadlock, or fake–original attack. One or many new watermarks are introduced on an already watermarked media which makes it difficult to detect the original watermark and the owner. Some kinds of attacks will produce a fake original media object with a watermark so that the detector will detect it as an original watermarked legit copy. Watermark from an already watermarked object is detected and transferred to another media object which is called copy attack, which is also very popular.

11.12 Limitations of watermarks and watermarking

Limitations of the watermarking schemes are discussed in this section. When a watermark is inserted into the original media object, it should be detected with ease if not tampered with. Even in the case of attacks, the watermark should be resistant. In this chapter, we discussed a lot about different kinds of watermarks and the characteristics. With the hardware watermarking coming into picture, the IoT integration is becoming easy. Different hardware modules that were discussed above can be integrated into IoT applications. But IoT devices need to be connected to the Internet all the time and some of them will be battery operated. So, the latency and the power consumption of the watermarking modules is a great challenge.

When it comes to the visible watermarking schemes, the copyright is clearly mentioned and need not be worried (Mintzer et al., 1996; Mohanty et al., 2000a). The watermark should occupy a significant portion of the original media object. Besides that the quality of the image should not be degraded. When removing the watermark it costs same as a new media object. This kind of security is sufficient for use in different applications. This also has some drawbacks where the watermark should be enforced with laws.

Invisible watermarking, unlike the visible watermarking techniques, is imperceptible and is more complicated for that reason. Robustness of the watermark is considered the highest characteristic that a watermarking algorithm has to meet. But this is not true in case of an invisible watermarking. Because, every watermark can be attacked using various techniques and invisible watermark is also not left out from that category. Any media can be subject to counterfeit production by attacking the watermark. So, invertible or quasi-invertible invisible watermark schemes are not able to resolve the rightful ownership. Without a standardized watermarking scheme, anyone can claim ownership.

Due to the advancements in the technology scaling and development of high-performance devices, signal manipulations are being introduced into various artworks and the indistinguishable noises are added to the media object. This makes it difficult to differentiate the manipulations and prove original ownership of the object. The additional data in the object is not known to occur due to the watermark or any new noise. In such scenarios, extracting watermark and authenticating the ownership of the object is a challenge. With the use of highly sophisticated DSP, this problem is further deteriorating. A watermarked image that is not protected properly cannot be used for authentication and hence cannot be used in a court of law. To avoid this situation, watermark can be embedded into the object during the acquisition phase directly using hardware modules.

For a satisfactory robustness of watermark image, in case of a c traitors out of N, the length of the codewords to be inserted into the watermark is given as: , where the probability of error is denoted by . The discussed amount of added noise embedded into the image will surely degrade the quality of the image which in turn reduces the commercial value of the object. Digital watermarking will not be able to prevent illegal activity but can only provide evidence that such an activity has been performed by a party. But cryptographic techniques can protect the data from such attacks. So digital watermarking should be used as a secondary protection layer.

11.13 Conclusion

This chapter discusses the watermarking schemes, some issues with watermarking and its limitations, and attacks and solutions on different watermarking algorithms. A big picture of watermarking from basics to deployment is presented in this chapter. Different hardware watermarking schemes along with some very-low-power chips which can be integrated into battery operated devices were discussed. With the introduction of a new watermarking scheme or a new cryptographic algorithms, the attackers are soon coming up with ways to attack them and breach the security. There are many counterfeit devices being produced and media content being shared without proper legalities being met. This has become a major issue that has to be addressed designing of high sophisticated and low-power security modules in both cryptography and watermarking.
