Chapter 12
Physical unclonable functions (PUFs)

It has been the practice to store information under lock and key for safeguarding it. Even today, we use cryptographic primitives to store information securely under lock and key, encryption, and decryption. For the process of cryptography, keys are necessary for any operation. But these keys should be stored in the memory so that they can be used whenever necessary. When a key is stored in the memory, it can be stolen by the adversary using various methods. Therefore, storing it in a non-volatile memory is not an option in this age of security threats. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are the promising security primitives used for generating the keys instead of storing them in the memory. These modules use the naturally occurring manufacturing variations in the fabrication process for generating the keys for cryptographic purposes. This chapter discusses different types of PUFs. Section 12.1 gives a brief introduction of PUFs. Section 12.2 discusses working principles of PUFs. Section 12.3 discusses different characteristics of a PUF design. Section 12.4 presents different classifications of PUFs. Various designs of PUF based on ring oscillators (ROs) are presented in Section 12.5, based on multiplexers and reconfigurability are presented in Section 12.6. Static random access memory (SRAM)-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.7, memristor-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.8, and diode-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.9. There are also non-silicon-based PUF designs, such as carbon PUFs, presented in Section 12.10. Microprocessors can also be used for implementing the PUF designs which are presented in Section 12.11. Magnetic material-based PUFs are presented in Section 12.12 and the FPGA implementations of PUF and security measures for FPGA are presented in Section 12.13. Some case study applications are presented in Section 12.14. Further the issues and challenges faced during the design of PUF modules are presented in Section 12.15. The conclusion and future directions are presented in Section 12.16.

12.1 Introduction

The first transistor was invented in 1948. With the introduction of the transistor, vacuum tubes occupying huge space disappeared and led to the invention of the IC in 1958 (Kilby, 1976). Along came the Moore’s Law which states that the number of transistors on an IC will double every two years. This came true until recently and the number of transistors on a single chip has exponentially increased since its first introduction. With the introduction of the new 10 nm technology, each square millimeter of an IC can be packed with 100 million transistors (Courtland, 2017). With technology improving at such a drastic pace, it has penetrated into almost every sphere of human life. Day-to-day activities such as communications, business, financial transactions, and so on depend on technology. Digital footprint of human being has become an inevitable and unavoidable parameter (Gencoglu et al., 2015). IoT has become an integral part of our lives. In an IoT environment, every device is connected to the network and will have a unique IP address (Mohanty et al., 2016). Smart cities, smart grid, smart healthcare, and so on are various forms of IoT.

With so many devices connected to each other, there are security concerns that are raised. The data that is being collected by various applications, sensors, and other devices should be stored securely. There are many attacks reported recently where security needs to be given the highest importance (Charette, 2018a, 2018b). To secure the data that is being generated, cryptography is used. It has been around for a very long time. Cryptography is the process of concealing a message or information by converting it into unreadable text and only the end user will be able to extract the original information from the text. It was found that in the year 1900 BC Egyptians used techniques such as steganography (2001). Various algorithms are available currently for encryption and decryption which can transfer the data securely. The National Bureau of Standards proposed DES algorithm which lasted for 20 years. Then came AES algorithm which is very popular now but there have been reports of AES being successfully broken (Mangard et al., 2005). An amount of $7.5 billion is estimated to be lost by the US semiconductor industry because of IC counterfeiting (Rose et al., 2013). In addition to all of this, in the case of many devices, sensors, or applications, the device itself will not be monitored all the time. It will be in a remote location transmitting and receiving necessary data to the cloud or a remote server. In such cases, the current practice of encryption and decryption is to store the necessary keys in a nonvolatile memory and use it (Herder et al., 2014) when required. The memory is subject to side-channel attacks where the attacker can get access to the physical device and retrieve data from it.

A PUF is a new primitive that is being introduced into various applications. Without storing a key in nonvolatile memory, it can provide keys for encryption and decryption (as shown in Figure 12.1) (Yanambaka et al., 2017). The cryptography key will be generated by PUF whenever necessary, based on the imperfections that are introduced into an IC while fabrication. There are various advantages to PUF. Fabrication of PUF components is much easier compared to the memory modules necessary to store the key. This also means the reduction in cost and chip area necessary for the memory modules like EEPROM. Side-channel attacks on the device itself will become more difficult. With some types of PUF, expensive cryptographic processors can be avoided. The number of keys generated by the PUF increases exponentially with the complexity of the architecture and design used. The same keys generated by a PUF module can also be used for IP protection where the input and output pair of PUF can be used to authenticate the ownership of a device. PUF uses the manufacturing variability of the IC to generate the output keys. Hence, the output keys generated by a PUF module should also be unique. The concept of PUF is shown in Figure 12.2. For the same PUF module, different inputs yield different outputs as shown in Figure 12.1. For different instantiations of a PUF circuit (logically same) on different chips, the same input yields different outputs as shown in Figure 12.1.

Figure 12.1 The concept of a PUF over traditional key stored in a nonvolatile memory

Figure 12.2 Concept of PUF

12.2 PUF: Principle

When an IC is fabricated, there is a process that will be followed from the beginning to the end. From the time silicon becomes an ingot to the final IC, these series deals with various fabrication steps such as masking, ion implantation, photolithography, chemical diffusion, polishing, electrolysis, and so on (Mohanty, 2015). During this process of fabrication, the devices that are being fabricated on the wafer will be affected due to various factors. Figure 12.3 shows the manufacturing variability of devices. The geometry of the devices such as length, gate oxide thickness, doping concentration, and so on will also be affected. Due to these variations, no two devices that are fabricated will look the same.

Figure 12.3 Working characteristics of the PUF

Even when the devices are fabricated on the same die, there will be variations in their geometry that will make them distinct from the others on the same wafer. A PUF will take advantage of these variations to generate the keys. The manufacturing variations that are introduced into the IC are unpredictable and unavoidable. A naturally occurring phenomenon will introduce unwanted changes in the geometry of the device. When two different transistors on the same die have variations in their geometry, the output of the two will also be different. The output from two different devices will be compared with each other to generate a single bit key of PUF.

The design of a simple PUF is shown in Figure 12.4. The input to a PUF is called the “Challenge” and the output from a PUF is called the “Response.” The pair of input and output of a PUF is called “Challenge Response Pair” (CRP). Figure 12.4 shows the design of arbiter PUF (Lee et al., 2004). As shown in the figure, the PUF uses two sets of multiplexers connected in series. The output from each set is connected to the D-input and clock signal of a D-flip-flop. The select lines of the multiplexers are the challenge input the user gives to PUF. Based on the challenge input, the multiplexers through which the input signal traverses will change. Once the input signal is given to the module, based on the challenge input, the delay will be added before it reaches the D-flip-flop. The output from the flip-flop will depend on the amount of delay added to the input signal by the devices it passes through. In this scenario, due to manufacturing variations, each transistor in the multiplexers will add various amounts of delay. This delay added is unpredictable. Thus, the PUF key generated is also unique to the module and secure. However, predicting the CRPs in the arbiter PUF is also not difficult. To avoid this, much complex designs of PUF are designed, which are introduced in the later sections.

Figure 12.4 Arbiter-based simple PUF

12.3 Properties or characteristics of PUFs

A PUF is used to generate keys for cryptographic purposes. Various properties should be satisfied by the outputs of PUF to be used for various applications. Figure 12.5 shows the different characteristics of PUF that should be satisfied for it to be ideal (Böhm, 2013; Chang et al., 2017; Maiti et al., 2013; Yanambaka et al., 2017) (Table 12.1).

Figure 12.5 Properties of PUFs

12.3.1 Uniqueness

A PUF module generates an N-bit key which should be unique. PUF uses the manufacturing variations on an IC to generate the output key. Hence, the same PUF key should not be generated by the same module for a different challenge input. The uniqueness can be considered to be calculated over different chips. Let us consider a pair of chips, i and j, where i is not same as j. The responses generated be and . Then the uniqueness can be given as (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Maiti and Schaumont, 2011):

Table 12.1 Comparison of various publications

HD is the hamming distance of the two response bits and n is the length of the response. The number of different elements that two strings of the same length have is called the HD. Initially, XOR is performed on the two strings and the result is added to get the HD. For example, consider the two strings “11001100” and “11100111.” The XOR of the string will be “00101011” and adding all bits will get us 4, which is the HD (Böhm, 2013). HD is also represented in percentage, where the result is divided by the length of the string and multiplied by 100. In the previous example, it is is 50%. The ideal HD for a PUF to be securely used for cryptographic purposes is 50%.

12.3.2 Reliability (correctness)

When necessary PUF will generate the keys for various purposes. But once it is implemented, for a single challenge input, the output response should not change. Various factors such as aging, voltage fluctuations, noise, and other factors should not affect the output of a PUF. This is the reliability or correctness characteristic of PUF where it will be able to generate the same key for a given challenge input. The reliability of a PUF can also be calculated using the HD. If the same key is given to a single PUF over a long period of time, the ideal HD should be 0%. No errors in the output bits should occur. As no design is ideal, various techniques were employed to avoid them, especially to avoid the aging effects of a design.

Let us consider a chip i from which an “n” bit response is extracted for reference at optimal conditions of environment. Now the same n-bit response is extracted from the same chip i at different environmental conditions, such as supply voltage and power supply, and let the value be , where x different samples are taken from the same i at different conditions. The reliability can be given as (Maiti and Schaumont, 2011):

12.3.3 Randomness (uniformity)

For the output of a PUF to be random, the key should contain equal number of 1’s and 0’s. This ensures that the output of a PUF is random and secure to be deployed in an application. Apart from the HD, the randomness parameter validates the keys generated by the PUF. In some cases, it is also useful in determining the error rate in the output.

12.3.4 Correlation (bit aliasing)

The correlation characteristics of a PUF are of two different types: (1) bit and (2) chip. There should be no correlation between any of the bits generated by the PUF module. If a different challenge is given to the PUF, the response should be different. And various chips on the same wafer should not affect the working of a PUF module and generate the same keys. In some cases, the manufacturing variations will be uniform across the wafer. In such cases, there is a chance that with the CRPs of one PUF chip, the other can be predicted.

12.3.5 Power consumption

A PUF is designed to be deployed in devices like RFID tags which consume very low power. In an IoT environment, there is a chance that the devices are battery operated and need to work with low power consumption. PUF is also being deployed in various smart devices which require a low-power operation. Hence designing the PUF with low-power consumption is vital.

12.3.6 Speed

There are various IoT environments depending on the place they are deployed and the application tasks they are supposed to perform. Based on the various tasks, there is a need that the environment has to send and receive the data in real time. In such cases, there is a need for security but the same cannot be a bottleneck to the processing speed or increase the transfer latency. Hence the speed with which the keys are generated is also going to play a major role in where the respective design is going to be deployed.

12.4 Classification of PUFs

PUFs can be classified based on the fabrication method and security strength as shown in Figure 12.6 (Chang et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2017; Škorić et al., 2005). In a broad sense, there are two categories of PUFs. They are categorized based on the types of devices used to design the PUF and the other category is based on the level of security provided by the module itself. Further, each of the categories has different types of PUFs. Various researchers around the world have proposed different types of PUF: these are silicon-based, non-silicon-based, electronic, and non electronic. Based on the level of security provided, there are three types of PUFs, strong, controlled, and weak.

Figure 12.6 Different types of PUFs

12.4.1 Device-based PUFs

Various devices are used by researchers to manufacture PUF. A PUF uses the manufacturing variability present in the devices to generate the outputs. Not all the devices in the world are ideal. Therefore, different varieties of devices can be implemented at the core of design to generate the PUF keys.

12.4.1.1 Silicon-based PUFs

Almost all the ICs are made from silicon and other materials. This category of PUFs is made on the silicon and fabricated on the same die as part of the IC. Various designs of PUF are proposed by researchers around the world depending on the implementation and the area of deployment. Examples of this type of PUFs are SRAM (Schrijen and Leest, 2012), butterfly (Kumar et al., 2008), arbiter (Lao and Parhi, 2011), RO (Rahman et al., 2014), and lightweight secure (Majzoobi et al., 2008). These PUFs will be extracting the manufacturing variations on the IC which can generate the keys for cryptographic purposes.

12.4.1.2 Non-silicon PUFs

PUFs that are not classified as silicon PUFs are referred as non-silicon PUFs. They are fabricated in silicon systems but require special fabrication techniques which are not part of a generic CMOS fabrication technology. The response is generated from the challenge set obtained from the random physical variation in the physical system rather than the ICs. Such types of PUFs are optical, acoustic, magnetic, radio frequency (RF), coating, etc.

12.4.2 Security-based PUFs

Once a PUF is fabricated, the design itself cannot be modified. Hence, various designs of PUFs will generate different number of CRPs. The CRPs will decide where the particular design of PUF can be deployed and used. Based on the category, PUF is of three types: strong, controlled, and weak.

12.4.2.1 Strong PUF

The strong PUF is the types of designs that will be able to generate more number of CRPs. The CRPs can also be not easily extracted from the device. A protection is provided through a complex input–output relations and an exponential number of CRPs. This type of PUF operates in the range of few MHz, so even a short duration of eavesdropping can collect many CRPs. However, all known strong PUFs are vulnerable to one or more types of attacks. This type of PUFs is frequently used for device authentication purposes. Some common example of circuits belonging to this class are arbiter, feed-forward arbiter, XOR arbiter, lightweight secure, and optical PUFs. This class of PUFs is also frequently referred to as super-high information content (SHIC) (Lugli et al., 2013; Ruhrmair et al., 2011).

12.4.2.2 Weak PUF

This category of PUFs will not be able to generate more number of CRPs. The least number of CRPs that can be generated is “1” in a worst-case scenario. Therefore, this design can be easily vulnerable to attacks. This is the reason that the design of this PUFs cannot be revealed publicly. These are mainly used to derive a secret key in cryptographic algorithms and are the least susceptible to modeling attacks. Some common examples of circuits belonging to this class are SRAM, coating, and butterfly PUFs. These are also known as physically obfuscated keys (POKs).

12.4.2.3 Controlled PUFs

This class of PUFs has a strong PUF as an underlying core additionally protected by control logic. Since the challenges are preprocessed first before passing to the strong PUF and the responses are preprocessed before coming out of the strong PUF, the CRPs of the strong PUF are never accessed directly. This preprocessing of challenges and responses significantly improves the security of controlled PUFs. A controlled PUF (Yu and Devadas, 2010) is only accessed via an algorithm which is fabricated in the same chip as the PUF such that the PUF and the algorithm are inseparable. This implies that the actual PUF outputs are never given to the outside world directly and the outputs that are given to the outside world are the processed outputs from the algorithm.

12.5 Ring oscillator–based PUFs

The design of a ring oscillator PUF is shown in Figure 12.7 (Suh and Devadas, 2007). There are two different sets of ROs that are connected to two multiplexers “Mux1” and “Mux2.” The two multiplexers are connected to two counters which are connected to a comparator, which gives the final output. The multiplexers will select different combinations of ROs and feed the oscillations to the counters. The number of oscillations over a selected period of time are given to the input and clock of the comparator. The comparator compares the two input values and gives out “1” or “0.” The input to the multiplexers is the challenge input given to PUF and the output from the comparators is the response of the PUF.

Figure 12.7 Ring oscillator PUF

Due to the manufacturing variations in the IC, all the ROs will not oscillate at the same frequency. This causes the counters to give out different number of oscillations for a same period of time. When different inputs are selected by the multiplexers, different ROs will give distinct oscillation frequencies, which generate different bits at the output of the comparator. Thus the keys generated by the RO PUF will be unique. If there are N different ROs, only N × (N − 1)/2 different comparisons will be possible. The main component in the RO PUF design is the inverter. Due to the manufacturing variations in the inverter, the delay added is different for each inverter. The delay of an inverter can be calculated as (Wang and Tehranipoor, 2010):

where is the supply voltage, is the load capacitance, W and L are the effective width and effective length of the channel, respectively, μ is the mobility of carriers, is the saturation source to drain voltage, is the oxide thickness, is the oxide dielectric permittivity, and is the threshold voltage. The oscillation frequency of the ROs with N inverters is given as:

There are some advantages to the implementation of ring oscillator PUFs. They are easier to build, evaluate, highly reliable, and relaxed layout and routing constraints in the design. There are some disadvantages also to the design. It is comparatively slow; to increase the number of bits, the chip area needs to be increase, which results in consumption of more power. In addition, aging is also one of the main issues that can affect the reliability of the ring oscillator PUF. Various factors like positive bias temperature instability (PBTI), negative bias temperature instability (NBTI), time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB), hot carrier injection (HCI), electro-migration (EM), and thermal cycling (TC) also affect PUF. Due to the aging effect, the change in the output oscillations of the ROs will affect the output bits of PUF module itself. This can become a major issue when implemented in the cryptographic applications. In a PMOS transistor, when a negative voltage is applied at gate-to-source terminal, an interface trap is generated at Si–SiO2 interface. Over a period of time, this results in the change of transistor parameters like transconductance, drain current, and threshold voltage. This effect is called NBTI. The HCI occurs due to the switching activity of the transistor (Mohanty, 2015). NBTI and HCI will depend on various factors, including workload of the transistor and technology.

TDDB is occurred due to the rapid scaling of the device. The high operating voltages at the gate terminal of the transistor will lead to the structural degradation of the device, like the gate oxide and its interface. With the continuity, the dielectric layer will lose the property to insulate and as a result, a conduction path will form between the gate oxide and the substrate. This effect has been addressed and reduced significantly with the implementation of high-κ material. Other parameters that affect the performance of the device are the temperature and supply voltage. With the variations in the supply and temperature, the output oscillations of the ROs will change. When the temperature of the chip increases, the threshold voltage of the device is reduced. The increase in temperature can also decrease the drain saturation current and the carrier mobility. But the operating temperatures of the chip and the supply voltages can be regulated and maintained. If the temperature increases, it can be decreased using various methods. But the effects caused by aging cannot be reversed and have a permanent damage on the device and hence the chip itself. This affects the performance and reliability of the chip over time.

To avoid these, aging-resistance designs are introduced. Figure 12.8 shows the design of an aging-resistant PUF (Rahman et al., 2014). The NBTI effect is decreased by introducing an NMOS transistor to connect two inverters in the RO as shown in the figure. The supply voltage is connected to the transistors which are activated using the ENABLE signal. These are introduced to avoid the logical “0” at the input of the inverter’s PMOS transistor. When the RO is not active, there is a chance that a “0” might be at the input of PMOS in the inverter and can cause power consumption. This design of PUF will reduce the NBTI effect in the off state. Various other designs of aging-resistant RO PUF designs were also introduced (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Rahman et al., 2015, 2016).

Figure 12.8 Aging-resistant RO PUF

There are various designs of PUF that are implemented for different applications (Yanambaka et al., 2017, 2018). One of the properties of PUF is the speed of key generation as discussed in Section 12.3. A PUF can be deployed in various applications, including network switches and routers. The speed with which the key is generated by the PUF is important in such cases. Figure 12.9 shows the design of hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF intended to be deployed in applications where the speed of key generation is pivotal. As shown in the figure, there are two sets of ROs in the design. Unlike the conventional ROs, multiplexers, counters, and the comparator are replaced with the D-flip-flops. The D-input and the clock input of D-flip-flops are connected with two ROs, one from each set as shown in the figure. Due to the manufacturing variations in the inverters of ROs, the delay added in each of the oscillator will be different and so will be the oscillation frequency. Based on the oscillation frequency of the ROs, the output bit from the flip-flop changes. Bits to give the key generated by the PUF.

Figure 12.9 Speed-optimized hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF

12.6 Reconfigurable or dynamic PUFs

The previous section presented a ring oscillator PUF and different designs which can be implemented in various applications. Some of the designs that are presented in the previous section are reconfigurable but the others generate a constant set of CRPs and the design itself is not reconfigurable. This section concentrates on the reconfigurability of the PUF design. Reconfigurability is an important aspect of PUF design. There is a chance that if the attacker gets hold of the device and perform attacks such as machine learning, emulation, man-in-the-middle and RE, he/she will be able to regenerate the CRPs. The reconfigurable or dynamic PUFs are introduced in order to increase the security of PUF against these attacks and to be able to generate new set of CRPs when necessary. A feed-forward structure is introduced in the arbiter PUF to avoid the attacks using linear modeling. This introduces some nonlinearity in the design and increases the security and robustness of the design trading-off the design complexity. This can also be achieved using other techniques like preprocessing the challenge input before feeding it to the PUF, postprocessing the output response from the PUF, and adding some components to the output of module which can be used for reconfiguring the response bits. The preprocessing challenge bits can be done by introducing an additional circuitry which can implement linear feedback shift register (LFSR) or by introducing some hashing. The postprocessing of response bits can mean the introduction of hashing to the bits. Figure 12.10 shows the design of arbiter PUF with an LFSR at the input. The challenge inputs given to the PUF are not directly fed to the arbiter PUF. Initially they are passed through the LSFR, preprocessed and then they are given as input to the PUF, “Real Challenge” as shown in Figure 12.10 (Lao and Parhi, 2011). With the introduction of the input-reconfigurable circuitry, the robustness of the overall design and also the reconfigurability can be increased.

Figure 12.10 Arbiter PUF with LFSR at input

To avoid various attacks on the arbiter PUF, different configurations of the design are implemented (Lao and Parhi, 2014):

  1. Feed-forward MUX PUF overlap structure (FFO): Design of FFO is shown in Figure 12.11. In this design, there is an overlap between the two feed-forward connections.

    Figure 12.11 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based overlap structure PUF

  2. Feed-forward MUX PUF cascade structure (FFC): Design of FFC is shown in Figure 12.12. In this design, the stage which got the input from feed-forward path will be the start of a new feed-forward path.

    Figure 12.12 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based cascade structure PUF

  3. Feed-forward MUX PUF separate structure (FFS): Design of FFS is shown in Figure 12.13. In this design, there will be no overlap between the feed-forward paths of the multiplexers.

    Figure 12.13 Arbiter feedforward MUX-based separate structure PUF

Figure 12.14 shows the design of a lightweight PUF. The design is presented by Majzoobi et al. (2008) with an improved robustness and increased security. In this PUF design, there are two networks at the input and the output, “Input Network,” which takes in the challenge inputs, and “Output Network,” which gives out the response outputs. The module itself will contain a number of parallel PUF structures which are run by the input and the output networks. For connecting the challenge inputs to a number of parallel PUF structures, an interconnect network is implemented. A single PUF will be satisfying the strict avalanche criterion (SAC). Any cryptographic primitive is said to satisfy the SAC if a complement in the single input bit induces a change in each of the output bits with a 50% probability. But when the overall parallel network of the design is considered, the SAC is not satisfied.

Figure 12.14 Lightweight PUF

Figure 12.15 shows a design of hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF which uses RO as a main component in the module and can also be reconfigured (Yanambaka et al., 2018). As shown in the figure, there are two different sets of ROs which are connected to two multiplexers “Mux 1” and “Mux 2.” The ROs will generate the oscillations which are fed to the multiplexers. Challenge input given to the PUF module acts as the select lines to the multiplexers. Based on the challenge input given, the multiplexers select different ROs. The output from Mux 1 is given as D-input to the D-flip-flop and output from Mux 2 is given as clock signal to the D-flip-flop. Due to the variations in the ROs, the oscillations produced will not be of the same frequency. Therefore, the output of D-flip-flop will change based on the input challenge. Different configurations of inputs can be achieved by changing the select line inputs. The robustness and security offered by the design can be increased by increasing the number of ROs in the design, but it also increases the complexity and chip are occupied.

Figure 12.15 Power-optimized hybrid oscillator arbiter PUF

12.7 SRAM-based PUF

Many devices and development board have SRAM which can be used to design a PUF. Figure 12.16 shows the circuit design of a 6T SRAM cell (Mohanty, 2015). The start-up value of the SRAM cell is used by the PUF to generate the output bits. When compared to the other designs of PUF, the reliability and uniqueness of the SRAM PUF are less. As shown in Figure 12.16, an SRAM cell can be designed using cross-coupled inverters and will be able to store a single bit of binary data, “1” or “0.” When the SRAM cell is powered up, its initial condition is taken as the advantage by the PUF to generate the unique output. But there are issues with the behavior of SRAM cells at the start-up. Different SRAM memory modules were compared and analyzed by Schrijen and Leest (2012), operating at different temperatures and supply voltages. The analysis was performed by calculating the reference bits at the starting, at various temperatures of 20 °C, −40 °C, and 80 °C by Schrijen and Leest (2012), which showed the stability of SRAM. The supply voltage of the SRAM was also varied by 10%. This does not affect the performance of the PUF as claimed (Schrijen and Leest, 2012) because the start-up conditions are attained during the initial few nanoseconds.

Figure 12.16 6T SRAM cell

In the case of an SRAM memory, one of the important challenges is to get a sufficient entropy into a key that is of a fixed length. In the case of an SRAM PUF, the generated keys will have noise and the entropy will be lost during the generation of helper data and the error correction (Koeberl et al., 2014; Maes et al., 2012). In some cases, the loss of entropy during the helper data will be considered where it is uniformly distributed. The entropy and the length of output are equal when the entropy density is multiplied by the error correction. In that scenario, the entropy of the raw PUF outputs, even when low, can be used for generation of keys. The entropy of the output of PUF is usually unknown and so the estimation of entropy should be performed using a more rigorous method in worst-case scenarios. In the syndrome constructions and the code-offset, when a binary linear code C(n, k, t), where the length of the dimension of code is represented by n and k and the maximum number of errors that can be corrected is represented by t, is considered. When a worst-case scenario is taken into account, the entropy lost can be calculated as bits which can be considered satisfactory (Maes et al., 2012). When the original bit entropy is less than /bit, entropy will not be present in the output in case of a worst-case condition. Therefore, PUFs are not suited for generating the keys under a worst-case condition. For calculating the min-entropy, NIST specification 800-90 (Barker and Kelsey, 2015) is usually used. Let p0 and p1 be the probabilities of binary source of outputs where , the maximum probability of p0 and p1 which can be used for the calculation of min-entropy is as follows (Liu et al., 2018):

where .

For increasing the entropy of the source bit, Von Neumann extractor is used to compress the bits (Leest et al., 2010). In the case of Von Neumann extractor, the process is as follows: a sample of the pattern is considered and is divided into successive nonoverlapping bits. When the pair of bits differ from each other, the second bit that is considered is discarded. If both the bits are equal, both of them are discarded. After the completion of processing all the bits, the remaining bit will be in order. A bias to “1” is considered for simplicity. Pair of bits A and B having a maximum probabilities of and are the probabilities due to the bit “1” occurrence, with the probabilities and , respectively. The ratio between the lengths of the output and input of extractor is called “Extraction Rate.” This can be given as (Liu et al., 2018):

12.8 Memristor-based PUFs

Technology scaling has led to designing high-performance, low-power chips and SoCs (Mohanty, 2015). Transistor sizes have reached 12 nm (AMD, 2018) and are going low still. There are speculations of 7 nm chips being released commercially. But there is a threshold that can be reached and alternatives to the transistors are being explored to replace them. Scaling has also led to many issues, including power consumption, fabrication, and switching speeds. High switching speeds and low power consumption have been achieved using the RRAM, resistive random access memory technology, and 3D arrays (Mohanty, 2015). These RRAMs are also called “Memristors.” It is a two-terminal device, whose resistance depends on the amount of voltage and the direction of current that passes through it. So taking this property of a memristive device as an advantage, multiple resistive levels can be achieved. A continuous variable resistance can also be achieved by switching states from one resistive to other states. The resistance change will also be dependent on the state that it is already in, that is, the voltage/current that has already passed through the device in the previous iteration. This proves that a Memristor has the properties of a “Resistor” and “Memory.” Hence the name “Memristor” (Memory + Resistor). The memristance of the memristor is given as (Rose et al., 2013):

where the maximum resistance () offered is represented as , the difference between the maximum and minimum memristance offered is represented as , and applied voltage polarity is represented by . is the mobility and D represents the device thickness.

In case of an analog model, the memristance offered by the device will change gradually from minimum to maximum and takes place from varying W and D. Figure 12.17 shows the device structure and working of a memristor. The doped and undoped regions of the device will change based on the direction and amount of current that is passing through it. The memristor contains two titanium dioxide layers, one of which contains excess amount of oxygens sandwiched between two metal electrodes. When a current is applied in the forward direction, the oxygen ions will be distributed all over the device, which increases the doped region as shown in Figure 12.17. Then the resistance offered by the device will reduce. Similarly, when current is applied in the opposite direction, the oxygen atoms will be concentrated at one place, which reduces the doped region as shown in Figure 12.17. Then resistance offered by the device will increase significantly. Thus, the memristance can be varied in case of a memristor.

Figure 12.17 A memrister device

The memristor-based PUFs use the variation of resistance in the device, which depends on the thickness of device, “D.” Due to the manufacturing variations, the device thickness will vary which will affect the read and write times of the device in a memory cell. In case of the memristor, a logical “1” can be written to it when it is set from high resistive state (HRS) () to a low resistive state (LRS) () for a write time above a minimum threshold of time ; else, a logical “0” will be written. T is called the SET time and when it is close to , the probability of having a “1” in the cell will be equal to that of a “0.” This uncertainty will make memristor much suitable for the design of PUF. Also, in this case of a binary memristor, where two states are considered, “1” and “0,” transition from one state to the other will take place very abruptly. In such cases, the tamper resistance of memristor-based PUFs will be very high. For the initialization process, a high voltage should be applied so that it will be in a SET state and then switching should be performed between the HRS and LRS at a lower voltage. Below this SET voltage threshold, the device will be operating as a normal resistor. This property can be used as a tamper resistive mechanism. Figure 12.18 shows a 1-bit memristor memory-based PUF (McDonald et al., 2011, 2012). This uses the write time variability of the devices for design of a PUF.

Figure 12.18 A 1-bit memristive memory-based PUF

As shown in Figure 12.18, there are two control signals in the design, where () is used to determine the write/read operation of the device and the NEG is used to determine the polarity of the writing operation. When a RESET operation should be performed on the device, and NEG should be supplied with a “1.” Memristor will go into an HRS with the signal. After this, SET signal can be applied for writing a “1” or a “0” by supplying “1” to and “0” to NEG. Reading can be done by supplying a “0” to . An XOR operation is performed on the output with the challenge input resultant of which will be the output of PUF.

In case of a lateral switching PUF cell designed using memristor (McDonald et al., 2011, 2012), forming step is highly important for the operations. During the forming step, the conductive filament of the device is supplied with a large voltage in the dielectric sheet. This gives an advantage of values being hidden even during the fabrication state in the foundry. Therefore, if a filament is not present in the dielectric of the device, then it can be assumed that the device has not been tampered with and is secure. In the case of a lateral switching configuration, when the device is SET, during the RESET operation, only one device can go to HRS while other will stay in LRS. Which devices stays in LRS and which goes to HRS is completely random.

Figure 12.19 shows the design of a lateral switching filament-based memristor PUF. Like the previous design, there are control signals that are used for various operations and is used for selecting formation step or operation modes of memristor devices, M1 or M2. When the signal “0” is applied to , either RESET or SET is applied to the devices, during which the nodes between them are floating. When a “1” is applied to , both the devices are driven with and memristors are loaded. The RESET operation will be done when the filament is formed and one of the memristors will go to HRS. Select signals of MUX will be given the challenge bit and response is read. Noise immunity of a binary memristor PUF is high compared to the others as it is forced either to LRS or HRS. Noise margin is high provided the states are far from the thresholds. But the operation of the memristor is near the threshold voltages which reduces the noise margin.

Figure 12.19 A 1-bit filament-based memristive PUF

Figure 12.20 shows the design of a hybrid memristor CMOS PUF (Chatterjee et al., 2016). As shown in the figure, the memristor array is connected to an arbiter at the end from which the response is collected. The delay produced by the memristors will decide the output bit that comes from the arbiter where a D-flip-flop can be implemented. Both the memristor arrays are given the same input at the same time. The signal that is present at the input of the arbiter at time of response collection will decide the output bit of PUF.

Figure 12.20 Hybrid memristor CMOS PUF

12.9 Diode-based PUF

There are various advantages to a crossbar array compared to other circuit designs which make them more suitable to be used in a PUF design. Figure 12.21 shows the design of a memristor crossbar array. Regular structure, low energy consumption, high packing density, and simple implementation of the designs are some of the advantages. Besides these, there are also some disadvantages to this design, like sneak current path and crosstalk. The sneak current is dependent on the reverse junction current.

Figure 12.21 Memristor crossbar array

There are two sets of wires in the crossbar array, horizontal and vertical, as shown in Figure 12.21. The intersection of the wires is separated by a thin material or by a molecular compound. The compound will be resistive to any voltage variations among the wires. Therefore, achieving different resistive states can be done using the intersection which is used for storing the data. Horizontal wires are the word lines and vertical are the bit lines with the voltages “Vword” and “Vbit”. The voltage applied for reading is high compared to that of the reading.

When the memristors in the figure are replaced with diodes, it becomes a diode-based crossbar array. In this case, there are three schemes: in floating schemes, the bit and word lines that are not accessed are kept floating. In the single-supply biasing scheme, the word and bit lines that are not accessed are kept at a voltage . When it is “0,” it is considered grounded scheme. In case of a double supply biasing scheme, the word lines that are not accessed are biased at a voltage and bit lines at . When they are equal, it will be in a single-supply scheme and when they are opposite polarity, they are called reverse biasing scheme. A crossbar array cell is a bistable element consists of two resistive states and , which are used to store “1” and “0.” The noise margin in this design can be calculated as (Ruhrmair et al., 2011):

where and are the junction currents.

In the case of a memristor-based crossbar array, the forward voltage applied will reduce the resistance offered by the device and the input voltage in opposite direction will increase the resistance of the device (Lugli et al., 2013) thus writing a “1” or “0” to the array. Another design of PUF is a super-high information content PUF (SHIC-PUF), which can be characterized by slow readout time and high information content (Ruhrmair et al., 2011). For storing information, a crossbar array is used in this case. But for using this, there are some requirements that should be met: the readout time should be low and this will be controlled by the construction of memory cell or slow-process modules. For higher security, the slow readout times should be due to the intrinsic construction of memory cell. Another requirement is that the circuit should be characterized completely and should be very large. The bits of information that are stored on the memory should also be random. Characterization time for a bits (~10 GB) and k = 100 bits/s circuit is . This array should also be able to fit in the small area which reduces the occupied chip area.

The bit and word lines are used for the addressing of bits at the intersection of vertical and horizontal lines. This is where the current will flow through the crossing. The word and bit lines will be biased at and and during this period, and the word and bit lines that are not accessed will be biased at and voltages. So, the junctions that are at the accessed word and bit lines are only made to go into forward bias and others are reverse biased in case of a diode-based crossbar array. Word lines are connected with a sense resistor and depending on the voltage at the word line, there are two states that are shown, high or low resistance. In this case, the information in the bits is random and is also important to see that the structural features are irregular. To achieve this, aluminum-induced layer exchange is considered. This gives an advantage of randomizing the distribution of conductivity which will result in an inhomogeneous conductivity. This can be taken as an advantage in case of PUF. When the array size is increased, reverse bias junction current will increase, which in turn will increase the power dissipation of the module. But the parasitic paths will avoid the accessed bit and word line. This reduces the noise margin and makes it suitable for PUF design. And large generator resistance values are required for readout cycles to be slow and for limiting the capacitive peak current. As an alternative, high-κ material can be used.

A crossbar array can also be used and a weak PUF and SHIC PUF can be implemented as presented by Lugli et al. (2013). In this case, rewriting and erasing the PUF response can be performed without the other responses changed. This is only possible in case of a crossbar array but not in the case of other PUF designs. An increased crossbar array will be a huge issue as the sneak current path becomes a problem and this also decreases the noise margin and degrades power dissipation. A rectifying element can be implemented for reducing the crosstalk and leakage between the accessed and unaccessed cells. The design of a crossbar can also contain a memristor in series with a diode which can reduce the noise margin and power dissipation. There is a compatibility issue in case of a traditional silicon process and transitional metal oxide memristors (Kim et al., 2010).

When the floating biased scheme was implemented, the size of the array was reduced and noise margin was also reduced because of the increase in sneak current. This is also same in case of power dissipation. Due to this, the size of memory is limited to a few megabits. External resistance effect is minimal on the noise margin and reverse-biased scheme is suitable for the noise margin and power dissipation. But when compared to the floating point scheme, the power dissipation is high due to the higher off currents. It can be inferred that the memory size can be increased if power consumption is not a problem, which also decreases the noise margin. Scaling also helps in reducing the diode current and wire resistance.

In case of an ALILE, the diodes that come from a weak-doped wafer will have high rectification ratio and high randomness. But noise margin is low when compared to a ZnO junction because of low rectification of about 108 at ±2 V.

An ALILE diodes of small size is suited for use in case of a weak PUF when compared to a ZnO Schottky diodes, as the randomness is high (Ruhrmair et al., 2010). The stability of ALILE diodes is also high over a long period and resistive to invasive readouts. Temperature dependency of the diode’s performance is high, which can be improved with the use of differential measurement techniques.

12.10 Carbon-based PUFs

In the current research trend, silicon devices are used widely for the development of PUF designs and are more focusing on the randomness, reliability, and robustness. But the power consumption of the devices is not being monitored or focused. Scaling of devices has led to a place where low-power consuming devices are more required and low-voltage operational devices are required, which becomes a challenge to the PUF design. Scaling of devices also makes it difficult to control the gate and charge carriers in the channel. This makes it necessary to explore post silicon device which can be used for scaling. Carbon derivative options such as the carbon nanotube (CNT) and graphene are promising candidates.

12.10.1 CNT-based PUF

CNT FET-based PUFs can be implemented for various advantages such as low-power consumption, high reliability, and low energy (Konigsmark et al., 2014). In case of a CNTFET, a CNT is used as a channel in the transistor. The configuration of a CNTFET changes depending on various properties of the CNT, such as diameter, chirality, growth density, misalignment, and doping concentration. Chirality is used for the generation of secret bits. The direction in which the graphene sheet is rolled decides the chirality of a CNT which decides the metallic or semiconductor nature of the device. Figure 12.22 shows the design of a CNPUF, which contains the CNTFETs connected in series. The parallel elements of the transistors, CNPUF-PEs, share a common gate voltage. In this case, there can be a large number of semiconducting CNTs and a small number of metallic CNTs. The ratio in which they are used is 10%–30% where the semiconducting current will dominate the metallic current. Each parallel element consists of a distinct state for high- and low-input gate voltages. Due to the process variation, this states will vary, which affects the output. The improvement of area can be achieved by 300% when compared to design of silicon-based arbiter PUF (Konigsmark et al., 2014). The interchip HD of 49.67% has been presented by Konigsmark et al. (2014). When the simulation was performed in different conditions, by giving random values to the temperature and the supply voltage of the devices, the performance of CNPUF-PE has been more reliable and stable compared to that of an RO PUF, current-based PUF, and SRAM PUF. For a higher security, a trade-off between security and power consumption should be made. An extended CNPUF adds an area overhead but is comparable to the Si PUF with higher security.

Figure 12.22 CNT-based PUF design

Even though the CNTFET has various advantages over the silicon transistors and allows more scalability, fabricating the CNTFET gives high difficulties. The planar geometry of the graphene makes it easier compared to the CNTs during fabrication and is also comparatively cheaper to silicon devices. Graphene is also compatible with the CMOS technology, which gives additional advantage of scaling and performance. Therefore, high-density SoC and higher performance can be achieved by combining the CMOS fabrication technologies with the graphene’s unique properties.

12.10.2 Graphene-based PUF

Figure 12.23 shows the design of a graphene nanoribbon transistor. Graphene has high electron mobility which has an added advantage to be used as a channel in case of FETs (Khan et al., 2014). It is a two-dimensional carbon atom network which is arranged like a honeycomb lattice. Graphene is a single layer of graphite structure which is interconnected in a lattice structure. It is highly strong in all the directions. A CNT structure can be formed by rolling a graphene nanoribbon and one with 12 pentagon defects will give a fullerene structure. Properties of graphene which makes it more suitable than silicon for future technology are two-dimensional one atom crystal, light and thin material with high flexibility and strength. It is transparent and nonflammable and highly conductive.

Figure 12.23 Graphene transistor

Besides these advantages, there are also some challenges in this graphene technology: it is highly sensitive to environmental changes and does not work easily with discrete electronic signals as there is a no band gap in the semiconducting graphene structure. Unlike a silicon transistor, the graphene-based transistor cannot be turned off as the bandgap is low. But the high bandgap makes it more suitable for use in RF applications, which controls the gate current in digital logic environment. Off-state leakage currents are high, which results in smaller ION/IOFF ratio. Saturation of drain voltage current is not readily available.

A measurement circuit is usually present in a PUF-based security modules. This can be used for measurement of the property of graphene devices such as resistance, capacitance, and voltages for deriving the output of PUF which can be used for cryptographic applications (Dimitrakopoulos et al., 2012). There are some points that should be used for graphene-based PUF designs:

  1. Properties of graphene-based PUFs should be stable over a wide range of time, temperature, and other environmental variables.

  2. During the fabrication process under extremely controlled conditions, there will be variations in the properties of the devices because of chemical processing, the presence of terrace edges, and growth process during growth of graphene. This results in device-to-device variations on the wafer. For the introduction of additional variations, different methods can be employed:

    • (a) Molecular doping, hydrogen inhalation, width/length scaling, contact treatments, and contact metal variation.

    • (b) Laser annealing can be introduced during the fabrication where beam width, energy, pulse duration, and wavelength can be varied.

    • (c) Contact treatment and contact metal variations.

    • (d) Different ambient conditions such as varied dopant quantities and types, oxygen levels, and so on can also introduce variations.

    • (d) For increasing the variability, a single graphene device can be packed with more layers. Which will vary the electrical properties of device.

  3. For an improved stability, passivation layers can be employed, which also does not affect the security of the device during attacks based on scanning electron microscopy (SEM). A higher yield can be achieved using the passivated graphene. Resistance is inversely related to temperature in case of an unpassivated graphene device, which can reduce the resistance with the increase in temperature.

  4. Array of devices that can be used for the implementation of PUF has a very low variability range almost close to threshold values of the core device used. In this case, reliability decreases with time and so will the temperature variation. This can cause to read errors while reading the output bits from the PUF module. There are also various solutions that can be implemented in this case. Some of them are:

    • (a) Error correction schemes can be employed but by sacrificing security.

    • (b) Average values of device in the array can be considered for setting the threshold value for digital fingerprint.

    • (c) Temperature-compensating algorithms can be used along with the temperature sensors for mitigating the temperature variance issues.

  5. Robustness against attacks can be increased by implementing the following:

    • (a) The device location in a large array can be changed randomly which makes it difficult for the attacker to correctly give the challenge input to get an appropriate response.

    • (b) A measurement circuit can be employed on the circuitry to make it difficult for the attacker to use probes for accessing the devices.

    • (c) Delayering the measurement circuits can also be implemented, which makes the circuit more robust. This makes it difficult for the attacker to convert the read values to digital outputs. Attempting to remove the delayering will render the device useless.

12.11 Microprocessor-based PUF

Until now, this chapter discussed different PUF circuits that were designed for security and need to be fabricated. This section discusses different components such as microprocessor, power rail, and so on for designing PUF circuits. Figure 12.24 shows the design of a microprocessor-based PUF (Kumar et al., 2017). Two 32-bit multiplexers and two PUF counters are used for designing the module. The output of the multiplier is connected to MUX as shown in the figure. The MUX will choose which PUF module will be driven by the bits of the multiplier. PUF counter is 32-bit long and the general-purpose registers of the microprocessor will store the 9th bit to 24th bit output from PUF counters. A 32-bit long output is generated from the two different PUF counters as shown in the figure (Kumar et al., 2017).

Figure 12.24 Microprocessor-based PUF

There are five select lines for each of the MUX for selecting the output of the multiplier. Part of the challenge input to the PUF module will be the select lines that go into the MUX. Different paths of the multiplier are selected using the assembly program, which becomes the later part of the challenge input to the PUF module. Response from the counters gets stored in the registers of the microprocessor. For an efficient CRP generation, the assembly program development is an important task. The interconnects will add delays with the manufacturing variations introduced during the fabrication stage.

In the design presented by Kumar et al. (2017), the openmsp430 design has been modified into two different modes of operation, normal and PUF. I/O pins of the microprocessor are given the 10 select lines and “En” pin. Multiplier output has been modified for generating the addition of multiplexer and PUF counter. Additional circuitry in the module will become active when the PUF mode is selected and during the normal operation, they will be separated from the microprocessor.

12.12 Magnetic PUF

Sections 12.10 and 12.8 presented two different types of non-silicon material-based PUF designs. This section presents another type of non-silicon-based PUF designs, magnetic PUFs. There are various devices which use magnetic properties of materials for performing operations (Gao et al., 2016).

Spin transfer torque magnetic random access memory (STT-MRAM) devices are one of them. Figure 12.25 shows the design of an STT-MRAM (Huai, 2010). When current passes through the fixed layer, a spin-polarized current is produced. If the current that is produced is directed toward the free layer, the angular momentum can be transferred to the layer which can change the orientation of the magnet. When the two layers are parallel (P) to each other, the resistance is low. When the two layers are anti-parallel (AP) to each other, the resistance is high.

Figure 12.25 Spin transfer torque magnetic random access memory PUF

A magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ)-based PUF was proposed by Marukame et al. (2014) which can extract the fingerprint of the spin transfer-switching properties. The characterized STS characteristics were measured experimentally by Marukame et al. (2014) and a method to extract the PUF signature was also presented. It was also observed that different programming voltages for AP to P state and P to AP state transitions were required by the MTJ. Extrinsic properties such as the process damage and junction resistance lead to the MTJ. Due to these variations, an operation sequence for the extraction of bits from PUF-based 4×4 array was implemented. Initially, the reset voltage is applied to initialize them into a state of parallelism. Then the precalibrated voltage is applied for inducing the switching with a probability of 50% for majority of the MTJs. The switching will result in a random distribution of the devices in an array in various states, AP and P. Signature extraction circuit will take care of the information resistance. After extracting the information, the entire array is set into P state. For increasing the reliability, the operation sequence is repeated for extraction of the bits.

Figure 12.26 shows a phase change material (PCM) which is similar to the previous one and takes advantage of the magnetic properties for designing the PUF. A PCM has amorphous and crystalline natures in the PCM. The difference in the resistance offered by the two states is largely different. To change the material to amorphous state, a pulse with high amplitude and fast fall time is supplied to heater to initially melt it and then quench it rapidly. So a region of high resistive amorphous material is formed in the PCM. A long fall time moderate amplitude pulse is supplied to the cell for converting it into a crystalline state which will anneal the active region at a temperature between crystallization and melting temperature which forms a crystalline material in the cell which offers low resistance. Figure 12.27 shows the structure of a PCM array. During the reading operation, the resistance of the cell is read by sending a small current to it. This pulse will not be disturbing the state of the cell (Wong et al., 2010). The resistance offered by the PCM cell can also be controlled by passing a small amount of current, a programming pulse with intermediate amplitude rise/fall time.

Figure 12.26 Phase change material

Figure 12.27 Phase change material memory array PUF

12.13 Practical implementation of PUF

Designing a PUF module can be half the problem but the implementation and deploying the same in an environment can pose additional challenges. Any design to be validated has to be implemented in a real-time scenario where it is subject to different real-time conditions. FPGA implementations of PUF are being explored by researchers for validation of the design and implementation of their proposed designs into different applications. Deploying the design on an FPGA opens up a lot of opportunities to the PUF design and adds more to the list of applications (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Ikezaki et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2015).

The FPGAs are also evolving day-by-day and adding more features for better integration into the IoT world (Johnson et al., 2015). One such capability is the dynamic partial reconfiguration (DPR) or runtime partial reconfiguration (RPR). With these features of an FPGA, the circuit design that is on the FPGA can be configured partially during the runtime. This ability is called “Partial Reconfiguration.” The power consumption of the FPGA can be reduced by using the DPR which makes them ideal for use in IoT applications. But these DPR-enabled FPGAs are subjected to various attacks by the adversary which can get the entire network of devices into jeopardy. A protection technique that can be used for protecting the DPR-enabled FPGAs was proposed by Johnson et al. (2015). An XoR PUF was employed in the paper for securing the protocol. Because of the complex nature of the PUF that is deployed in the application, modeling an attack by the attacker will be difficult as there will be no access to the PUF responses. If that access is gained by the adversary, attacking the PUF with a modeling attack will become easy and successful in some cases.

There are also many different aging-resistant PUFs designs that are implemented on the FPGAs (Chowdhury et al., 2017). The aging effects on the FPGA are presented by Maiti and Schaumont (2014). It was also presented that a change in the location of the output response bits and the devices that are affected by the aging are also random. There are also many designs of PUF that are implemented based on SRAM on the FPGA that use the aging effects on the design to an advantage. An aging resistant RO PUF is proposed for reliable key generation in (Rahman et al., 2016). With the FPGA lacking the ability to change the circuit architecture, implementing this idea becomes more difficult.

12.14 PUF: case study applications

All the above sections discussed different designs of PUFs. This section discusses different applications of PUF in various domains. There are many applications and domains where PUF can be used and implemented. One such major issue that is becoming a problem is counterfeiting. Figure 12.28 shows a big picture of counterfeiting in the case of an IC. When an IC is designed by a manufacturer, there can be many clones designed by various third parties to be sold in the market (Chang et al., 2017; Mohanty, 2015). But this is a major issue economically and also in terms of security. The ICs that are created by the counterfeiting party can be malicious and might contain trojans. A PUF can be implemented in the IC design so that it can be used for authenticating the original device (Yan et al., 2017).

Figure 12.28 Securing against IPR PUFs

A PUF module that contains on-chip hash function can increase the cost of the entire chip but can also increase the robustness of the entire design. An index-based syndrome encoding has been shown to be implemented with RO PUF for a better reliability (Yu and Devadas, 2010). There are also variations in the output bits that get flipped due to the environmental and operational conditions. So error correction mechanisms can also be implemented with a PUF so that the output can be read without errors. But error correction mechanism can increase the chip area and hence the total cost of the chip. There is also a power trade-off that has to be considered while adding additional circuitry. A comparison of built-in hash functions and their effects is shown in Table 12.2.

Table 12.2 Comparison of different types of hash functions in terms of chip area and clock (Majzoobi et al., 2008)

Man-in-the-middle attacks can be controlled by implementing PUF modules in various applications like distributed computing (Gassend et al., 2002). Different steps involved in such an attack are as follows:

  • “A” should interact with the PUF module by using the CRPs shared between A and PUF.

  • “B” is an attacker who has access to the PUF module. Therefore, B will be able to gather the responses from the module by giving the challenge inputs that are chosen by B. B wants to use it with the identity of “A” and impersonates with fake results.

  • A gives out PUF challenges from CRP list and compares responses that come from the output of PUF module with a private list.

  • B has access to the challenges and PUF, so gets the response from PUF for that specific challenge.

  • B will be able to fool A by pretending that A has PUF access and can impersonate the PUF as if it is A.

The applications of PUF are very broad as shown in Figure 12.29. They can also be used in applications or devices where randomness is needed. PUF modules are elegant solutions in various applications such as RFID tags, random number generation, secret key generation, device authentication, and so on (Gunlu and Iscan, 2014; O’Donnell et al., 2004; Suh and Devadas, 2007; Suh et al., 2005). PUF has also been used in consumer electronic devices where authentication is needed at a low cost (http://www.eecs.mit.edu/news-events/media/mit-spinoff-verayo-developed-srini-devadas-gains-increased-use-commercial).

Figure 12.29 Typical applications of PUFs

In case of the cryptographic and security applications, the random number generation can be used for generating the encryption and decryption keys, initial seed values, and in some cases, where required, introduce some randomness to the padding schemes and protocols. Pseudo-random number generation (PRNG) is not truly random and in that case, the pattern will repeat after a certain number of iterations. Each of the number generated by the PRNG has to go through a very complex algorithm. Initial seed value should be kept highly secret in case of PRNG. Due to all these different issues with the PRNG, hardware random number generation (HRNG) has been implemented in various cases (O’Donnell et al., 2004). In case of an HRNG, an initial seed is not required for generating a truly random number. A delay-based PUF circuit will have the rising edge of the input signal and challenge bits as select lines to the multiplexers. Input will propagate through the series of multiplexers and depending on the delay offered by each of them, a D-flip-flop will generate the output bit “1” or “0.” An unbiased output response will be given by a meta-stable PUF. A Von Neumann correction gives a 32-bit output response from an N-bit input. Similarly, there are various designs of PUF which can be implemented based on the requirements of application. Figure 12.30 shows a key generation system using PUF modules.

Figure 12.30 Secure key generation system using PUFs

For using the authentication schemes of PUF on a chip, a trusted party or the manufacturer should store the CRPs which are exponential in number in a secure database which can be matched for authentication (Suh and Devadas, 2007). For an input challenge, the output of PUF is the same, in that case, the device that has been challenged will be authentic. But when using the challenge inputs, the man-in-the-middle attack should be avoided by discarding the challenge once used.

A controlled PUF module can also be used for certified execution. It is a process of executing or running a program on a remote server where the client can rely on the results produced by the server (Gassend et al., 2002). Figure 12.31 shows the process of authenticating a person over the network using PUF. In this case, the PUF device will generate a challenge input and has the response respectively. When authentication is needed, the response is sent to the server where it confirms the identity of the client. This can help avoid identity fraud and rendering the results of the client useless. This can also avoid an attacker from generating different malicious results and sending it to the user. This scenario is often seen in case of a distributed computing where one processor cannot handle the workflow. This type of PUF modules can also be used to restrict the usage of a specific software to a respective amount of processors.

Figure 12.31 Authentication of user using PUFs

Figure 12.32 shows the design of a secure digital camera which has a PUF module that is built into it (Haider et al., 2016). Secure boot of sensor controller of the camera is used to ensure the integrity of the platform at booting. PUF-based secure key generation and storage module provides key for sensed data attestation to ensure integrity and authenticity. In system architecture of the secure camera, the PUF-based key generation and storage module has two cascaded components, a PUF source and a helper data algorithm (HDA). The choice of the HDA depends on the selection of the PUF source. The HDA is used to obtain: (1) a perfectly reproducible PUF response under a range of environmental and operating conditions, in other words, the HD between any two responses from the same PUF is zero, and (2) an almost uniformly distributed PUF response.

Figure 12.32 Secure camera using PUFs

IoT applications have become more necessary nowadays. Many situations are arising where the devices have to be deployed in places where they cannot be monitored or have human interaction. Such cases are more often prone to attacks by the attacker who has access to the device without security. PUF can be used to stop attacks in such situations where the entire network of devices can be secured (Mohanty et al., 2016; Yanambaka et al., 2017).

12.15 PUF: issues

The understanding of this chapter so far is that a PUF provides better security and robustness to the entire application. But there are many issues and challenges that have to be addressed while designing and implementing the PUF in an application (Chang et al., 2017; Wan et al., 2015; Wen and Lao, 2018; Ye et al., 2017, 2018). There are various attempts for providing better security and robustness by implementation of PUF, but some of the common attacks are:

  • There is a chance that the attacker can create a large number of chips with the similar design to the PUF module used in a respective application for obtaining the response. In cases where the design of PUF is simple, this can be very successful.

  • It is also possible to predict the response of the PUF or calculate it using mathematical modeling techniques (Ma et al., 2018; Mispan et al., 2018; Tanaka et al., 2018). Adding a nonlinearity to the PUF design can avoid these kinds of attacks.

  • There are different types of attacks, invasive or semi-invasive, which can determine the time delay and power of the devices. Tamper-resisting packaging can avoid these attacks.

  • Introducing errors into the module can also be performed by the attacker to tamper with it and render it useless.

These attacks are common and there are many different kinds of solutions that are suggested. Improvements can also be made to the PUF designs to make them difficult to attack by the attacker.

  • A hash function can also be implemented before or after the PUF module which can prevent the attacker from gaining knowledge of the CRPs. This can prevent the modeling attacks on the modules.

  • Error correction mechanisms can be implemented in the PUF modules which can make them more reliable and avoid bit-flips due to environmental variations and operational disturbances.

  • Control of PUF response is often desired by the client who is using the module. Additional secret keys for the input of the modules can be implemented, which is totally in hands of the user or client.

  • Tamper-resistant packaging should be used for the ICs and PUF modules. This will increase the cost of the entire application and will increase the robustness also.

Attacking the PUF modules is a kind of attack that has to be performed by an adversary with an ill intent. But there are also other challenges faced during the design of PUF modules (Ganta and Nazhandali, 2014; Sahoo et al., 2018; Wang and Tehranipoor, 2010; Yanambaka et al., 2017, 2018). Some of the challenges include crosstalk, noise in the signals, noise in power supply, and so on. Noise sources can also originate from an unusual input pattern which varies with a different input. Such a noise can be taken as an advantage by the user in designing different input challenges which will increase the robustness of the module against the attackers.

When a large switching activity is triggered due to the input pattern, a power supply noise can occur. The dynamic power is increased due to this and will be responsible for a voltage drop in the power line and an increase in voltage at the ground. Such changes in the supply voltages can cause the change in gate voltages and induce unusual delays in the circuitry. Then the entire circuit operation changes which affect the output response inducing more errors into it. Parasitics should also be taken into consideration during the design of a PUF module.

Aging is another issue that is present in the PUF designs. With the aging effects, the integrity of the circuit degrades over time and renders it useless. Over a period of time, the circuit health degrades and the output responses of a set of challenges can also be affected due to these changes (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Ganta and Nazhandali, 2014; Meguerdichian and Potkonja, 2011; Rahman et al., 2015, 2016). The aging effects on the PUF module depending on the frequency of turning the device on have been presented by Ganta and Nazhandali (2014). An RO PUF was subjected to the study and some of the observations presented by Ganta and Nazhandali (2014) are:

  • The bit error rate (BER) in the case of PUF, which is always on is the highest. But when the device is turned on during the day only once, the BER is 2%. A 35% reduction in BER can be achieved by turning on the device once a day.

  • The manufacturing variations of the devices are modeled during the simulation as threshold voltage variations. A mismatch was observed by Ganta and Nazhandali (2014) in identical circuit elements, and when the process variation is high, the PUF is stable.

  • For the effects of temperature and the aging of the modules, and their effects on the stability of design, the PUFs were operated at various temperatures and ages. The effect of aging on the PUF design was not observed to be significant on the stability of the device due to the differential nature. The correlation on stability is shown as 70% of the aging effect and the temperature.

  • Supply voltage and the noise in the supply voltage are also the challenges in the designs. The PUFs’ performance is measured in the presence of these issues and aging by Ganta and Nazhandali (2014). The effect of supply noise is less than 0.2% in the presence of aging. But the BER of the PUF that is operating at a subthreshold voltage with aging is high.

  • The stability of the PUF depends on the ring oscillation configuration highly where with an increase in the stages, there is also an increase in the susceptibility to the environmental changes.

12.16 Conclusion

This concept of a PUF was initially proposed in 2001 as physical one-way function. Since then, there are various concepts of PUF that were designed using different architectures, devices, and materials. Many of the PUFs are highly robust and others are not secure which can be easily broken with the implementation of a simple machine learning algorithm.

Research is being conducted for designing more robust and secure designs of PUFs for better security. But with the high implementations of IoT architectures, there is more necessity and scope for the development of low-power designs of PUF. There are low-power-consuming designs being implemented and proposed by many researchers around the world but the main focus of research has been the increase in the robustness and resistance to attacks. As a future research, low-power design of PUF can also be implemented for better wide range of implementation and integration.

There are also the threats and attacks on the PUF that are yet to be addressed. With the introduction of new applications every day, it is necessary to secure them against attacks that come with it. Side-channel resilient PUF designs are yet to be more saturated and better designs are yet to come into the consumer-level market. PUFs are being implemented in many enterprise domain applications like servers, but commercial market is still open to the implementations of PUF. This can also be considered as a future research of the PUFs.
